You can also type a query straight into the search box (Ctrl+K): it lists the matching tasks and offers to open them as a new view.

  • g then f opens the page with the cursor in the query input, at the bottom of the filter panel. Results update about 150 ms after you stop typing. Under the header, the toolbar repeats the query's conditions in words, with the filter and display buttons on the right.
  • Results are grouped and ordered as a saved view would show them: by project (Inbox first, then projects in sidebar order, each heading showing the project's path, Work › Client A), then by due date and priority. Display options changes the grouping, the order, the layout, completed tasks and what rows show before you save.
  • Enter in the input runs the query at once and moves to the first result; Esc returns to the input. In the list, the usual keys work: j / k, Enter to open, c to complete, 1–4 for priority, L for labels, Delete.
  • ↑ / ↓ in the input step through the last 20 distinct queries you ran on this device. The history lives in the browser's local storage for the app, is never synced, and is cleared when you sign out.

Build a filter without typing#

In the filter panel, above the query input, the builder shows the same query as conditions you can read: Label is errand, Due on or before tomorrow, Priority is P1, No project.

  • Conditions. + Condition opens a small dialog: choose what to filter on (label, project, priority, one of the five dates, a state such as Due earlier or Waiting on another task, text in the title or notes, origin, workspace (with more than one), tracked time or a custom field), then its value. Labels and projects are picked from a searchable list. Click a condition to change it.
  • Groups. A group is a block headed All of these (every condition must match, &) or Any of these (one is enough, |). + Group adds one inside, up to three levels deep. Change the heading to switch between the two.
  • Not. The Not switch in a condition's dialog, or the Not button on a group, matches the tasks it would otherwise leave out (!).
  • Keyboard. Tab reaches every control. Inside a group, the arrow keys move between conditions, and Delete or Backspace removes the focused one.
  • Both ways. The query input stays under the builder (Edit as text jumps to it). Every change in the builder rewrites it, with only the parentheses the grammar needs, and anything you type that parses updates the builder. What is saved is always the query text, so saved filters, ot and the API see exactly what they saw before.
  • What it cannot show. A double !!, or groups nested deeper than three levels, stays editable as text; the builder shows a short notice instead.
  • Show or hide it. The filter button at the right of the toolbar folds the panel away; the conditions stay in the toolbar. The choice is kept on this device, separately for the New view page (shown by default) and for saved views (hidden by default).

The panel's header says how many tasks the query matches.

Saving views#

A query you come back to can be saved as a view: it keeps the query and its display options, and syncs to all your devices like your tasks do.

  • Save. On the New view page, press s while the results have focus (or choose Save as view). The header becomes a card: type a name and press Enter, or Esc to cancel. The view is created with the current query, grouping, order and display options, listed under Views in the sidebar and pinned to Favourites, and opened at /views/<id>. Saving works offline; other devices show the view after they sync.
  • Edit. A view shows its conditions in the toolbar. The filter button, a condition chip or / opens the same filter panel as the New view page, with a count for the changed query before you save. Enter or Save saves a changed query for every device, Esc discards the change. A query that does not parse shows the error and is not saved.
  • Display options. The sliders button at the right of the toolbar opens them, reachable with Tab: List or Board (one column of cards per group), Group by (project, due date, priority, label, none), Order by (due date, priority, manual order, created, title), Completed tasks (hide or show) and Show on rows (date, project, labels, estimate, assignee, deadline, start, origin); the direction is under More options. Defaults are list, group by project, order by due date ascending with undated tasks last, completed hidden, everything shown. Grouping by due date shows Earlier, Today, Tomorrow, then each later date and finally No date; grouping by label lists a task under each of its labels. For priority, descending puts priority 1 first. Show completed lists finished matches too, unless the query already names a state (completed, open or a completion date); the sidebar still counts open tasks. Every choice is stored on the view at once and syncs.
  • Sidebar. The Views group appears with your first saved view. Pinned views are listed under it with a live count of their open tasks, computed on the device. The ⋯ menu of a view renames, moves it up or down, unpins or deletes it, and sets it as this device's start view. g then v opens the overview of every view, pinned or not, where views can be pinned again.
  • Start view. Each device can open on a different view: choose it in Settings → General → Start view or from a view's menu. The choice stays on the device (it is not synced). If the saved view is deleted, for example on another device, the app opens the Inbox and says so once.
  • Dashboards. New dashboard in the overview creates a view that shows up to six other views side by side as panels, each with its name, open-task count and first ten tasks, updating live. Add panels from the header, reorder or remove them with Arrange. Tab / Shift+Tab move between panels, j / k select a task inside one, Enter opens it (or the view when nothing is selected) and o opens the panel's view. A panel whose view was deleted shows View removed with a button to remove it. Panels stack on narrow screens. A panel whose view has an on-drop rule (set with Rule in Arrange) is a drop target: dragging a card onto it, or Shift+→ / Shift+← on the selected card, applies the rule (labels added or removed, priority, a due date of today, tomorrow, next week or none, Someday or no start, a project and section, complete or reopen) as one undoable change; the rule's wording is the panel's description, and panels without a rule take no drops. A task that still does not match the panel's filter afterwards stays shown there, marked Not matching, until you leave the board. New board offers an empty board or the Eisenhower matrix: the filters (p1 | p2) & (due <= tomorrow | deadline <= tomorrow), (p1 | p2) & !(due <= tomorrow | deadline <= tomorrow) & !someday, !(p1 | p2) & (due <= tomorrow | deadline <= tomorrow) and !(p1 | p2) & !(due <= tomorrow | deadline <= tomorrow) & !someday with the rules priority 1 and today, priority 2 and next week, priority 3 and today, priority 4 and no date, on one pinned board.

A saved view evaluates its query exactly like the New view page: open tasks only unless completed or open appears, tasks of archived projects left out, unknown names reported as warnings. If a view was saved by a newer version with a term this version does not understand, it shows the parse error instead of wrong results. When two devices change the same view while offline, each option keeps the newer value: a grouping changed on one device and a sort changed on the other both survive, and so do a layout and the properties a view hides. A dashboard's panel list is replaced as a whole, so concurrent panel edits keep the newer list; so is a view's on-drop rule. Scripts can manage views through /api/v1/views (see docs/api.md); the server checks that the query parses with the same grammar.

Examples#

1. Work due by tomorrow, high priority#

@work & due <= tomorrow & p1

2. Anything overdue that is not filed in a project#

overdue & no project

3. Errands or calls, outside the Work project#

(@errand | @call) & !#Work

4. Everything under Work, including its sub-projects, due this week#

##Work & due <= 6 days

5. Tasks for a client whose names contain spaces#

#"Client A" & @"follow up"

6. Captured in the last week and still unscheduled#

created > 7 days ago & no date

7. Due on Friday, either priority 1 or 2#

due = friday & (p1 | p2)

8. Find a task by a phrase in its title or notes#

search: "oat milk" | search: groceries

9. Completed subtasks of the Home project#

#Home & subtask & completed

10. Due before the end of November, unlabelled, with no fixed time#

due before 2026-12-01 & no labels & no time & !today

11. A deadline this week, but no plan yet#

deadline <= 6 days & no date

12. Waiting on others, without the parked ones#

@waiting & !someday

13. Waiting for (save it as a view)#

blocked

14. What can be done today#

unblocked & today

15. Habits still to do today#

habit & due <= today

16. What I finished last week#

completed = last week

17. Work done this month, high priority#

##Work & completed >= this month & (p1 | p2)

18. Expensive renovation items ordered by Friday#

#"Home renovation" & cost > 1000 & "Order date" <= friday

19. Quotes still missing a client#

status = "Quote" & no client

20. Open issues from GitHub#

origin: github & open

21. Captured pages and mail still unfiled#

(origin: url | origin: email) & no project

22. Anything I have spent time on#

tracked

23. Over an hour tracked and due by today#

tracked > 1h & due <= today

24. Work not started yet#

!tracked & #Work

25. Due this week at home and at work, from any workspace#

(workspace: Home | workspace: Work) & due = this week

26. Urgent side projects#

workspace: "Side projects" & p1

pages.title: The Android app
pages.summary: The OpenTodo app for Android: connect it to your server, reminders without a push service, sharing, widgets and fingerprint unlock.
pages.html:
The Android app

The OpenTodo app for Android opens your own OpenTodo server, like the installed web app, and adds what only a phone app can do: reminders on time without a push service, sharing files from other apps, home-screen widgets and fingerprint unlock. It needs Android 8.0 or later and an OpenTodo server; it talks to nothing else.

Connect to your server#

On first start the app asks for your server's address, the one you open in the browser (for example todo.example.com). It checks the address and says what is wrong when it can't connect:

  • No connection: the first start needs the network; the screen tries again when it's back.
  • Not an OpenTodo server: the address answers, but not like OpenTodo. Check for typos.
  • Certificate not trusted: the phone doesn't trust the server's certificate. If your server uses its own certificate authority, install it in Android's security settings; the app trusts certificates you installed there.
  • Address refused: the app needs https://. Plain http:// works only for addresses on your own network (such as 192.168.1.4:8080 or nas.local), after a warning.

Then sign in as usual. After the first start the app also opens offline, with your local copy.

To use another server, long-press the app icon and choose Change server. This removes the current server's data from the phone (the offline copy, scheduled reminders, widget data and fingerprint unlock); changes not yet synced are lost.

Reminders#

In Settings → Notifications, turn on Notifications through the app. The app schedules the next seven days of reminders on the phone itself and refreshes them about once an hour, so a reminder you add on your computer reaches the phone too. Details in Notifications.

Sharing#

The app appears in Android's share menu for links, text, photos and files, also on phones without Google Play services. See Capturing pages.

Widgets#

Two home-screen widgets: Today shows your tasks for today with the time of the last update, and Quick add opens the app's quick add. The widgets show what the app last saw; open the app to refresh them. While an encrypted account is locked, the Today widget shows only counts.

Fingerprint unlock#

With end-to-end encryption, the unlock screen offers Unlock with fingerprint or face next time.

Privacy#

No trackers, no analytics, no advertising. The app stores the server address, the scheduled reminders, the widget data and, if you turned on fingerprint unlock, the encrypted account key, only in its private storage, excluded from Android backup.

pages.title: Time tracking
pages.summary: Track the time you spend on a task with a start and stop, add past work by hand, compare it with the estimate, and export it as a CSV.
pages.html:
Time tracking

A task can carry an estimate; time tracking records what it actually took. Each stretch of work is one time entry: when it started, when it ended (nothing while it runs) and an optional note. Entries are stored on your device first, work offline and sync like your tasks.

Start and stop#

  • In any task list, select a task and press y to start tracking it; press y again to stop. With the task panel open, y acts on the open task.
  • The row's actions menu (.) and the panel's ⋯ menu offer Start tracking or Stop tracking.
  • Only one entry runs at a time: starting another task ends the running entry at that moment.
  • Completing the task you are tracking stops the entry in the same step.

Completed and deleted tasks offer no start, and viewers of a shared project cannot track.

The running indicator#

While an entry runs, a pill in the sidebar's bottom row takes the place of your name: the elapsed time and the task's name, 1:05 · Write the report, with a Stop button inside it; activate the pill to open the task. With the sidebar collapsed to icons it shows the time alone and opens a menu with Open the tracked task and Stop. On a phone the bar shows the time as a pill that opens a sheet with Open and Stop. The time counts in minutes, then as hours and minutes from one hour, and turns to a caution colour after 12 hours in case you forgot to stop. Screen readers hear it once when tracking starts and once when it stops.

If you stop the entry on another device, the indicator disappears here after that device syncs.

The Time tab#

The task panel's Time tab lists the task's entries, newest first, with their day, times, duration and note, and in a shared project who tracked each one. It shows the total, Start tracking or Stop tracking, and Add time:

  • Type a duration, 45m, 1h30 or 90 (minutes). On today it ends now; on another day it ends at 17:00.
  • Or choose Enter a start and an end and type both times.
  • Add a note if you like.

An end before the start is refused. The ⋯ menu of each of your own entries edits its start, end and note, or deletes it. Other members' entries can be read, not changed. The start, the end and the note are separate fields, so edits made on two devices at once are both kept.

Tracked against estimated#

Once a task has entries, its row shows the tracked time with the estimate, 35m / 1h, or 35m tracked without one. It takes the estimate's place in the line under the title, as one item. A running entry counts up to the current minute. Rows and the Time tab show the task's total, everyone's entries included.

Today's header adds 3h planned · 1h 20m tracked: the estimates of the open tasks listed, and your own entries that started today, each counted whole on the day it started even across midnight, with your day start applied.

Statistics, filters and quick add#

  • Statistics shows the time you tracked in the period, per day and per project.
  • The filter terms tracked and tracked > 1h list tasks by their tracked time; see Filter queries.
  • In quick add, 30m/2h means 30 minutes already spent and a two-hour estimate.

Export#

Export time entries in Statistics downloads a CSV of the chosen period, made on your device. Its columns are date, start, end, minutes, task, project, labels (joined by ;) and note, then one column per custom field of the projects present. Times are in your time zone, a running entry has no end and counts up to the export, and the file starts with a byte-order mark so spreadsheets read it as UTF-8. The server writes the same file for ot time export and the API; see Command-line client and the HTTP API.

Shared projects and encryption#

In a shared project every member reads every entry, and each entry names its author. Only the author edits an entry; the author, project admins and the owner can delete it. Statistics and Today count only your own entries.

With end-to-end encryption the note is encrypted on your device; the times stay readable so the server can total and export them. The server's CSV and AI assistants then show [encrypted] for the note.

pages.title: Recurring task rules
pages.summary: The repeat rule grammar, how the next date is worked out, and what completing, skipping and detaching do.

toc.text: How the next occurrence is computed

pages.html:
Recurring task rules

A task can repeat. The rule is a short English phrase stored in the task's recurrence field, for example every weekday or every 3 days after completion. The same grammar is implemented by the server (internal/recurrence) and the web app (web/src/lib/recurrence.ts), and both are tested against one shared file of test vectors (web/src/lib/recurrence.vectors.json), so every device and the REST API compute the same dates. Every example on this page is one of those vectors.

Grammar#

every <pattern> [after completion] [until YYYY-MM-DD | for N times]

Rules are case-insensitive and extra whitespace is ignored. A rule is at most 200 characters. What gets stored is the canonical form: lowercase, single spaces, weekday names spelled out, ordinals with the correct suffix. Every 2nd Tuesday is stored as every 2nd tuesday.

Pattern Examples Meaning
day, N days every day, every 3 days Daily, or every N days (1–999).
week, N weeks every week, every 2 weeks Every 7 × N days.
weekday every weekday Monday to Friday.
month, N months every month, every 6 months Same day of month; a day the month does not have becomes its last day.
year, N years every year, every 2 years Same date; 29 February becomes 28 February in common years.
weekday names every monday, every mon, wed, fri, every tuesday and thursday Any set of weekdays, full names or three-letter abbreviations, separated by commas or "and".
day of month every 1st, every 15th, every 31st That day of each month; in shorter months the last day.
last day every last day The last day of each month.
last weekday every last weekday The last Monday–Friday of each month.
ordinal weekday every 2nd tuesday, every first monday, every last friday 1st/first to 4th/fourth or last of that weekday in each month.

every 2nd is the 2nd day of each month; every 2nd tuesday is the second Tuesday.

Completion-relative rules#

Add after completion to a day, week, month or year interval to count from the day the task is actually completed instead of from its due date: every 3 days after completion, every week after completion. Calendar patterns (weekdays, days of month, ordinals) cannot be completion-relative.

End conditions#

  • until YYYY-MM-DD: no occurrence after that date, e.g. every day until 2026-12-31.
  • for N times: the series has N occurrences in total, e.g. every weekday for 10 times. Skipped occurrences do not count.

Only one end condition per rule.

How the next occurrence is computed#

All dates are floating calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD), like due itself; the computation never converts through a time zone, so daylight saving changes have no effect. The due time, if any, is kept.

A deadline on the series moves by the same number of days as the due date: every monday due 12 October with the deadline 14 October is next due 19 October with the deadline 21 October, also when an overdue series catches up. Skipping and "this occurrence only" move it the same way. The completed occurrence and a detached copy keep the deadline they had. A start date moves the same way, so a task deferred until two days before it is due is deferred again before the next occurrence. This Evening stays on the series. Parking a repeating task in Someday clears its due date and so ends the repetition.

  • Calendar rules: the next occurrence is the first matching date strictly after the current due date. If that date is already in the past (the task was overdue), it is instead the first matching date after today: overdue tasks catch up rather than piling up, and no missed occurrences are generated. Interval rules keep their rhythm while catching up (every 3 days due on the 1st, completed on the 10th, moves to the 13th).
  • Completion-relative rules: the next occurrence is counted from the local date of completion. every 3 days after completion due Monday and completed on Wednesday is next due Saturday; completed on the Sunday before, it is next due Wednesday.
  • Month ends: every month due 31 January moves to 28 (or 29) February. The rule has no memory of the original day, so the following month is the 28th too; use every 31st or every last day to stay at the end of the month.
  • A rule set on a task without a due date gives it one: the first matching date from today on.

Completing, skipping and editing#

  • Complete: a completed copy of the current occurrence (the occurrence record) goes to Completed, and the task moves to its next occurrence. When the end condition is reached the task completes like any other task.
  • Skip (Shift+K, or Skip in the detail panel): moves the task to the next occurrence without recording a completion. Completion-relative rules skip as if completed today. Skipping the last occurrence is not possible; complete or delete it. For a habit, a skip also writes that day's occurrence record marked skipped, in the same batch as the move, so the history can tell a skipped day from a missed one. A skipped record is not a completion: it is not listed in Completed, does not match completed filters and does not count towards for N times. A task that is not a habit skips exactly as before, with no record.
  • This occurrence only (Shift+O, or the button in the detail panel): makes a standalone copy of the current occurrence, without a rule, and moves the series to its next occurrence. Edit or move the copy freely.
  • Every other edit (title, notes, project, priority, labels, due time, rule) applies to the series, because the series is the task.
  • Reopen an occurrence record and it becomes a standalone open task; the series is not moved back. Reopening a series that ended keeps its rule, so its next completion continues the schedule.

Projected occurrences in the Plan#

The calendar's Plan draws the occurrences that would follow the current one inside the days it shows, dimmed, and counts their estimates in each day's total. They are computed on each device from the rule, the due date and the completed count with the same calculation as the preview, so every device draws the same ones. They are never written: no operation, no row, nothing to sync. They can't be moved, selected or completed; move the task itself and they follow. An end condition stops them. Every other view shows the current occurrence only.

Sync and convergence#

The rule is stored in task.recurrence and occurrence records point back with task.series_id (see sync.md). An occurrence record's id is derived from the series id and the occurrence date (SHA-256, formatted as a UUID), and the next due date is a pure function of the rule and dates every device shares. Two devices that complete the same occurrence offline therefore write the same record and the same next due date, and end with one Completed entry once they sync. A for N times count is the number of occurrence records, so it converges without a counter; skipped records of a habit are left out of the count on every device and on the server.

A habit's skip writes the same record id a completion writes, with every field of the record in one batch under one timestamp. Two devices that skip the same day therefore end with one skipped record, and when one device completes a day while another skips it, per-field last-writer-wins keeps the later batch whole: the day reads as done or as skipped, never as a mix, and the streak is unbroken either way. A completion through the REST API, CalDAV or an assistant writes no skipped field; if it lands after a device's skip of the same day, the record keeps skipped: true with the server's completion time, and the day still reads as skipped.

Skipped a day by mistake? Set the task's date back to that day and complete it: the completion writes the same record with skipped: false, so the day reads as done. The history grid itself is read-only.

The REST API behaves the same: PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id} with a non-null completed_at on a recurring task records the occurrence and moves the task (see api.md).

Clients older than this feature keep working: they store the new fields without showing them and complete a recurring task as a plain completion, which is recovered by reopening it on an updated device.

Habits#

A recurring task with a calendar rule (any rule except after completion) can be tracked as a habit: turn on Track as a habit under the repeat rule in the detail panel. The task stays an ordinary recurring task; the flag is the boolean habit field, synced like any other. Its streaks and month history are computed on each device from the series and its occurrence records (web/src/lib/habits.ts, pinned by web/src/lib/habits.vectors.json); nothing about them is stored and the server computes nothing, so two devices with the same rows show the same numbers, offline too. A task whose rule is removed or made completion-relative keeps the flag but shows no habit statistics until it has a calendar rule again.

The rules:

  • Scheduled days are the dates the rule matches plus every date that has an occurrence record: a record proves the day was scheduled even if the rule changed since. Weekday and month rules match the date itself; interval rules (every day, every 2 weeks, every month) step back from the current due date by the interval, months clamped to the month's length (every month due on the 31st was due on 28 February). Days before the habit's first record are not part of its history.
  • Done and skipped days have a record. A missed day is a scheduled day before the current occurrence without one.
  • The current occurrence (the task's due date) is pending: it never breaks the streak, whatever today is. Once the day has passed the streak chip says it is at risk.
  • The streak counts done days walking back from the scheduled day before the current occurrence, until the first missed day. A skipped day keeps the chain without adding to it. Unscheduled days (Tuesday for every mon, wed, fri) are never missed.
  • The best streak is the longest such run in the habit's history.

Catching up after being overdue leaves missed days, because that is what happened: every day due Monday and completed on Wednesday records Monday and moves to Thursday, so Tuesday and Wednesday read as missed and the streak starts again. A rule change rewrites only which past days without a record read as missed; done and skipped days stay.

With a day start after midnight, "today" for a habit is the day you are living in. A habit due on the 14th and done at 01:30 on the 15th with a day start of 04:00 records the 14th, its usual record (the record's day is always the occurrence's due date), counts in the streak, and the 15th is pending and not at risk until 04:00 on the 16th.

The month grid marks each day as done (check mark), skipped (dash), missed (dashed outline), pending (circle) or upcoming, with the date and state as each day's accessible name ("6 October, skipped"). Arrow keys move by a day or a week, Home and End jump to the month's first and last day, and Page Up and Page Down change the month.

The REST API, CalDAV and assistant tools complete a habit like any recurring task, which records a done day; none of them skips. The API reads and writes habit as a plain boolean, assistant results carry habit: true, and CalDAV serves a habit as an ordinary recurring VTODO.

pages.title: Reminders reference
pages.summary: How relative, deadline and absolute reminders fire, web push and its privacy, snooze, shared projects and the Trash.
pages.html:
Reminders reference

A task can carry any number of reminders (OpenSpec change reminders). Open a task, then use the Reminders section of the detail panel.

You can also type reminders in quick add: Dentist tomorrow at 15:00 remind me 30 min before (see Repeat and remind).

  • Relative reminders fire a number of minutes before or after the task's due time ("30 minutes before"). A task with a date but no time counts as due at 09:00. A task whose time is fixed to a time zone fires relative to that exact instant, wherever your devices are. When the due date or time changes, on any device or through the API, the reminder moves with it; recurring tasks carry their relative reminders to the next occurrence. Without a due date a relative reminder is kept but does not fire.
  • Deadline reminders fire a number of minutes before or after 09:00 on the task's deadline ("1 day before the deadline"), in your device's time zone. They follow the deadline when it changes, on any device or through the API, and never move with the due date. Without a deadline the reminder is kept but does not fire. A device on an older version leaves them untouched.
  • Absolute reminders fire at a moment you pick and never move with the due date. They work on undated tasks and are shown in each device's local time.

Shared projects#

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project your reminders are yours alone: other members never see or receive them, and you can add them with any role, viewer included. When someone else moves the task, your relative reminders follow as soon as one of your devices syncs.

Delivery#

In the app. While the app is open, a reminder whose time has come appears as a notification in the corner with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss (focus moves to it; Esc dismisses). This needs no network and no permission, and is skipped for completed or deleted tasks. When the tab is in the background and the browser allows notifications, a system notification is shown instead.

Web push. In Settings → Notifications each device can enable push so reminders arrive while the app is closed. Enabling asks for the browser permission and registers the device with the server; disabling or signing out removes it. The server checks for due reminders every 30 seconds and sends each one once per firing time to every enabled device of the reminder's owner (reminders are personal), then records the delivery on the reminder (an op by device server) so all devices know it fired. A reminder that falls due on a completed task is not sent; the server records it as dismissed instead (also an op by device server), so it is not checked again. Reopening the task does not bring that firing back; set a new time or snooze it to be reminded again. System notifications offer Snooze 10 min and Dismiss; these work offline and are uploaded on the next sync. Their text and the due date are written in the account's interface language, which the service worker reads from the synced preferences row on the device (English when there is none). If the app is focused when a push arrives, the reminder is shown in the app only.

Privacy. A push payload carries only the reminder id, the task id and the firing time, encrypted end to end (RFC 8291) so the push service cannot read it. The device shows the title from its own copy of the task. Enable Include task titles if a device should be able to show the title before it has synced the task; the description is never sent.

Trash#

A reminder does not fire, in the app or by push, while its task is deleted or while the task's project, or any project above it, is in the Trash. It is not marked as delivered either, so restoring the task or the project brings it back: a reminder whose time is still ahead fires on time, and one whose time passed while it was in the Trash is delivered once, late, on the next check (the same rule as for reminders that fell due while the server was down). Dismiss or snooze it if you no longer need it. Purging the task from the Trash removes its reminders.

Snooze and dismiss#

Snoozing sets a new firing time (in 10 minutes, in an hour, or tomorrow at 09:00) and the reminder fires again, also by push. Dismissing silences the current firing. Both are ordinary synced edits: when one device dismisses and another later snoozes the same reminder, the later edit wins on every device.

End-to-end encryption#

For an account with end-to-end encryption the server never puts a title in a push, even for devices that opted in to titles: it cannot read it, and ciphertext would be useless. The notification uses the content-free text; in-app reminder toasts still show the decrypted title from the device.

For operators#

Nothing to configure. The VAPID key pair is generated on first use at <data>/push_vapid.pem and travels with backup archives. OPENTODO_PUSH=off turns push off entirely (routes answer 404, no outbound requests); in-app reminders keep working. Push requires the app to be served over https (OPENTODO_BASE_URL), as browsers only allow push subscriptions on secure origins. See self-hosting and API.

pages.title: Capturing pages
pages.summary: Save pages, selected text, files and screenshots from other apps: the share sheet, the bookmarklet and the browser extension.
pages.html:
Capturing pages

Many tasks start as "deal with this page later". OpenTodo can receive a page from three places, and all of them open the same capture screen at /share on your own server:

From How Works offline
Phone or desktop share sheet Install the app, then choose OpenTodo in the share menu Yes, once the app has been opened online
Any desktop browser The bookmarklet from Settings → Capture The popup opens from the app's offline cache once the app has been loaded in that browser
Chromium and Firefox The browser extension in extension/ Same as the bookmarklet in Capture screen mode

The capture screen proposes:

  • Title: the page title, or the link's host name when there is no title. The title field is a regular quick-add line, so typing tomorrow #work p1 into it sets the date, project and priority.
  • Description: the selected or shared text, followed by the link. The link is also kept as the task's origin.
  • Project: the Inbox by default; pick any project.
  • Files: anything shared along with the page (photos, PDFs, documents) or a screenshot from the extension, each with its name, type and size and a thumbnail for images. Remove any you don't want; they're saved as attachments of the new task. A share that carries only a file proposes the file's name as the title.

Press Enter to save or Esc to cancel. Nothing is saved until you confirm. Saving creates an ordinary task on the device first and syncs it like any other quick-add task, so it works with no network and reaches your other devices when the network returns.

When the capture screen was opened as a popup (bookmarklet, extension) or in a window opened just for the share, it closes itself after Save or Esc. Otherwise it takes you to the Inbox or to the project you picked.

Where a task came from#

A task saved from a shared link also remembers that link as its origin. The task's row shows a small chip with the link's host (example.org), and the task panel an Origin chip; both open the page in a new tab, and the page title you shared is their tooltip. On a row the chip is quiet, like the counts at the end of the row; on a board card it ends the line under the title. A link to an issue on GitHub, GitLab, Jira (*.atlassian.net) or Linear is recognised on your device, without opening it: the chip reads the issue (owner/repo#7, ENG-123) and the task is listed by origin: github, origin: gitlab, origin: jira or origin: linear in a filter. Self-hosted trackers are kept as ordinary links. The link still ends the description, so your notes read as before.

To forget the origin, remove the Origin chip in the task panel; the description keeps the link. The command palette also finds a task by its issue id (eng-123) or the shared page title. Tasks from email carry an Email origin without a link, and imported tasks carry their source (origin: todoist). A message saved from Gmail or Outlook on the web with the extension's Quick save reads Gmail or Outlook, opens the message, has the subject as its tooltip, and is listed by origin: gmail or origin: outlook.

Share sheet (installed app)#

The web app manifest declares a Web Share Target (POST /share with title, text, url and files), so the app is offered for links, text, images and documents. The browser adds OpenTodo to the share menu once the app is installed:

Platform Install Share
Android, Chrome / Edge / Samsung Internet Menu → Install app (or Add to Home screen) Share from any app → OpenTodo
Android, other browsers (Vivaldi, Brave …) or a device without Google Play services (GrapheneOS, /e/OS, LineageOS) Usually only a home-screen shortcut, which Android cannot list in the share menu See below
Windows, ChromeOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Share from apps that use the system share dialog
macOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Support for receiving shares varies by version; use the bookmarklet or extension
iOS and iPadOS, any browser Share → Add to Home Screen Safari does not support share targets for web apps; use the bookmarklet in Safari instead
Firefox (all platforms) Firefox does not install web apps as share targets Use the extension or bookmarklet

From the Android app#

The Android app is in the share menu as soon as it is installed, also on phones without Google Play services. Links and text open the capture screen as above; photos and files (up to ten, 20 MB each, 25 MB together) are handed to it the way the browser extension hands over a screenshot, and stay on the phone until you save. A share that arrives before you have entered a server waits until you have.

OpenTodo is missing from the share menu on Android#

Android lists a web app in the share menu only when it was installed as a real app (a WebAPK), not as a home-screen shortcut. Chrome creates that app through Google Play services, Samsung Internet through its own service. Other browsers such as Vivaldi or Brave, and any browser on a device without Google Play services (GrapheneOS without sandboxed Google Play, /e/OS, LineageOS), add a shortcut instead. OpenTodo then opens normally from the home screen but cannot receive shares. Nothing on your server can change this.

To check: open Android Settings → Apps. If OpenTodo is listed there, it is installed as an app; if not, it is a shortcut.

What works instead:

  • Install from Chrome: remove the shortcut, open your server in Chrome and choose Install app. On GrapheneOS this needs sandboxed Google Play installed in the same profile.
  • Email to task: share the page to your email app and send it to your secret inbox address, if the owner turned email capture on.
  • Copy and paste: share → Copy, then paste the link into quick add.

Some apps put the link inside the shared text instead of the link field. The capture screen then takes the last http(s) link from the text and moves it to the end of the description.

After an update that adds or changes the share target, the browser may need the app to be opened once (or reinstalled) before the share menu entry appears. If a share reaches the server before the app has been opened since the update, the title, text and link still arrive, and the capture screen says the files did not: open the app once and share again.

Shared files never leave the device before you save. The app's service worker receives the share on the device, also offline, and keeps the files in a separate local store (opentodo-share) only until the capture screen is saved or cancelled. Anything left there is removed after ten minutes and at sign-out. Saving creates the task and its attachments in one step, on the device first; the files upload with the next sync.

The service worker only takes a share from the system share sheet or from the app's own pages: a form on another website that posts to /share just opens the app and nothing is stored. A share larger than 100 MB in total (files and text together) is not stored either.

Bookmarklet#

Settings → Capture shows an Add to OpenTodo button generated for your server's address. Drag it to the bookmarks bar (or use Copy bookmarklet and paste the code as the address of a new bookmark). Clicking it on any page opens a small popup with the capture screen, prefilled with the page's address, title and the text you selected.

The bookmarklet contains no password or token. It only opens your server's /share page in a popup, where your normal sign-in applies. Its source, with your server's address in place of https://todo.example.com:

javascript:(function () {
  var e = encodeURIComponent
  var s = String(window.getSelection ? getSelection() : '').slice(0, 16384)
  var u = "https://todo.example.com/share" + '?url=' + e(location.href) + '&title=' + e(document.title) + (s ? '&text=' + e(s) : '')
  if (!window.open(u, 'opentodo-capture', 'popup,width=480,height=640'))
    alert('Allow pop-ups for this site to capture it to OpenTodo.')
})()

If nothing happens, the browser blocked the popup: allow pop-ups for the site you are on. Some sites block bookmarklets with their own security policy; the extension works there.

Browser extension#

extension/ holds a small Manifest V3 extension for Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi) and Firefox 128 or later. The toolbar button and Alt+Shift+O (change it at chrome://extensions/shortcuts or in Firefox's Manage Extension Shortcuts) open a popup: one line with the page's title, the text you selected, a project and a label picker, the page as the task's origin (remove it with its cross), and Save. Enter saves, Esc closes without keeping anything.

Right-click to start from something else with Add to OpenTodo: on a link, the link's text is the line and its address the origin; on an image, the file name is the line and the image's address starts the description (the extension never downloads the image). On a message open in Gmail or Outlook on the web, the subject is the line and From: with the sender starts the description; the message body is never read.

Two modes, chosen in the extension's options:

  • Capture screen (the default): Save opens your server's capture screen in a popup window with the line, the text and the address, where you check and save as above. The extension holds no token and sends nothing itself.
  • Quick save: paste a full-access API token (create one per browser, so you can revoke it alone). Save then creates the task at once and shows Saved with a link to it. While you type, the line is previewed as chips (date, project, labels, priority, reminders) in your account's language; a #name that is no project shows a grey chip and stays in the title. A label that does not exist yet is created. If the server cannot be reached or refuses the token, the popup keeps your text and offers Open capture screen. On an account with end-to-end encryption, save from the capture screen, which encrypts on your device. A read-only token previews but does not save.

The extension's own texts follow the browser's interface language in English, German, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, and English otherwise; the chips and the capture screen follow your interface language.

Install (it is not published in the browser stores yet): download opentodo-browser-extension-chrome.zip or opentodo-browser-extension-firefox.zip from a release (or run make extension) and unzip it.

  • Chromium: open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the unzipped folder.
  • Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, Load Temporary Add-on…, pick manifest.json in the unzipped folder. Temporary add-ons are removed when Firefox restarts.

First use: if no server is set, the extension opens its options page and asks for your server's address (for example https://todo.example.com); the capture you started continues once it is saved.

Screenshot: right-click a page and choose Add screenshot to OpenTodo. The visible part of the tab is handed to the capture screen as a PNG under Files; nothing is saved until you press Save. This needs access to your server's address, which the options page asks for.

Privacy: the extension talks only to the server address you enter. It stores that address and the mode in the browser's extension sync storage, and the token, in Quick save mode, on this device only (browsers never synchronise it); a token travels only over https (or to localhost). It has no content scripts and opens no connections while idle. Permissions: activeTab (the clicked tab's address, title and selection), contextMenus, scripting (read the selection or a mail's sender, hand a screenshot over), storage, and, optional, access to your server's address only.

Signed out#

If the device is not signed in, the capture screen first shows the sign-in form with a note, then continues to the capture screen with the shared page intact. Until you save, the shared title, text and link stay in the page's memory only: they are removed from the address bar and are not written to storage or sent to the server (the server's request log records paths, never query strings). Reloading the sign-in page therefore loses the shared content; share it again.

Limits and safety#

  • The title is cut to 500 characters, the text to 16 KB with a [truncated] note.
  • A link is kept only if it starts with http:// or https://; anything else (javascript:, data:, file: …) is dropped and the rest of the share is shown normally.
  • Shared content is shown as plain text, never as HTML, and the capture screen never opens the shared link.
  • There is no auto-save: a link to /share cannot create a task without you pressing Save.
  • At most 10 files per share, none larger than the server's limit per file (25 MB unless the owner changed it); a larger file is listed as refused and the task is saved without it. On the public demo, files are not attached.
  • Shared files are listed by name, type and size and never shown as web pages; an HTML file is attached as a file that downloads.

pages.title: Import formats
pages.summary: Every import format in detail: your own export, CSV and other apps' JSON exports, mapping rules, duplicates and undo.
pages.html:
Import formats

OpenTodo imports tasks, projects, sections, recurrence rules and reminders from files: its own JSON export (for moving between instances or recovering), CSV from a spreadsheet or a script, and the JSON exports of other task managers. Open Settings → Data → Import data in the web app (or press g then Shift+I), or drive the same endpoints from a script; see API below.

Every import works in two steps:

  1. Preview. The server reads the file and reports, row by row, what would happen: create, update, skip (with a reason) or error (with the row number and the reason), with totals that also count new sections, recurring tasks and reminders, and file-level notes (for example comments that are not imported). Nothing is written.
  2. Import. The server runs the import as a background job. Every created or changed field becomes an ordinary operation in the op log, stamped with server time and the device id import, so every device receives the imported data on its next sync under the usual last-writer-wins rules. A whole import can be undone later.

Import runs on the server, so it needs a connection: the Import screen disables the file picker while offline and keeps showing the last loaded job list.

Formats#

The format is detected from the content, in this order; the preview shows what was detected and the format option overrides it.

Format id Recognised by Notes
opentodo a top-level "format": "opentodo-export" Exact round trip, see below
things-db a SQLite database with Things 3's tables a copy of Things' main.sqlite, see Things
google-tasks-json "kind": "tasks#taskLists", or items of kind tasks#taskList Google Takeout's Tasks.json, see Google Tasks
trello-json top-level id, name and lists, cards, checklists arrays one Trello board, see Trello
microsoft-todo-json lists with wellknownListName, or with tasks that have importance and dueDateTime or isReminderOn written by a PowerShell script, see Microsoft To Do
apple-reminders-json an array whose every element has identifier and isCompleted written by a Shortcut, see Apple Reminders
anydo-json categories and tasks arrays, tasks with categoryId and status Any.do's data request, see Any.do
json-items top-level items and projects arrays "projects / sections / items" backups
json-lists a top-level lists array lists of tasks; each list becomes a project
json-generic a top-level array of objects, or a tasks array a generic task list

ZIP files. A ZIP whose files are all of one format is imported as one job, one preview and one undo; each preview row shows the file it came from. Folders, __MACOSX/ and hidden files are skipped. An archive with more than 1,000 files, mixed formats, an unsafe file name, or more than ten times the upload limit when unpacked is refused with 400 invalid_file before anything is written. A zipped Things Database.thingsdatabase folder is read as a Things database.

A file matching none of these is refused with 400 unsupported_format, naming the supported formats. If a JSON export from another app is not recognised, convert it to the CSV columns below; every field the data model holds can be expressed there.

Own export (opentodo)#

The file from Settings → Data → Download export or GET /api/v1/export. Labels, projects (with their sub-project tree), sections, custom field definitions (fields, deleted ones included), tasks (with subtasks, completion, tombstones and their fields values), reminders and saved views are recreated with their original ids and field values, so importing an export into an empty account and exporting again gives an equivalent file (comments aside, see below).

Because ids are kept, nothing needs remapping: a task's section_id, a recurring series and its occurrence records (series_id, whose ids are derived from the series id), a reminder's task_id, a task's blocked_by and a dashboard's panels all point at the same entities as before. Every task field is carried: recurrence (stored in canonical form, for example Every Monday becomes every monday), series_id, section_id, notes_doc (rich-text notes), due including a zoned tz, estimate_minutes, ical_extra, origin (where the task came from, unchanged) and every custom field value in fields, including values of definitions that were deleted or belong to another project. The preview counts the definitions it creates as fields.

What is handled differently, and why:

  • Comments are not imported. A comment keeps its author, and the sync engine only accepts comments whose author_id is the account writing them; the authors in an export are accounts of the exporting instance (and other members of shared projects). Comment creation is also rate-limited per account. Rewriting every comment to you would misattribute other people's words, so the preview shows a note such as "12 comments are not imported" and nothing is written for them.
  • Assignees are kept only when they are you (a restore into the same account). Any other assignee_id names an account that is not a member here, so it is dropped with a warning on the task.
  • Reminders keep their delivered_at and dismissed_at, so a reminder that already went off stays quiet. A live reminder whose time has already passed and that was neither delivered nor dismissed for that time is imported dismissed at import time (with a warning), so restoring an old export does not push a burst of stale notifications. Future reminders fire normally. A reminder whose task is neither in the file nor in your account is an error row.
  • Attachments keep their ids, names and types and become yours: author_id is rewritten to you, comment_id is cleared (comments are not imported) and uploaded_at is set by the server once the file is stored. Links are always imported. A file needs the ZIP export (GET /api/v1/export?format=zip): the importer reads export.json and the files under attachments/<id>/<name>, checks each file against its size and sha256, and applies the server's per-file limit and your attachments total; a file that does not fit is left out and listed among the job's errors. From the JSON alone, file attachments are skipped and the preview says how many ("3 file attachments are not imported").
  • The read-only role and owner_id the export adds to shared projects are not data and are skipped silently; the end-to-end encryption key record is not imported.

A template file is an own export with one more top-level key, "template": {"day": "YYYY-MM-DD"}, written by Save as template… (OpenSpec project-templates). Import treats it like any export (it creates the contents once, with the file's ids and dates) and adds a note to the preview pointing to From a template…, which makes a fresh copy on the device with new ids and dates moved so template.day lands on the chosen start day. A file without template (such as the downloads on the website) uses the date of exportedAt as its reference day there. See Templates.

When an id already exists in the account the row is skipped (exists), unless the existing option is overwrite: then only fields whose value differs are written (update), and fields that are unchanged keep their original clock, so a concurrent edit on a device is not clobbered needlessly. An entity that is deleted in the account is never resurrected (skip, reason deleted). Fields unknown to this server version are dropped with a warning.

json-lists#

{"lists": [{"id", "title", "tasks": [...]}]}; each list becomes a project with its title. Tasks read title, notes (description), due (RFC 3339; converted to the chosen time zone), status: "completed" and completed (completion time), parent (a task id) or nested subtasks, and starred / important (priority 1). recurrence (string, RRULE array or {pattern: {type, interval, daysOfWeek}}) becomes a rule and reminderDateTime (or the other reminder keys of json-generic) a reminder. links are dropped with a warning; tasks marked deleted are skipped.

Mapping rules#

  • Projects are matched by name, ignoring case, against existing non-deleted projects; otherwise created. Tasks without a project go to the target project (option) or the Inbox.
  • Sections: see Sections.
  • Recurrence and reminders: see Recurrence and Reminders.
  • Subtasks are resolved after the whole file is read, so row order does not matter. A subtask joins its parent's project. A parent that is missing, invalid or would form a cycle leaves the task at the top level with a warning.
  • Labels are matched by name, ignoring case; missing ones are created.
  • Dates: plain dates stay dates; date-times without a zone keep their wall clock; date-times with a zone become the wall clock of that instant in the chosen time zone (default: the browser's zone in the web app, UTC through the API). Due dates are always stored floating. A deadline is a date only: a time on it is dropped with a warning, keeping the day as written. The preview counts the tasks that get a deadline.
  • Completion: a completed row keeps its source completion time, or the import time when the source has none.
  • Unsupported attributes (attachments that are not web addresses, comments, assignees, links, location reminders, recurrence rules the grammar cannot express) never block a row: the task is imported and the row carries a warning naming what was dropped.
  • Custom fields: see Custom fields.

Custom fields#

Trello custom fields, Asana's extra columns and Linear estimates become custom fields of the task's project. A field of the same name (ignoring case) and type in that project is reused; otherwise one is created, and the preview counts it under new fields. A choice field gets the values in the order they first appear. A value is dropped with a warning when the project already has a field of that name with another type, when the project already holds 30 fields, or when the task goes to the Inbox (fields belong to a project). Undo removes the fields the import created and leaves fields that were there before.

Sections#

With sections: section (the default) a row's section becomes a real section of the task's project: an existing live section with the same name (ignoring case) is reused, otherwise one is created once per project, after the existing ones. A subtask's section is looked up in the project it ends up in. Tasks without a project (the Inbox, when no target project is chosen) cannot hold sections, so their section becomes a label, with a warning. sections: label turns every section into a label named like it (the behaviour before sections existed), sections: ignore drops them. Re-importing a file finds the sections it created by name (and, for json-items, by source id), so nothing is duplicated.

Recurrence#

A recurrence becomes a rule of the recurrence grammar, stored in canonical form, when the grammar can express it. Accepted, in this order:

  1. The grammar itself: every day, every 2 weeks, every monday, friday, every 15th, every last friday, every 3 days after completion, … until 2027-01-01, … for 10 times.
  2. An iCalendar RRULE, with or without the RRULE: prefix (FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2, FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR), when it maps exactly onto a rule (as for CalDAV).
  3. Common spellings: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, annually, biweekly, fortnightly, every other day|week|month|year, weekdays, every workday, every weekend, each … and ev … for every …, and every! … for "after completion" (every! 3 days → every 3 days after completion). A trailing time of day (every tue 4pm, every day at 09:00) is removed: the due time carries it.
  4. A structured object {frequency|freq|type|unit, interval, days|daysOfWeek|byday} (also under pattern), e.g. {"frequency": "weekly", "days": ["MO", "TH"]} → every monday, thursday, and an array of RRULE strings.

Anything else (hourly rules, starting …, every other monday, an interval combined with weekdays, free text) is shown in the preview as a warning on the row, recurrence "every 3 hours" not supported; imported without a rule, and the task is imported without a rule. A recurring task without a due date gets the rule's first date from today in the chosen time zone, as in the app. Imported recurring tasks are series of their own (no series_id).

Reminders#

Reminders are created together with their task (a task that is skipped, for example as already imported, brings none) and belong to you, like every reminder.

Value Becomes
a number, or a string of digits relative reminder that many minutes before the due time
30m, 1h, 2 days, 15 min before relative reminder before the due time
an ISO 8601 duration (-PT15M, -P1D) relative reminder; a negative duration is before the due time
a date-time (2026-10-20T08:00, with or without zone) or a date absolute reminder at that time (floating values in the chosen time zone, a date at 09:00)
an object with offset_minutes (negative = before), minute_offset / minutes_before (minutes before) or offset / trigger (a duration) relative reminder
an object with datetime, at, remind_at, fire_at, time, date or due.date absolute reminder
type: "location" dropped with a warning

A relative reminder fires at the due time plus its offset, with a date-only due counting as 09:00, in the chosen time zone. On a task without a due date it is kept but does not fire (the row says so). A reminder whose time has already passed at import time is imported dismissed, with a warning, so no stale notification is sent. Offsets beyond one year are dropped with a warning.

Origins#

Tasks from Todoist, TickTick, Things, Linear, Google Tasks, Trello, Asana, Microsoft To Do, Apple Reminders and Any.do keep where they came from as their origin, written in the import's operations like every other field and shown as a chip on the row. Tasks from a generic CSV or JSON file get none, and the preview has no origin column. Duplicate detection still uses the importer's own memory (below), not the origin.

Duplicates#

Checked in this order:

  1. Own export: an id that already exists is skip (exists) or, with existing: overwrite, update.
  2. A source row recorded by an earlier, not undone import of the same format for this account is skip (already_imported). Importing the same file twice therefore creates nothing the second time. CSV rows without an id column are recognised by their content.
  3. A row whose title (trimmed, ignoring case), project and due date match an existing open task is skip (possible_duplicate), unless the duplicates option is import, in which case it is created with a warning.

Options#

Option Values Default
format a format id from the table above detected
targetProject id of one of your projects Inbox
timeZone IANA zone, e.g. Europe/Rome UTC (the web app sends the browser zone)
sections section, label, ignore section
duplicates skip, import skip
errors skip_rows, abort skip_rows
existing skip, overwrite (own export only) skip

With skip_rows, bad rows are reported and everything else is imported; a bad row never leaves a partial task. With abort, any row in error fails the job before anything is written and names the first bad row.

Jobs, limits and undo#

  • One import job per account runs at a time; starting a second one answers 409 conflict naming the running job.
  • Files may be at most OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB megabytes (default 20, allowed 1–200) and 50,000 rows; larger files answer 413 too_large.
  • Ops are written in batches of at most 1,000 and progress is saved after each batch. If the server restarts mid-import, the job shows failed with the counts of what was written, and undo removes it.
  • Undo tombstones every project, task, label, section, reminder and saved view the job created, through the op log: they disappear from every view and from other devices after their next sync, and stay in the export with deleted_at. Entities the job only updated are left alone. As when deleting in the app, open tasks you later added to an undone project move to the Inbox, open tasks you later put into an undone section move to "No section", and undone labels are removed from your other tasks. Undo is idempotent. After an undo the same file can be imported again.
  • Webhooks see an import as one import.completed delivery per finished job and one import.undone per undo, not one event per task. See Webhooks → Imports.

Job records (status, options, counts, row errors) are operational metadata kept in the server database; they are not part of the export.

Memory#

The preview reads the whole file once. CSV is streamed record by record; a JSON file is decoded in one piece and takes roughly five times its size in memory, so the largest default file (20 MB of JSON) peaks around 100–120 MB during the preview and the start of the job, released afterwards. Typical imports of a few thousand rows stay under 10 MB. On a 1 GB Raspberry Pi keep the default or lower OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB.

API#

All routes require a session or a bearer token, like the rest of the API. Uploads are multipart/form-data with a file part and the options either as one JSON options part or as individual fields named like the options.

# Preview (nothing is written)
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/preview" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F file=@tasks.csv -F timeZone=Europe/Rome

# Start the job → 202 {"job": {"id": "…", "status": "running", …}}
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F file=@opentodo-export.json -F 'options={"existing":"overwrite"}'

# Follow it, list jobs, undo
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -sS -X POST "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>/undo" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

See docs/api.md for the response shapes and error codes.

pages.title: End-to-end encryption
pages.summary: What encryption hides from the server and what it does not, the threat model, devices, recovery and limits.

toc.text: What is encrypted, what is not
Enabling, plaintext that appears later, purging, disabling

pages.html:
End-to-end encryption

Optional, per account, off by default (OpenSpec change e2ee). When it is on, your devices encrypt the content of your tasks before it is synced, so the server, its backups and every server-side integration hold only ciphertext for it. Sync, offline use and conflict-free merging keep working because ciphertext travels through the unchanged operation log as an ordinary string value.

Turn it on in Settings → Account → Encryption.

Automation rules work with encryption: their conditions and actions use ids and dates. Only the comment action is unavailable.

What is encrypted, what is not#

Encrypted, in your personal data (Inbox, your own projects, labels, saved views):

Entity Encrypted fields
task title, description, ical_extra, notes_doc (the rich-text note document, encrypted as one opaque string; its ciphertext must fit the 256 KB document limit, so an encrypted note document is capped at about 196 KB), origin (where the task came from: the whole object, serialised as JSON and encrypted into one ciphertext string, because its title, link and id name the page, mail or issue; the server accepts that string wherever it accepts the object)
project name, description and notes_doc (the project's note)
label name
section name
saved view name, query
comment body (your comments on your own tasks)
attachment name, mime (the file type), url (a link's address), and the file itself, as an encrypted file (see below)
custom field the field's name and options, and every text, link, date and choice value on a task (fields.<id> with a string value)
time entry note (the time entry's note)
review tomorrow_note (the line for tomorrow you leave when you close the day)

Everything else stays plaintext, because views sort and group by it, reminders and calendars schedule with it, and the server needs it to merge and authorize: due (date, time, zone), priority, completed_at, deleted_at, created_at, position, project_id, parent_id, section_id, labels (the list of label ids on a task), recurrence, estimate_minutes, assignee_id, number and checkbox values of custom fields, a custom field's type and project_id, project color and archived, reminder times, the review record's times and today's focus (completed_at, daily_at, monthly_at, closed_at, focus_date, focus), a time entry's task_id, user_id, started_at, ended_at, device_id, created_at and deleted_at (so the server can total and export tracked time; its CSV and AI assistants show [encrypted] for the note), an attachment's size and sha256 (of the encrypted file) and encrypted flag, a comment's reactions (reactions.<account id>: who reacted with which of six names) and a task's note_mentions (the members its notes mention; the mention itself, like every table and image in the note, stays inside the encrypted notes_doc), and all timestamps and device ids of operations. An image embedded in a note or comment names its attachment; the device downloads the encrypted file and decrypts it to show it, and a locked device shows "Encrypted image".

Empty values ("") and null are not encrypted. The length of a ciphertext reveals the approximate length of the text.

Shared projects are never encrypted. A project that was shared before you enabled encryption, and projects other people share with you, stay plaintext for every member. While encryption is on you cannot share a project that is not shared yet (409 encryption_enabled): the members would hold no key.

Threat model#

Protected against:

  • Someone who reads the server's disk, database file, backups (local, S3, WebDAV) or database dumps: they see ciphertext for the fields above.
  • The server operator browsing the data, and server-side integrations (CalDAV, the MCP endpoint, webhooks, the REST API with an API token): they see ciphertext or a placeholder.
  • A server or a bug moving a ciphertext to another field or task: the value is bound to entity, entityId and field and fails authentication; the app shows "[Cannot decrypt]" and keeps the operation.

Not protected against (honest limits):

  • Metadata. Everything in the plaintext list above, plus how many tasks, projects and labels you have, when you edit what, from how many devices, and the approximate length of each text.
  • A malicious or compromised server serving tampered JavaScript. The web app is delivered by the same server it protects you from. A server that changes the code can capture the passphrase or the key on the next load. This is inherent to web-delivered end-to-end encryption; a future change may verify release signatures in the service worker.
  • Your devices. The device is the trust boundary: local storage (IndexedDB) holds plaintext and the account key (as a non-extractable CryptoKey). Malware, a browser extension with access to the page, or someone with your unlocked device can read everything. "Lock this device" forgets the key and pauses sync but leaves already synced data in local storage; Sign out clears local data.
  • Weak passphrases. The server holds the passphrase-wrapped key. Someone with that record can try passphrases offline; PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations slows this down but is not memory-hard. Use a long passphrase (at least 12 characters are required). The app refuses a key record whose iteration count is below 100,000 or above 10,000,000 and stays locked with an error, so a broken or hostile server can neither weaken the derivation nor hang the device.
  • Rollback of a value. The authenticated data binds a ciphertext to its entity, id and field, but not to a version or time. A server can serve an older ciphertext of the same field again (for example the title a task had last month, or a whole older state from a backup), and the app cannot tell: it decrypts correctly and wins by its clock as usual. Encryption guarantees that the server cannot read or forge content, not that it shows you the latest content.
  • Turning encryption off by forgetting the key record. A server cannot switch a device back to plaintext: a missing key record (a server restored from a backup made before encryption, another device that turned encryption off, or a hostile server) pauses sync on every device that encrypts until you choose (see Devices, locking and offline use). If you choose to turn encryption off there, the server sees your content in plaintext again.
  • Plaintext that existed before. Content written before encryption was enabled, or written in plaintext later (REST, email), stays in older backups and in the server's history until you purge it (see below).
  • Your account itself. Encryption protects content, not access: anyone who can sign in can delete, reschedule or tombstone your (encrypted) tasks, and can read the plaintext fields.

How it works#

Key hierarchy, all generated and used in the browser with the built-in Web Crypto API (no dependency):

  • Account key: 256 random bits, AES-256-GCM. Kept on each unlocked device as a non-extractable key in IndexedDB.
  • Passphrase key: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 over your passphrase (NFC-normalised) with a 16-byte random salt and 600,000 iterations, producing an AES-KW key.
  • Recovery key: 256 random bits, shown once as 56 base32 characters in 14 groups of four (52 for the key, 4 for a checksum). HKDF-SHA-256 (fixed salt, info opentodo/e2ee/recovery-kek/v1) turns it into an AES-KW key.
  • The account key is wrapped (AES-KW, RFC 3394) under both. The key record — {version, kdf, salt, iterations, wrappedByPassphrase, wrappedByRecovery} — is the only key material the server stores (encryption_keys table). It never receives the passphrase, the recovery key or the account key.

Value format (a string in the existing op value):

"enc:v1:" + base64url( nonce(12 bytes) || AES-256-GCM(utf8(plaintext)) || tag(16 bytes) )
additional authenticated data = utf8(entity + "\0" + entityId + "\0" + field)

Nonces are 96 random bits per encryption. Known-answer vectors shared by the Go and browser test suites are in web/src/lib/e2ee.vectors.json.

Attached files are encrypted on the device in 1 MiB chunks, so a large file is never held in memory twice:

header  = "OTAT1" || chunk size (4 bytes, big-endian) || file prefix (8 random bytes)
chunk i = AES-256-GCM(chunk i of the file) || tag(16 bytes)
nonce i = file prefix || i (3 bytes, big-endian) || 0x01 on the last chunk, else 0x00
additional authenticated data = utf8("attachment\0" + attachment id + "\0") || header

The id in every chunk binds the bytes to their attachment, and the marked last chunk means a cut-off file is detected. The server stores and serves the encrypted file as opaque bytes (always as a download), and its size and sha256 describe the encrypted file, never the original. Opening a file downloads it to the device, checks and decrypts every chunk, and only then shows it: a chunk that fails the check means nothing is shown. An encrypted file is about 16 bytes per MiB larger than the original, so a file just under the per-file limit can be refused once encrypted. Thumbnails are not shown for encrypted images.

Where it happens on the device:

  • Every edit is applied locally in plaintext and queued. The sync engine encrypts content fields at the single point where operations leave the device (just before upload), so nothing reaches the server in plaintext whichever path created the operation (edits, re-seeding after a server restore, the migration, encrypt-on-sight).
  • Incoming operations are decrypted before they are applied, so search, filters and views work on plaintext locally.
  • Convergence is unchanged: winners are chosen by (timestamp, device), never by value. Two ciphertexts of the same text differ, which does not matter.

Content larger than 48,000 bytes (UTF-8) in one field is refused before an operation is created, because its ciphertext would exceed the server's 64 KiB value limit.

Devices, locking and offline use#

  • New device: sign in, then enter the passphrase (or the recovery key) on the unlock screen. Nothing is pulled or pushed before that; the sync status reads Locked. Afterwards the device works offline and does not ask again.
  • Wrong passphrase: an error, and after 5 failures within a minute further attempts are delayed for the rest of that minute (on this device).
  • Lock this device (Settings): forgets the key and pauses sync until unlocked.
  • The command-line client: ot encryption unlock unwraps the key with the passphrase (or --recovery) on your computer and keeps it in an owner-only file next to the CLI's configuration, so ot mcp --decrypt can let a local AI assistant read and write your text. The passphrase and the key never reach the server; the assistant's AI provider does receive the plaintext it reads. ot encryption lock deletes the key file, and a passphrase change elsewhere makes it stale until you unlock again.
  • Offline unlock works once the device has seen the key record.
  • Unlock with a fingerprint (Android app): see below.
  • A device that did not know encryption had been enabled notices the first ciphertext it receives, checks the key record and locks itself without applying the batch.
  • Key record missing: only you can turn encryption off on a device, never an answer from the server. When the server says it has no key record while the device encrypts (the server was restored from an older backup, another device turned encryption off, or the server misbehaves), the device stops syncing and nothing leaves it, not even the re-send after a server restore. A screen explains it and offers three choices: Restore the key record from this device (uploads the copy the device kept; same passphrase and recovery key; a device without the key asks for the passphrase first), Turn off encryption on this device (your content is uploaded in plaintext again), or Sign out.

Unlock with a fingerprint#

In the Android app, on a phone with a fingerprint or face unlock, the unlock screen offers Unlock with fingerprint or face next time. After you unlock with the passphrase, the app keeps a copy of the account key encrypted by Android's keystore under a key that opens only with your fingerprint or face; from then on the unlock screen shows Unlock with fingerprint or face, and the passphrase still works. The copy never leaves the phone. It is deleted when you sign out, change or reset the passphrase on this phone, turn encryption off, or when the account key changes; Android makes it unusable when fingerprints or faces are added or removed. Lock this device keeps it, so the next unlock can use the fingerprint.

Passphrase change, recovery, losing both#

  • Change passphrase (needs the current one and a fresh sign-in confirmation): re-wraps the account key; content is not re-encrypted; other devices keep working; new devices use the new passphrase.
  • Reset with the recovery key (forgotten passphrase): sets a new passphrase and issues a new recovery key; the old one stops working.
  • Lost both: the content cannot be recovered by anyone, including the server owner — there is no server-side reset. Settings and the unlock screen offer only to turn encryption off and delete the encrypted content: the key record is removed and every item whose content cannot be decrypted is moved to the Trash as it syncs. Plaintext fields (dates, structure) are kept.

Enabling, plaintext that appears later, purging, disabling#

  • Enabling re-writes every content field of your personal data as ciphertext through ordinary operations, with progress in Settings; the job is resumable after a reload. 500 tasks produce roughly 1,500 operations. A link attachment cannot change its address on the server, so each personal link is replaced by a copy with the address and name encrypted, and the plaintext link moves to the Trash. Then each attached file is downloaded, encrypted and uploaded again as a new attachment that replaces the plaintext one ("Encrypting your files: 3 of 40 files"). This part needs a connection: it stops when the network goes and continues after the next sync, and files not done yet keep their old form meanwhile.
  • Plaintext written later — through the REST API, the CLI, email-to-task or an import — is accepted by the server and shown with a small "not yet encrypted" marker; the next unlocked device that syncs it re-writes it as ciphertext ("encrypt-on-sight"). Two devices doing that at once produce two ciphertexts of the same text; one wins and nothing is re-written again.
  • Purge plaintext history (POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history) deletes the superseded operations of the content fields in your personal data, including the plaintext from before encryption. Winners stay, so every device still converges. The deletion runs with SQLite secure_delete, then the database is vacuumed and the write-ahead log truncated. Revision history for those fields is gone afterwards. Backups made before the purge, and copies of the database, may still contain plaintext: delete them if that matters to you.
