  • Disabling (needs an unlocked device and a fresh sign-in confirmation) first re-uploads every encrypted file decrypted, while encryption is still on, and waits until the last one is stored on the server, so no file becomes unreadable. Then it deletes the key record, so other devices stop encrypting, and re-writes all content as plaintext, replacing each encrypted link with a plaintext copy. Devices that still hold the key decrypt ciphertext that arrives late and re-write it as plaintext too.

Server-side reads and integrations#

Workspace names, members and groups are server data in plaintext, like project members; with encryption on you can create workspaces and move things between them, but not add members, groups or invite links yet.

The server cannot decrypt. Each feature that needs content degrades explicitly:

Feature Behaviour for an encrypted account
REST API reads Return the ciphertext string in content fields, plaintext elsewhere. Scripts need the key to decrypt (format above).
REST API writes Accepted in plaintext; encrypted on sight by the next unlocked device.
Export (GET /api/v1/export) Ciphertext content, plaintext scheduling fields, and the wrapped key record under encryption, enough to decrypt elsewhere with the passphrase. Importing it into another account keeps the ids (so the binding still matches), but that account needs the same key record to decrypt.
Import Writes plaintext like REST; duplicate detection by name/title cannot match encrypted labels and projects, so an import may create duplicates.
Backups Hold ciphertext and the wrapped key record (plus any plaintext not yet purged).
CalDAV Refused: /dav/ answers 403 for the account and creating an app password answers 409 encryption_enabled. Calendar clients can neither read ciphertext nor write it back, and placeholders would overwrite real titles.
Calendar feed URL Encrypted titles appear as "Encrypted item" in calendar apps; dates, times, estimates and recurrence are served as stored.
Subscribed calendars Events fetched from other calendars are stored on the server unencrypted, like any data the server fetches for the account. The settings panel says so.
MCP (assistants) Encrypted titles, descriptions, project, label, section and custom field names and text values of custom fields read as "Encrypted item" with "encrypted": true; search_tasks never matches them. Dates, priorities and structure are still reported. A task's origin is left out (origin: null). Text arguments of write tools accept only ciphertext envelopes and plain text is refused with encryption_enabled; scheduling, completing, moving, priorities, labels, colours, icons and order still work. On your own computer, ot mcp --decrypt decrypts and encrypts for an assistant (see below). For a cloud connector, a device you opt in can answer for it: the key stays on that device, but the text the connector asks for passes through the server's memory, never stored, logged or audited, capped at 5,000 values an hour by the device.
Issue connections Refused: creating or enabling a GitHub or GitLab connection answers 409 encryption_enabled, because every poll would write issue titles and bodies into the history in plaintext. Turning encryption on stops the account's connections (encrypted_account) and the encryption screen names them; tasks already created stay and are re-written as ciphertext like the rest. See Issue import.
Email to task Creates plaintext Inbox tasks (the mail crossed mail servers in the clear anyway); encrypted on sight; purge removes the plaintext operations.
Webhooks Payloads carry the stored value: ciphertext for encrypted fields.
Reminder pushes An encrypted title is never put in the push payload, even for devices that opted in to content; the notification shows the content-free text.
Notifications (assignment, mention) Use "Encrypted item" instead of a ciphertext title (only relevant if ciphertext ever reaches a shared project).
Revision history, activity Served as stored; the web app decrypts values for display.
Sharing First share of a project refused with 409 encryption_enabled.
Filters Evaluated on the device on plaintext; nothing server-side.
Markdown vault ot vault decrypts on your computer with the key stored by ot encryption unlock and encrypts what it sends, so the server sees ciphertext; the vault's files hold plaintext. It refuses to sync without the key (encryption_enabled).

API#

See api.md: GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/encryption/keys, POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history, encryption and minClientVersion in GET /api/v1/me and GET /api/v1/auth/status.

pages.title: Feedback and support
pages.summary: Where to report a problem or suggest an idea, where to talk to other people who use OpenTodo, how to star it on GitHub, and how to buy the maintainer a coffee.

toc.text: Report a problem or suggest an idea

pages.html:
Feedback and support

OpenTodo is free and open source, made by one person in the open. These are the ways to reach that person and to help the project.

Report a problem or suggest an idea#

Open an issue on GitHub. Say what you did, what you expected and what happened instead, and which version you run (the Help page shows it at the top). Every report is read. Before reporting a problem, the troubleshooting guide may already have the fix.

If you found a security problem, do not open a public issue: follow SECURITY.md in the repository instead.

Talk to other people#

Join the OpenTodo server on Discord to ask a question, show how you use the app or see what other people build. It is the place for conversation; a bug report is still best as an issue, so it is not lost in the chat. Nothing in the app talks to Discord: the link opens it in a new tab only when you choose to.

Help other people find it#

Star OpenTodo on GitHub. Stars are how many people discover open-source projects, so a star is a real help. Telling a friend who pays for a task app works too.

Buy me a coffee#

If OpenTodo saves you a subscription, a coffee helps keep it going. It is entirely optional: OpenTodo has no paid plan and every feature is free.

Settings → About#

Settings → About has all of these in one place: the version your server runs, Help, the documentation and the website, the issue tracker, the Discord server, the source code and the coffee button.

The welcome note#

The first time the owner opens a new server, a short note thanks them and shows these links. It appears once per account; closing it on one device closes it on all of them. People invited to the server do not see it, and neither does the public demo. The owner can open it again from Settings → About → Welcome note.

pages.title: Issue import
pages.summary: Bring the open GitHub and GitLab issues assigned to you into OpenTodo as tasks that complete when the issue closes.
pages.html:
Issue import

Connect a GitHub or GitLab account and the open issues assigned to you become tasks. They show up in Today, Next and your weekly review next to everything else, and they follow the issue: when it closes, the task is completed; when it reopens, the task reopens; when it is renamed, the task is renamed. Nothing is ever written back to GitHub or GitLab.

The server owner turns issue import on under Settings → Integrations → Issues. Until then the panel says so and nothing is fetched.

Connect an account#

  1. Create a personal access token that can read issues:
    • GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens, with Issues: Read-only on the repositories you want (or a classic token with repo for private repositories).
    • GitLab: Preferences → Access tokens, with the read_api scope. On a self-hosted GitLab, use its own address. Give the token an expiry date; you can replace it at any time.
  2. Open Settings → Integrations → Issues and choose Connect issues.
  3. Pick the provider, keep https://github.com or https://gitlab.com or enter your own instance, and paste the token. The token is stored on your server, outside the database and its backups, and is never shown again.
  4. Choose which issues: all issues assigned to you, or only those in up to 20 repositories or projects. You can also require up to 10 labels.
  5. Choose the project the tasks go to (or the Inbox), whether issue labels become OpenTodo labels, and how often to check: every 15 minutes to once a day.

The connection checks the token at once and shows the account it belongs to. Test token checks it again later.

What follows the issue#

  • A new open issue becomes a task with the issue's title, its text as notes and a link back to the issue. Issues that were already closed are not imported.
  • Closing the issue completes the task on the day it closed; reopening it reopens the task; renaming it renames the task.
  • Your own edits win until the issue changes the same thing again. Complete a task yourself and it stays completed; rename it and it keeps your title until the issue is renamed.
  • The notes are written once. Later edits to the issue text are not copied.
  • Nothing is ever deleted. A task you moved to the Trash stays there. An issue that is unassigned from you, or loses a label you filter on, leaves its task as it is.
  • With label mapping on, each issue label becomes the label of the same name, created when missing. Labels you add yourself are kept.

Tasks arrive on your devices with their next sync, like tasks from any other device, and work offline like every task. Pull requests and merge requests are never imported.

The connection card#

Each connection shows its state first: up to date and when, failed with the last error, or stopped with the reason. Then the host and account, the project, the filter and what the last run did. Use Sync now to check at once; checks and syncs are limited to 12 an hour.

A connection stops, and waits for you, when the provider refuses the token, when the host turns out to be on a private network the owner has not allowed, or when no token is stored. A restored backup never contains tokens, so after a restore enter each token again with Edit → Replace token. When the host is down, the wait between checks doubles, up to six hours.

Limits#

  • Up to five connections per account, at most 1,000 new tasks per check; a larger backlog arrives over the next checks.
  • Hosts on your local network work only when the owner allows private network targets (Settings → Integrations → Webhooks).
  • Accounts with end-to-end encryption cannot use issue import: the server would write issue text into the history unencrypted. Turning encryption on stops existing connections; their tasks stay.

Deleting a connection removes its token. The tasks it created stay as ordinary tasks.

pages.t: Other calendars in Day and Week
What AI assistants can and can't do
What the assistant sends and keeps

s: This guide takes you from your first visit to a task added, dated and ticked off. Follow along in the demo or on your own server.

Go to demo.open-todo.app and select Try the demo. You get a private sandbox with sample projects and tasks that only you can see. It is deleted after two hours without activity and every night, so keep personal things on your own server, which takes one container. In the sandbox, one line at the top says so: Details shows the full text, Learn more opens this section and Dismiss hides it until you close the tab.

The first person to open a new OpenTodo server creates the owner account: enter your name, email and a password of at least 10 characters, then select Create owner account. From outside its network, the form also asks for the Setup code from docker logs opentodo (details). After that, sign-up is closed: other people join with an invitation from you (see Sharing and comments).

Open the invitation link, choose a name and password, and you're in. If your server offers single sign-on or passkeys, the sign-in screen shows those buttons too. Once you're signed in, the app is stored on your device. You can keep using it without a connection, and it catches up with the server when you're back online.

The sidebar on the left lists your views and projects; its groups fold with a click on their name. The magnifier by the OpenTodo name searches everything (Ctrl+K); the one by Projects finds a project, label or filter. On a phone, the bottom bar goes to Inbox, Today and Upcoming and opens Search; the menu at the top left opens a drawer with everything else; the round + adds a task from any page with the page's defaults (today's date in Today, the project in a project). Inbox collects tasks that don't belong to a project yet. Today shows what's due today, earlier days first. Upcoming shows the days ahead, grouped by date. Projects are your own lists, like "Home renovation" or "Work". The circle to the left of each task completes it. More on all the views in Views.

Press q (or click the Add a task box at the top of the list), type Call the dentist and press Enter. The task appears straight away. Your first task walks through this step by step, starting with the start guide that opens on your first visit.
Quick add understands everyday words: type Call the dentist tomorrow at 9am and a chip under the box shows the date it understood. See Give it a date.
Click the circle next to the task, or select it and press c. It moves to Completed in the sidebar, where you can reopen it. See Complete it.

Every guide on this site is also in the app: choose Help in your name's menu (sidebar, bottom), or press g then ?. It works offline and matches your server's version. Page headers have a Help action that opens the right section beside what you're doing.
Continue with Your first task: the start guide, the full quick add line and completing. Then install the app on your phone or computer.
You are signed in (see Getting started). This page adds a task, gives it a date and ticks it off.

The first time an account opens the Inbox, a start guide opens over it, one step at a time: add your first task (the guide has its own box, and the task lands in the Inbox behind it), choose how you work (Lists only, Companion or Open Loops first) and light or dark, and install the app. On a phone it is a sheet at the bottom, with the Inbox visible above. Every step has a Skip button, and Skip all, the × button, Esc or a tap outside close it at once. It never comes back on its own on that account, on any of your devices; Open the start guide in the Start guide row of Settings → Account → How you work opens it again over the Inbox. The first step also offers Start with three sample tasks, marked "Sample" and never counted in Statistics. Remove sample tasks, in a sample's panel or the Inbox's menu, trashes them all at once, with Undo. The guide ends on Your first day: add a task, plan today, get OpenTodo on another device. Until all three are done, Start guide under More in the sidebar reopens it; Hide in its menu removes it.

Press q, or click the Add a task box at the top of the list. Type what you need to do, for example Call the dentist. Press Enter. The task appears straight away, and the box stays open for the next one. Where the task goes depends on where you are: in a project it goes into that project, in Today it's due today, and in the Inbox it waits there until you sort it.

You can schedule a task while you type it. Quick add understands everyday words: Call the dentist tomorrow at 9am As you type, small chips appear under the box to show what OpenTodo understood: a date chip for "tomorrow at 9am", and below them the title that will be saved. If a word was picked up by mistake ("May" as in the name, not the month), click the × on its chip and it stays part of the title. The same line can also set a project with #, a label with @, a priority from p1 (highest) to p4, and how long it will take with +, like +15m. The quick add reference lists everything it understands, in six languages. To change the date later, open the task (click it, or select it and press Enter) and use Due in the panel that opens.
When you're done, click the circle next to the task, or select it with j and k and press c. It moves to Completed in the sidebar, where you can reopen it.
OpenTodo runs in the browser, and you can install it like an app on your phone, tablet or computer. It then opens in its own window and works offline. See Installing the app.

Tasks and projects: notes, subtasks, priorities and organising your work. Views: Today, Upcoming, the calendar and views you save yourself. Recurring tasks and reminders: repeat a task every week and get a nudge on time. Keyboard shortcuts: press ? in the app to see them all.

OpenTodo is a web app you can install. Once installed it has its own icon, opens in its own window without browser bars, starts without a connection, and on most platforms can show reminders while it's closed. There is no app store involved: you install it from your server's address, and updates arrive by themselves. On a phone the app is built for one hand: the bar at the bottom switches between Today, Inbox, Upcoming, Search and More (the sidebar), the + button adds a task from anywhere, a task opens as a full-screen page you close with Back or by swiping its header down, a project's board shows one column at a time (swipe sideways, or tap a dot), and the Week calendar is a day-by-day list. Before you start, open your OpenTodo address in the browser and sign in once. Installing needs a secure address (one starting with https://); if your browser offers no install option at all, ask whoever runs your server to set that up.

In Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen and Add. Open OpenTodo from the home screen from now on: on iOS 16.4 and later, push notifications for reminders work only in the installed app. The steps are in Install on your phone.

In Chrome (Edge and Samsung Internet work the same way), open the browser menu and tap Install app or Add to Home screen. Afterwards OpenTodo also appears in Android's share menu. The steps are in Install on your phone.

In Chrome or Edge: Open your OpenTodo address. Click the install icon at the right end of the address bar (a small screen with a down arrow), or open the browser menu and choose Install OpenTodo (in Edge: Apps → Install this site as an app). Confirm with Install. OpenTodo opens in its own window and gets an entry in your Start menu, Dock or app launcher. You can pin it to the taskbar like any other app. In Safari on macOS (Sonoma or later), choose File → Add to Dock. Firefox on the desktop doesn't install web apps. You can still use OpenTodo in a Firefox tab with everything working, including offline use once the page has loaded.
On a tablet or an e-ink display
Open display mode and make it the device's start view. For a shared screen, use a viewer account and kiosk mode; see Set up a shared screen.

The installed app keeps a full copy of your tasks on the device. You can open it on a plane, add and complete tasks, and it syncs when you're online again. The status at the top right tells you where things stand. More in Offline and sync.

When your server is updated, the app fetches the new version in the background and switches to it on its own, usually with one quick reload. If you think you're still on an old version, close the app completely and open it again.

Remove it the way you remove any app on that device: long-press the icon and choose Remove App (iPhone) or Uninstall (Android), or use Uninstall from the app window's menu on a computer. Your tasks stay on your server. Signing out (Settings → Account → Sign out here) clears the copy of your tasks on that device. Changes that haven't reached the server yet are uploaded first when you're online.

Sign in once in the browser first, at your server's https:// address; then add the app to your home screen. The general picture, and the steps for computers, are in Installing the app. Once installed, the round + at the bottom right adds a task, and the menu button at the top left opens a drawer with your projects, labels and views.

Open your OpenTodo address in Safari. Tap the Share button (the square with an arrow pointing up). Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen, then Add. OpenTodo now has an icon on your home screen. Open it from there from now on. On iOS 16.4 and later, push notifications for reminders work only in the installed app, not in a Safari tab; turn them on in Settings → Notifications inside the app. See Notifications. Recent iOS versions also offer Add to Home Screen from the share menu of other browsers. If you don't see it, use Safari.

Open your OpenTodo address in Chrome (Edge and Samsung Internet work the same way). Open the browser menu (⋮). Tap Install app. On some versions it's called Add to Home screen. Chrome sometimes shows an install banner at the bottom of the screen on its own; tapping it does the same thing. After installing, OpenTodo also appears in Android's share menu, so you can send a link or some text from another app straight into a new task. See Capturing pages.

Instead of installing from the browser, you can install the OpenTodo app from Google Play or F-Droid and enter your server's address on its first screen. It works the same and adds reminders without a push service, sharing on phones without Google Play services, home-screen widgets and fingerprint unlock. See The Android app.

An open loop is anything that has your attention and has not been dealt with: a call to return, an idea for the garden, the tax form on the desk. Kept in your head, open loops nag. Open Loops is a calm method for closing them: everything that has your attention gets a home you trust, so your head is free for the work in front of you. It is OpenTodo's own method, inspired by David Allen's GTD and simplified. You can use as much of it as you like: the app works the same without it.

Catch: get whatever is on your mind into the Inbox the moment it appears. Clarify: decide once what each item is and what it needs. Place: give every item one home: a project, a date, Waiting or Someday. Do: work from your next actions, by context, one step at a time. Review: look over the whole system on a rhythm, so you can trust it.

Catch everything. If it is on your mind, it goes in the Inbox. Decide once. Each item gets one decision, the first time you look at it. Do it if it is quicker than filing it. A task of a minute or two is done on the spot, not filed. One next step. Every project always shows its very next action. Hide what is not now. Deferred, waiting and someday items stay out of sight until they matter. Review on a rhythm. A system works only while you trust it, and you trust it by reviewing it. Your loops, your server. Everything stays on your devices and your own server, private by design.

Places: the seven homes a task can have, and the screen for each. Rhythms: the Daily check, the weekly review and the Monthly look. Horizons: next steps, projects and areas. Set up in ten minutes: turn the method on and start. Coming from GTD: the words you know, and where they live here.

The Loop home (g Shift+L, and the start view in Open Loops first) is the method on one screen: a capture field at the top, then the five moves in order, each with its count and a link to its screen. One move is lit, the first in the loop that needs you, and it carries the page's only button: Clarify while the Inbox has items, then Place while a project has no next action, then Review while a rhythm is due, then Do. When the Inbox is empty, every project has a next action and nothing is due, the page says the loop is closed. Below the moves are today's focus with how many of the chosen tasks are done, and the Loop pulse: tasks done this week against last week, how many of the items caught in the last fourteen days have left the Inbox, the age of the oldest Inbox item, and completions per day. The pulse uses the same definitions as Statistics, is computed on your device and sends nothing anywhere. In Settings → You → How you work you choose how much the app shows the method: Lists only (no method words at all), Companion (screens name the move they serve and link here) or Open Loops first (the Loop home opens first and the sidebar is arranged by the Places). See Set up in ten minutes.
Get whatever is on your mind into the Inbox the moment it appears. Do not decide anything yet: catching is fast precisely because it asks for nothing but the words.

Press q anywhere and type. Dates and labels typed in the title are understood (Quick add), but you do not need them. Forward an email to your personal address, share from another app, use the browser extension, or speak (Capture from anywhere). In a terminal, ot add "Call the plumber" (Command line). Everything lands in the Inbox, on every device, offline too.

The method only works if the Inbox holds everything. Small things count: "buy light bulbs" nags as much as "plan the move". When you notice something you have not caught, catch it now. Once a week the review's Mind sweep asks a few questions ("Calls to return", "Promises to someone") to find what slipped through. See Review.
Caught items wait in the Inbox until you Clarify them, ideally once a day.
Decide once what each item is and what it needs. Clarifying turns "stuff" into decisions, so you never read the same item twice wondering what it means.

For each item in the Inbox: Is it something to do? If not, trash it, or keep it as a note in a project. What is the very next step? If it takes a minute or two, do it now and complete it. Otherwise give it a home: that is the next move, Place. If the item is really an outcome with several steps ("Paint the bedroom"), it is a project: create one, and make the first step its first task.

Press g p (or Process in the Inbox header) to see one item at a time with one key per decision: c complete, t today, s schedule, m move to a project, a delegate, y Someday, l add a context label, Delete trash. See Process the Inbox.
Once a day keeps the Inbox small; the Daily check reminds you. An Inbox at zero is a good feeling, but the point is that nothing in it is undecided for long.
Give every item one home. When each task lives in exactly one place, you know where to look, and anything not in front of you can safely be ignored.

If the item Place it How belongs to an outcome with several steps a project m in triage, or the project chip must happen on a day Scheduled give it a due date (s in triage) cannot start before a day Later a start date (Shift+N in a list) waits for someone or another task Waiting assign it (a) or set Blocked by (b) is a maybe Someday y in triage, n in a list The full list, with the screen for each, is in Places.

Waiting (g Shift+W) lists everything assigned to someone else, grouped by person, and everything blocked by another open task. Look at it in the weekly review and follow up where something has stalled.
Someday and deferred tasks stay out of Today, Upcoming and Next until they matter. You lose nothing: Someday has its own view and the review shows it once a week.
Work from your next actions, by context, one step at a time. Choosing what to do is easy when every option is small, concrete and possible right now.

Next (g Shift+N) shows the next action of every project: its first task, in the project's order, that you can do now. A task is left out while it waits for another open task, is assigned to someone else, is deferred to a later start date or parked in Someday. Complete one with c and the project's following step takes its place.

A context is any label whose name starts with @: @home, @computer, @calls, @errands. Next groups its tasks by context, so at the computer you look at @computer and in town at @errands. Tasks without one are under Anywhere. Add a context in triage with l, or in a list with Shift+L.
Due dates still matter: Today shows what must happen today. The Daily check lets you pick up to three tasks as today's focus, shown on the Loop home.
A project without a next action is stuck. The weekly review's project walk finds them and asks for the next step. See Review.
Look over the whole system on a rhythm, so you can trust it. Trust is what lets you stop holding things in your head: you know that everything is caught, placed and will come back when it matters.

Daily check (5 minutes, g Shift+R): the Inbox, what is open from earlier, today's focus. Weekly review (30 minutes, g r): the whole system, in three phases. Monthly look (20 minutes): your areas, old Someday items and the four-week trend. Details are in Rhythms and in Weekly review.

Get clear: empty the Inbox, then a Mind sweep to catch what is still on your mind. Get current: what you completed and what is still open from earlier, what is Waiting, every project one at a time, and the week ahead. Get creative: skim Someday and promote what you now want to do. The project walk is the heart of it: one card per project, with its outcome, its next action and whether it has stalled. Press r when it looks right, q to add a next step.

The sidebar's Review entry shows Due when a review is late. In Open Loops first, the app offers the Daily check once a day. A skipped review is not a failure: the next one simply takes a little longer.

Every task lives in exactly one Place. The Place says what the task is waiting for: a decision, a moment, a person, or just you. Place Means Where you see it Inbox Caught, not yet decided. Inbox (g i), triage (g p) Next The next action of every project, by context. Next (g Shift+N) Waiting Waits for someone or something else first. Waiting (g Shift+W) Scheduled Has a day: Today and Upcoming. Today (g t), Upcoming (g u) Later Not before its start date. The Later group of its project Someday Maybe one day: parked without a date. Someday (g o) Projects Outcomes that take more than one step. The sidebar's Projects
How a task moves between Places

Clarifying moves a task out of the Inbox. A task in a project is in Next when it is the project's first actionable task. The others wait their turn in the project's own list. Assigning a task to someone else, or making it wait for another open task with Blocked by, puts it in Waiting. Completing the blocker brings it back. A due date puts it in Scheduled; a future start date in Later until that day comes. Someday keeps it out of the way until a review promotes it.

Next (g Shift+N) lists the next action of every project you can edit, grouped by context (labels starting with @; a task with two contexts is under both, one without under Anywhere). Waiting (g Shift+W) lists open tasks assigned to someone else, under each person, then the ones blocked by another open task, each naming what it waits for. Both are under More in the sidebar, can be pinned there in Settings → Appearance, and can be the view a device opens on. The list keys work as in any list, offline too.

A project is without a next action when none of its open tasks can be done now, waits for someone or another task, or starts later. A project is stalled when it has open tasks, the oldest created more than three weeks ago, and nothing in it was completed in the last three weeks. The weekly review and the Loop home show both, and the weekly email digest lists the first.
Reviews keep the system trustworthy. Open Loops has three, each short enough to actually do, and an optional step to end the day.

Five minutes, usually in the morning: open it from the Review screen's menu, the Loop home or g Shift+R. Process the Inbox if anything is in it. Look at what is still open from Earlier: complete it, or give it a new date. Pick today's focus: press f on up to three of today's tasks. They are shown on the Loop home on every device, with how many of them are done. To work through them one at a time with a timer, press g Shift+F for Focus. The check opens with the same briefing as Today: what is late, a full day and replies waiting. Done for today records the check. In Open Loops first, the app offers it once a day. If you closed yesterday with a line for tomorrow, it is shown right under the briefing. A day here ends at your day start: with 04:00, a check done or a focus picked at 00:30 still belongs to the evening before, and the focus stays until 04:00.

A few minutes in the evening: open it from the end of the Today list, the Review move on the Loop home, the command palette or g Shift+D. It has three steps; [ and ] move between them. The day you close is the day you opened it on: start at 23:59 and finish after midnight, and it is still that evening that gets closed. How the day went: one sentence with how many tasks were planned (what Today lists plus what you finished), how many you completed (the same count as Statistics) and how much of today's focus is done. Carry over: the unfinished tasks of Today, one at a time, each with its whole title. Choose Tomorrow (the default), Pick a day, Someday, Keep in Today or Done already with t, p, y, h or d, and the next task comes up. The list below the card shows your decisions; select a line to change one. Nothing changes until you move on to the next step; then every task moves at once and Undo (or Ctrl+Z) puts them all back in one step. A note for tomorrow morning: an optional line; the step shows how tomorrow's Daily check will start with it. Close the day records the close and ends on Done for today: the time, the day's figures ("5 done, 3 moved to tomorrow, 1 kept") and your line for tomorrow. No streak, no score. Back to Today (or Esc) returns to Today, which then ends with Day closed and the time; so does the Review entry in the sidebar. You can close again later the same day. Close the day is never due: nothing reminds you of it. Changed your mind? Until your day ends, Reo

Thirty minutes, on a day that suits you (g r). Seven steps in three phases: Get clear (Inbox, Mind sweep), Get current (Look back, Waiting, Projects, Look ahead) and Get creative (Someday). See Weekly review.

Twenty minutes, once a month, from the Review screen's menu or the Loop home: Areas: each top-level project that holds sub-projects, with how many of them need attention. Old someday: Someday tasks older than three months. Promote, complete or trash them. Trend: what you completed, created and let slip over the last four weeks.

Rhythm Due when Marker shown in Weekly review last finished more than 7 days ago every mode Monthly look last finished more than 30 days ago Companion and Open Loops first Daily check not done today Open Loops first Close the day never none; the Review entry says Day closed Each finish syncs to all your devices: a Daily check on the phone clears the marker on the laptop.

You can look at your work from three heights. Each answers a different question, and each has its rhythm. Horizon Question In OpenTodo Looked at in Next step What do I do now? a task, the project's next action Next, the Daily check Project What am I trying to finish? a project, its note holds the outcome the weekly review's project walk Area What do I keep up? a top-level project that holds sub-projects the Monthly look

Open a project's note (Shift+P) and write in one sentence what done looks like: "The car fits in the garage". The weekly review shows it on the project's card, so you can tell whether the next step still leads there.
Areas are projects that hold projects

Make "Home", "Work" or "Health" a project and nest the projects that belong to it (Projects and sub-projects). An area itself rarely has tasks; it is finished never, but its projects are. The Monthly look lists each area with how many of its projects need attention.

In Settings → You → How you work (or in the start guide on your first visit): Lists only: OpenTodo as a plain task app, no method words. Companion: your sidebar stays as it is; screens name the move they serve and link to the method. Open Loops first: the Loop home opens first, the sidebar shows Loop home, Inbox, Today, Next, Waiting and Review, and the app offers a Daily check each day. The choice syncs to all your devices and changes no task. You can switch any time. Choosing Open Loops first also offers to open on the Loop home on this device.
When you choose Companion or Open Loops first and have no context yet, the app offers @home, @computer, @calls and @errands. Accept, or make your own: any label starting with @ is a context.
Press q and catch everything on your mind, one line each, for five minutes. Do not sort anything yet.
Press g p and decide each item: do it, schedule it, move it to a project, delegate it, park it in Someday or trash it. See Clarify.
Open the weekly review (g r), go to Projects, and give each project a next step with q. From now on, work from Next and come back to the review once a week.

Open Loops is inspired by GTD (Getting Things Done) and keeps its core: capture everything, clarify once, organise by what the next step needs, review weekly. It is not affiliated with David Allen or the David Allen Company, and it is simpler in places: three horizons instead of six, and contexts as ordinary labels. GTD Open Loops In OpenTodo Capture, collect Catch quick add q, email, share, voice, CLI In-basket Inbox the Inbox Process, clarify Clarify triage g p Two-minute rule Do it if it is quicker than filing it c in triage Organize Place project, date, start date, Waiting, Someday Next actions Next the Next view g Shift+N Contexts Contexts labels starting with @ Waiting for Waiting assigned to someone else, or Blocked by Someday/maybe Someday y in triage, the Someday view Tickler file Later a start date Calendar (hard landscape) Scheduled due dates, Today, Upcoming, the calendar Projects list Projects projects, and the review's project walk Project support material the project note Shift+P Areas of focus Area a project that holds projects Weekly review Weekly review g r Trigger list Mind sweep the review's second step Horizons 3-5 (goals, vision, purpose) not modelled write them in a project note if you like Your existing @context labels become contexts automatically. If you used a "Waiting" label or a far-future date for someday items, switch to assigning or Blocked by, and to Someday: they keep those tasks out of the planning views.
Your projects, sections, subtasks, labels, priorities, due dates and recurring tasks come with you. It takes a few minutes, and you can undo the whole import with one click.

Use a backup: it holds every project and keeps their names. In Todoist, open its settings and find Backups. Download the latest backup. It is a ZIP file such as Todoist_backup_2026-09-19.zip. A single project can also be exported as CSV from the project's menu, but a lone CSV file does not say which project it was, so its tasks go to the project you choose when importing.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the ZIP file. The preview shows Todoist backup (ZIP) and lists every project, section and task. Check the warnings, choose a time zone if your tasks have times, and select Import. Projects that were boards in Todoist open as boards on this device. Your other devices receive everything on their next sync.

Projects, sections and subtasks (by their indent), in the same order. Priorities: Todoist's red flag is p1, as you saw it. Labels written in tasks (@errands), removed from the title. Descriptions and estimates (task durations in minutes). Due dates and times, in the language you used Todoist in (English, German, French, Italian, Spanish or Portuguese). Dates without a year take the year of the backup. Recurring dates such as every monday or jeden Montag, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Reminders with a time or an offset. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Comments are added to the task's description under "Comments", because their authors cannot be kept. Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description; OpenTodo has no deadline field yet. Assignees are dropped; invite people and share the project instead. Dates or rules OpenTodo cannot read leave the task without a due date, with a warning that quotes them. Changed your mind? Undo the import from the list of past imports.
Things 3 has no export button, but OpenTodo can read a copy of its database directly. Your areas, projects, headings, to-dos, checklists, tags and notes come with you.

On a Mac, as Cultured Code's support article "Accessing the Things database" describes: Quit Things. The copy must be made while the app is closed. In Finder, choose Go → Go to Folder and open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/. Open the ThingsData-… folder and copy (do not move) Things Database.thingsdatabase to your Desktop. Right-click the copy, choose Show Package Contents, and find main.sqlite. Alternatively, compress the whole folder into a ZIP. On iPhone or iPad, the same article lists a diagnostics code (Settings → General → Diagnostics → Enter Code) that sends Things Database.aar. Save it to Files, tap it to unpack it into Things Database.thingsdatabase, and use the main.sqlite inside.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose main.sqlite (or the ZIP). The preview shows Things 3 database. Check the warnings and select Import. The file is read on your server from a private copy, read-only, and deleted right after the preview or import.

Areas become parent projects; projects stay inside them. Headings become sections; to-dos keep their heading. Checklist items become subtasks, completed ones included. Tags become labels (nested tags as parent/child). Notes, the start date ("When") as the due date, and reminder times. Repeating to-dos, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Completed and canceled items (canceled ones get the label canceled). The full mapping is in Import formats.
Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description. Someday and This Evening are not imported as such; the to-dos arrive with a warning. Trashed items are skipped.
Your folders, lists, board columns, checklists, tags, priorities, due dates, reminders and repeating tasks come with you.
TickTick creates a backup as one CSV file from its settings (look for Backup). Download it; it is named like TickTick-backup-2026-10-14.csv.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the CSV file. The preview shows TickTick backup (CSV). Check the warnings and select Import. Lists you used as a board (kanban) open as boards on this device.

Folders become parent projects; lists become projects inside them. Board columns become sections. Checklists become a task with one subtask per item; checked items are completed. Subtasks, tags, descriptions and priorities (high, medium, low, none become p1–p4). Due dates and times as you saw them, all-day tasks as dates. Reminders and repeat rules, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Completed tasks; abandoned ones are completed with the label canceled. The full mapping is in Import formats.
Attachments, habits, focus records and comments are not part of the CSV backup. Repeat rules OpenTodo cannot express are dropped with a warning; the task is kept.
OpenTodo is a good fit for small teams and personal work that want speed without process. Your issues come with their projects, statuses, priorities, labels, due dates and sub-issues.
Linear exports a workspace's issues as one CSV file from its workspace settings (look for Import / Export).

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the CSV file. The preview shows Linear export (CSV). Check the warnings and select Import. Each project opens as a board on this device, with one column per status.

Projects (or teams, for issues without a project). Statuses become sections, in the order they appear, so the board shows the same columns. Titles, and descriptions that start with the issue identifier (ENG-123), so you can still find it. Priorities (Urgent, High, Medium, Low and No priority become p1–p4), labels and due dates. Sub-issues as subtasks. Completed issues; canceled ones are completed with the label canceled. Issues assigned to you stay assigned to you. Estimates become a number field "Estimate" on the project (see Custom fields). The full mapping is in Import formats.

Blocked by relations between issues in the export become Blocked by on the tasks. Cycles, milestones, initiatives, SLAs and the other issue relations (related, duplicate) are dropped with a warning. Issues assigned to other people arrive unassigned; share the project and assign them again. Comments and attachments are not part of the CSV export.
Your lists, subtasks, notes, due dates, completed tasks and links come with you.

Open takeout.google.com and select Deselect all. Tick only Tasks, then Next step and Create export. When Google's email arrives, download the archive and unpack it. Inside Takeout/Tasks/ is Tasks.json.
Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose Tasks.json. The preview shows Google Tasks (Takeout JSON). Check the warnings and select Import.

Each list becomes a project. My Tasks, your default list, goes to your Inbox, or to the project you choose as the target. Titles, notes (as the description) and subtasks. Due dates, exactly as Google Tasks shows them. The file has no times, so none are set. Completed tasks, with the time they were completed. Links attached to a task (for example the email it came from) become link attachments. Each task remembers it came from Google Tasks (origin: google-tasks). The full mapping is in Import formats.

Google Tasks has no priorities, labels or reminders, so imported tasks have none. Repeating tasks: Takeout writes only the next occurrence, without the rule. Set the repeat rule again on the task. Deleted tasks are in the file but skipped; the preview says how many.
Each board becomes a project that opens as a board, with the same lists as columns.

Open the board and its menu (…). Choose Print, export and share → Export as JSON. Your browser saves or shows the file; save it as board.json. Repeat for each board. You can put several board files in one ZIP and import them together.
Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the JSON file (or the ZIP). The preview shows Trello board (JSON). Check the warnings and select Import.

Lists become sections, in board order; archived lists come too, and their cards arrive completed. Card titles and descriptions, labels (named, or by colour when unnamed), due dates with their time, start dates. Cards marked complete or archived arrive completed. Checklists: each item becomes a subtask; checked items are completed. Comments are added to the description under "Comments", with who wrote them and when. Links attached to cards become link attachments. Cards you are a member of stay assigned to you. Custom fields (number, text, checkbox, date and dropdown) become custom fields of the project. Each task remembers its card, with a link back to Trello. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Uploaded files are not part of Trello's export; links to them are dropped with a warning. Download the files you need first. Other members are dropped with a warning; share the project and assign them again. Power-Up data other than custom fields, stickers, cover images and votes.
Each project comes with its sections, subtasks, tags, dates, priorities, dependencies and custom fields.

Open the project and its menu (the arrow next to the project name). Choose Export/Print → CSV. Repeat for each project. The file name becomes the project name in OpenTodo, so rename the file if you like. Several project files in one ZIP import together.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the CSV file (or the ZIP). The preview shows Asana project (CSV). Check the warnings and select Import. When every task has a section (a board project in Asana), the project opens as a board on this device.

Sections, in the order they appear. Task names, notes (as the description) and subtasks. Tags as labels; High, Medium and Low priority as p1, p2 and p3. Due dates (with the time when there is one), start dates, completion and creation times. Dependencies: a task blocked by another task in the same file becomes Blocked by it. Tasks assigned to you stay assigned to you. Every other column becomes a custom field of the project: numbers become a number field, Yes/No a checkbox, dates a date field, a column with ten different values or fewer a choice, and anything else text. The preview shows how many fields will be created. Each task remembers its Asana task id (origin: asana). The full mapping is in Import formats.

Tasks assigned to other people arrive unassigned, and collaborators are dropped; share the project and assign them again. A task that is in several projects is imported once, into this project. Comments, attachments, likes and approvals are not in Asana's CSV. A field's type cannot be changed later; if a column became the wrong type, delete the field and create it again.
Microsoft To Do has no export button, but Microsoft Graph, the service behind it, lets you read your own lists. A short PowerShell script saves them to one file that OpenTodo imports.

You need PowerShell 7 (Windows, macOS or Linux). Run these lines in it: Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Authentication -Scope CurrentUser Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Tasks.Read" function Get-All($uri) { $items = @() while ($uri) { $page = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri $items += $page.value $uri = $page.'@odata.nextLink' } return ,$items } $lists = Get-All "v1.0/me/todo/lists" foreach ($list in $lists) { $list["tasks"] = Get-All "v1.0/me/todo/lists/$($list.id)/tasks?`$expand=checklistItems,linkedResources" } ConvertTo-Json -InputObject @($lists) -Depth 10 | Set-Content -Encoding utf8 todo.json Disconnect-MgGraph Connect-MgGraph opens a Microsoft sign-in page and asks you to allow reading your tasks; nothing is changed in To Do. The script writes todo.json in the current folder. No PowerShell? In Graph Explorer, sign in and run GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/todo/lists to see your lists and their ids. For each list, run GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/todo/lists/{id}/tasks?$expand=checklistItems,linkedResources and paste the value array of the response into a text file shaped like [{"displayName": "Groceries", "tasks": [ … ]}], one object per list.
Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose todo.json. The preview shows Microsoft To Do (JSON from the PowerShell script). Check the warnings and select Import.

Each list becomes a project. Tasks, your default list, goes to your Inbox or the target project; flagged emails go to a project "Flagged emails". Titles, notes (as plain text) and steps, as subtasks. Important tasks become p1; categories become labels. Due and start dates as To Do shows them, reminders at their moment, completed tasks with their time. Repeats every few days, on weekdays, on a day of the month or once a year. Linked resources (such as the email a task came from) become link attachments. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Repeats like "the second Thursday of the month", and repeat end dates, are dropped with a warning. File attachments are not in the file; they are dropped with a warning. Shared lists come as your own projects; share them again.
Apple Reminders has no export button. There are two ways over.

If you want to keep using the Reminders app on your iPhone or Mac, connect it to OpenTodo with CalDAV: your OpenTodo projects appear as Reminders lists, and what you add on either side shows up on the other. Then move reminders into those lists. Nothing needs to be exported.
Or: save your reminders with a Shortcut

To bring everything in at once, build this Shortcut in the Shortcuts app (iPhone, iPad or Mac): Find Reminders where Is Completed is any value (leave the other filters empty). Repeat with Each item in Reminders. Inside the repeat: Format Date of Repeat Item → Due Date, format ISO 8601, Include ISO 8601 Time on. Do the same for Creation Date and Completion Date. Dictionary with these keys (all Text unless stated): identifier = the formatted creation date followed by Title; parent = Parent Reminder → Creation Date (formatted) followed by Parent Reminder → Title; list = List; title = Title; notes = Notes; dueDate, creationDate, completionDate = the formatted dates; isCompleted (Boolean) = Is Completed; priority = Priority; flagged (Boolean) = Is Flagged; tags = Tags; url = URL. After the repeat: Combine Repeat Results with ,, then Text with [, the combined text, and ]. Save File with that text, named reminders.json (turn off Ask Where to Save to put it in your Shortcuts folder in Files or iCloud Drive). Run it once. The file holds every reminder of every list.
Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose reminders.json. The preview shows Apple Reminders (JSON from the Shortcut). Check the warnings and select Import.

Each list becomes a project. Reminders, the default list, goes to your Inbox or the target project. Titles, notes (as the description) and subtasks. Priority High, Medium and Low become p1, p2 and p3. Flagged reminders get the label flagged; tags become labels. The URL becomes a link attachment. Due dates, with the time when the reminder has one; completed reminders with their time. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Shortcuts does not give access to repeat rules, early reminders, location alerts, images or the sections of a list, so those are not in the file. Set repeat rules and reminders again in OpenTodo where you need them.
Any.do has no export button, but it sends you a copy of your data when you ask for it.

In Any.do, open Settings → Privacy (on the web: your profile, then Privacy), and choose Request my data (or write to Any.do's support asking for a copy of your personal data). Any.do emails you a download, usually within a few days. Unpack it if it is a ZIP; the tasks are in a .json file. Any.do does not document this file, and its format may change without notice. If the import does not recognise your file, tell us and attach a copy with the personal text removed.
Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the JSON file. The preview shows Any.do (JSON from a data request). Check the warnings and select Import.

Each list becomes a project. Your default list (usually Personal) goes to your Inbox or the target project. Titles, notes (as the description) and subtasks. High priority becomes p1. Due dates, with their time unless the task was due "any time" that day. Daily, weekly, monthly and yearly repeats. Tags as labels, and the reminder as a reminder at the same moment. Completed tasks, with their time. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Deleted tasks are in the file but skipped; the preview says how many. Shared lists: other members are dropped with a warning; share the project again. Attachments are not in the file. The "My Day" plan is dropped; use Today instead.
A task is one thing to do. A project is a list of tasks that belong together. Each section below links to its full guide.

Press q anywhere in a task list, type, and press Enter. One line can also set the date, project, label, priority and estimate: Order new taps friday #Home @errand p2 +20m New tasks without a project land in the Inbox. See Work from the list and the quick add reference.
Click a title (or press F2) to edit it in place; click the rest of the row, or press Enter, to open its panel. Changes save as you make them. See The task panel and Notes, subtasks and dependencies.
Select a task and press a key: c completes it, 1 to 4 set the priority, L adds labels. The full table is in Work from the list.
A due date is a calendar day; a time is the clock time where you are. Type them in words like tomorrow or 3pm, pick them from a calendar, or fix a time to a time zone. See Dates and times.
A deadline is the day a task must be finished by, separate from the day you plan to work on it; the task's row shows a countdown. See Deadlines and start dates.
Start defers a task until a date or parks it in Someday, and This Evening puts a task due today in its own group. See Deadlines and start dates.
Blocked by makes a task wait for other tasks: it is dimmed with a lock until they are done. See Notes, subtasks and dependencies.
Tick tasks with x or their checkboxes, then Actions (or .) changes all of them in one go, with Undo afterwards. See Change several tasks at once.
Click the circle next to a task, or press c; reopen it from Completed in the sidebar. Deleting a task moves it and its subtasks to the Trash. See Work from the list and Trash and history.
Open the task and type in Add subtask, or select it in the list and press a. Subtasks appear indented under their parent, which shows your progress, like 1/3. See Notes, subtasks and dependencies.

Create a project with + next to Projects in the sidebar; pick a parent to make it a sub-project. The Project menu colours, moves, renames, duplicates, archives or deletes it. See Projects and sub-projects and Sections and boards.
Every project can carry a note above its tasks; Shift+P edits it. See Project notes.
In the Inbox and in projects, you decide the order: drag a task, or select it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. See Work from the list.

Keep the Inbox as a landing spot: capture fast, then sort into projects once a day. Use priorities sparingly. If everything is P1, nothing is. A task with an estimate shows it on the row, like 30m, which makes it easy to spot quick wins. The Filter action in a list's header can show only tasks of 15 minutes or less (Quick wins).

Select a task with j / k and press Enter to open its page; a click edits the title in place, and its arrow (or Shift+Enter) opens the page. Every change is saved as you make it; there is no Save button.

The top of the page says where the task lives (its project, and its parent for a subtask) and where it sits in the list you opened it from, such as 2 / 5. Press j or k (or the ↓ and ↑ buttons) for the next or previous task of that list, and Esc or × to go back to the list, with the task selected where it was. On a phone, Back in the bar does the same. Opened from a reminder, a notification or the search bar, the page goes back to the task's own list. From 1024 px wide, the Inbox and Process the Inbox keep the task beside the list or the card instead: in the Inbox, Enter then opens its page.

The ⋯ menu holds Copy link, Attach, Delete and the less frequent actions. Under the breadcrumb are the task's checkbox and its title (edit it in place), then Notes: one quiet line until you click it, then an editor (see Write notes).

Beside the notes (under them on a narrow screen) are the task's facts, in the words the list uses: Schedule: Do (the date and time, and evening), Start, Deadline, Reminder and Repeat. Details: Priority, Estimate, Assignee, Blocked by, Blocks (when something waits for this task) and Location. Labels. Project: the project, the section, the parent task and where the task came from. On a phone the facts are one card of rows: those with a value, Do and Deadline, then More properties for the rest. A fact without a value reads as what sets it, such as Set a deadline or Add a place. Click a fact, or Tab to it and press Enter, to open its editor next to it; click it again or press Esc to close it. Every editor has Clear and Done. The When editor shows one part at a time (Do on, Start, Deadline, Repeat, Reminders), starting with the one you clicked; This Evening and the time zone are in Do on. Press 1 to 4 anywhere on the page for the priority. See Dates and times, Deadlines and start dates and Assign tasks.
If you are a viewer of a shared project, the lines read as text and can't be changed, and the checkbox and Delete are disabled. You can still comment.
Close the panel with Esc or the × at the top. On a phone the panel covers the list; close it to go back.
A due date is just a calendar day, and a time is the time on the clock where you are. A task due Tuesday at 09:00 shows Tuesday at 09:00 on every device, even when you travel.
Type or pick a date and time

Click the date on a task's When line. Today, Tomorrow, This weekend, Next week or No date sets it in one click. Or type in the field, which previews what it understood ("→ Fri 23 Oct"), or pick a day in the calendar. Add time suggests 09:00, 13:00 and 18:00. Formats follow Settings → General → Date and time: Date: a date in your format (14/10 or 10/14, with or without a year), an ISO date (2026-10-14), or a word: today, tomorrow, a weekday such as fri, next week or 3 Nov. A date without a year that has already passed this year means next year. Press Enter or leave the field to save it. If the date doesn't exist (31/02), the field says so and the task keeps its date. Calendar: always shown under the field, with weeks starting on your first day of the week. Arrow keys move by day and week, Page Up and Page Down by month, Home and End to the start and end of the week, Enter picks the day and Esc closes it. Time: 15, 1530, 15:30, 3pm, 3:30 pm or noon, whichever clock you use. ↓ in the field shows times in 15-minute steps to pick from. Clear at the bottom removes the due date; Remove time keeps only the day.

For the app, a new day begins at midnight. If you often work past midnight, set Settings → General → Date and time → My day starts at to a time up to 06:00. With 04:00, at 01:30 on Thursday it is still Wednesday: Today still lists Wednesday's tasks, nothing moves to Earlier, and Thursday's tasks are Tomorrow in Upcoming. A task you complete now counts for Wednesday in Completed, Statistics and the Loop pulse, and a habit keeps its streak. today, tomorrow and overdue in quick add and filters mean the day you are living in. At 04:00 the views move on by themselves. Nothing stored changes: due dates stay calendar days, and reminders and times fixed to a zone still happen at their real moment.
Fix a time to a time zone

Once a due has a time, a line under it says how the time is meant: Floating time (the same clock time wherever you are) or Fixed to New York (one moment worldwide). Choose Change to: Fix to my zone: tie the time to your current time zone, for things that happen at a fixed moment. Press z with the panel open to do the same, and again to release it. Fix to another time zone: search any city or zone, for example a call at 15:00 in New York. The panel shows how that reads for you ("15:00 in New York = 21:00 your time (Berlin)") before you choose Fix to New York. Your own zone is listed first, then the zones you used recently. Make floating: release a fixed time to the clock time you currently see. Devices elsewhere show a fixed time converted to their local time, with the original time and city as a hint. Without a time the button is off: a due date alone always stays floating.
The due date is when you plan to work on a task. Two more dates say when it must be done and when it becomes relevant.

A deadline is the day a task must be finished by, and the two are separate: you can plan a report for Tuesday that is due to your boss on Friday. Moving or clearing the due date never changes the deadline, and you may even plan a task after its deadline; the countdown then turns red. A task with a deadline shows a countdown on its row, next to an hourglass: 3d for three days to go, Today on the day, and 2d over once it has passed. It turns amber in the last week and red on the day and after. Hover it to see the full date. The countdown follows the calendar on your device, so it moves on at midnight even offline. Deadlines also bring tasks into Today and Upcoming, and you can add a reminder before the deadline (see Reminders). In the panel, Deadline in the When editor offers End of week, End of month and In 2 weeks, a field and a calendar. From the list, d sets the deadline (fri, 2026-11-06).

Not every task is for now. Start, in the panel's When editor, says when a task becomes relevant: No start date, the default: the task is in your lists as usual. Clear in the editor brings a task back to it. A start date defers the task until that day: it disappears from Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts, and its project lists it at the end under Later, with a Starts 21 Oct chip. A deferred task without a project leaves the Inbox; without a due date it is listed in Upcoming on its start day (where planned tasks go). On its start day it appears in Today with a Started chip and stays there until you deal with it. The start date can't be after the due date. Someday parks the task: it moves to the Someday view and its project's Later group, and its due date is cleared (a repeating task stops repeating). Giving it a due date or a start date brings it back. A due date or a deadline that has come always shows the task in Today, even if it is deferred or parked. This Evening (the Evening switch in the same editor, or Add › This Evening) moves a task due today into its own group below the day's tasks in Today, and shows a moon on its row elsewhere. It says nothing about the time of day. From the list: n parks a task or brings it back, Shift+N asks for its start date, and Shift+E toggles This Evening.

In the task panel, Notes sits under the title. Below the property lines are the Subtasks as a checklist, with an Add subtask… line under them, the attachments once there is one (attach from Add or the ⋯ menu, or paste or drop files on the panel, see Attachments), and the Comments, Activity and History tabs. The comment box rests as one line at the bottom of the panel while Comments is shown and opens when you click it or press Shift+C. Activity starts with when the task was created and completed.

The notes field formats as you type: - starts a bullet list, [ ] a checklist, # a heading, and / opens a menu with tables, quotes, code, images and more (see Format notes and comments). If two of your devices edit the same note at the same time, both sets of changes are kept.

Big tasks are easier as a few small steps. To add one: open the task and type in Add subtask, or select the task in the list and press a. Subtasks appear indented under their parent, and the parent shows your progress, like 1/3. You can nest subtasks inside subtasks. To turn an existing task into a subtask, select it and press Tab: it moves under the task above it. Shift+Tab moves it back out. You can also pick a Parent task in the panel. Use ← and → to fold and unfold a parent's subtasks. Completing a parent completes all its open subtasks too. When you tick off the last open subtask, OpenTodo asks whether to complete the parent as well; press Enter for yes.

Some tasks can't start until another is done: you can't book flights before the dates are confirmed. Open the task, choose Add › Blocked by (or select it in a list and press b) and pick the tasks it waits for. The list offers open tasks you can link: the task itself, tasks that already wait for it and tasks shared differently are left out, so you can't make two tasks wait for each other. While at least one of those tasks is open, the task is blocked: its row is dimmed and shows a lock with the number it's waiting for, on boards too, and in Today it moves to a folded Blocked group at the end. As soon as the last one is completed (or deleted), the task is ready again, on every device. You can still open, edit and complete a blocked task; completing it doesn't touch the tasks it waited for. A repeating task keeps blocking until its series ends, and Blocked by says "repeats" next to it. "blocks 2" on the Who line counts the open tasks waiting for this one; click it to see them and select one to open it. In a shared project, blockers are tasks of the same project, and the person a blocked task is assigned to gets a notification when it's ready to start. Filter for blocked or unblocked to list them (see Labels and filters).
Notes and comments use the same editor, so everything here works in both (except Make subtask, which only notes have). Everything also works offline.

Start a line with - for a bullet list, 1. for a numbered list, [ ] for a checklist, # for a heading or > for a quote. Type ``` and press Enter for a code block: inside it, what you type stays exactly as typed. Select text and press Ctrl+B for bold, Ctrl+I for italic or Ctrl+K for a link (⌘ on a Mac).

Type / at the start of a line or after a space to open a menu of everything the editor can insert: headings, lists, a table, a quote, a code block, a link, an image, today's date and a mention. Keep typing to filter it (/tab finds the table), move with ↑ and ↓, press Enter to insert, or Esc to keep what you typed. On a phone, a row of buttons (bold, italic, link, lists and More) sits above the text while you write. In the comment box on a computer, the Formatting button shows the same row, and the @ button starts a mention.

Choose Table from the / menu. Tab moves to the next cell and adds a row at the end; Shift+Tab goes back. Right-click a cell, or type / in it, to add or delete rows and columns or turn the header row off. A table holds up to 10 columns and 100 rows of plain text per cell, and scrolls sideways on a narrow screen.

Paste a screenshot, drop a picture, or choose Image from the / menu. The file becomes one of the task's attachments and shows where you put it. Select it to type a description for screen readers. A picture whose file was removed shows Removed image. Pasting a web address of a picture adds a link, never the picture: OpenTodo loads nothing from other sites. With end-to-end encryption the picture is decrypted on your device; on a locked device it reads Encrypted image.

In a shared project, type @ and a few letters of a member's name and pick them. Mentioning someone in a task's notes sends them a notification "mentioned you in the notes of …" once; later edits don't notify them again. After the people, the list offers the groups of the workspace, shown with a group icon: @Adults notifies everyone in the group who can see the task.
Make a checklist line a subtask

In a task's notes, put the caret on a checklist line and press Ctrl+Shift+Enter (or choose Make subtask from the / menu). The line becomes a link to a new subtask with its text; a ticked line makes a completed subtask. The link always shows the subtask's current title. Ctrl+Z right after takes both back.

Notes and comments are stored as Markdown text too, so the API, the command line, exports and email show them as | pipe | tables |, > quotes, fenced code, ![name](attachment:…) for pictures and @name for mentions.
Most of the day happens in a list: the Inbox, Today or a project. You can do a lot there without opening a task.

Press q anywhere in a task list, type, and press Enter. The box stays focused so you can add several in a row. You can fill in details as you type: Order new taps friday #Home @errand p2 +20m This creates "Order new taps", due Friday, in Home, with the label errand, priority 2 and a 20-minute estimate. Chips under the box show what was understood. The quick add reference has every word and symbol it knows. New tasks without a project land in the Inbox. Tasks added inside a project go into that project, and tasks added in Today are due today.

Click a task's circle or press c. On a phone, swipe right to complete, left to schedule; hold to select. Completed tasks move to Completed, where you can reopen them. Deleting a task (the Delete button in the panel, or Delete in the list) moves it to the Trash, along with its subtasks. You can restore it from there. See Trash and history. Completing, deleting, moving, rescheduling or parking a task shows a toast with Undo for a few seconds (Ctrl+Z outside a text field also undoes).

A row leaves out what the view already says: no "Today" in Today, no date under an Upcoming day, no project inside that project. Times stand in a column before the titles (a deadline's countdown when there is no time). Dates are grey for later, darker for tomorrow, the accent for today and red when past; only P1 and P2 colour the circle. Labels are small chips, two at most and "+2". The project and counts end the row, faint until hovered. With a mouse on a wide screen, hovering a row shows Schedule, Priority and More at its end; Tab reaches them. On a touch screen, long-press a row to select it, or swipe it.

You don't have to open a task to change it. Select it and press: Key Does 1 to 4 Set the priority c Complete or reopen L Add labels (type to search, Enter to add or create) e Set the estimate (20, 45m, 1h30) d Set the deadline (fri, 2026-11-06) n Park in Someday, or bring back Shift+N Defer: type the start date Shift+E Toggle This Evening x Tick for a bulk action (see Change several tasks at once) s Schedule it on the Day calendar Delete Move it to the Trash

In the Inbox and in projects, you decide the order. Drag a task to a new place (on a touch screen, press and hold first), or select it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. Alt+Shift+↑ sends it to the top. Dropping a task on the middle of another one makes it a subtask. Projects in the sidebar can be reordered the same way. Today, Upcoming, labels and filters sort themselves by date and priority; there a drag only goes to the sidebar (see Drop on the sidebar).
Tick tasks, then act on all of them in one go.

Keyboard: press x (or Space) to tick the selected task, Shift+↓ or Shift+↑ to extend the range, and Ctrl+A (⌘+A) to tick the whole list once something is ticked. Esc clears the ticks (after closing the panel). Mouse: Ctrl/⌘+click a task to tick it without opening it, Shift+click to tick a range. Once a task is ticked, every row shows a checkbox in place of its circle until the selection is cleared; otherwise the circle always completes the task. Touch: press and hold a task to tick it and show every checkbox, or choose Select tasks in the page menu; tap Done in the bar to hide the boxes. Hold a ticked task and move to drag the selection.

While tasks are ticked, a bar above the list says how many and offers Actions (or press .): complete or reopen, priority, labels (added to all, or removed from all), a date (today, tomorrow, next week, none, or one you pick), move to a project or section, assign, and move to the Trash. The usual keys work on the whole selection too: c, 1 to 4, L, Shift+A and Delete. With nothing ticked, . opens the same menu for the selected task. It works in projects, the Inbox, Today, Upcoming, the Filter view and saved views, also offline.

Moving and assigning show the changes first, task by task, because they can change who sees a task or notify someone: Enter applies the checked ones, Esc changes nothing. Everything else applies at once, and a notice with Undo stays for ten seconds (Ctrl/⌘+Z works too). Undo puts every task back in one step, except a task someone changed again since, which keeps the newer value and is named. See also Undo a bulk action.

Today's Earlier group has two actions in its header: Move all to today and Reschedule… (today, tomorrow, next week or a day you pick). They change every task of the group as one batch, with the same Undo, and leave your ticked tasks alone. A task you can only view is left as it is and counted ("3 of 4 tasks moved to today"). The palette offers both as Move earlier tasks to today and Reschedule earlier tasks….

From any list or board, drag a task onto a project in the sidebar (or onto Inbox) to move it there, or onto a label to add that label. If the task is ticked, every ticked task goes along, as one change that Undo takes back. A project you can only view doesn't accept drops, and dropping a task on the label it already has changes nothing. Without a mouse, use Move to project in the task's menu (.) and Shift+L for labels.

All next to Projects in the sidebar (or g then Shift+P) opens the Projects page. It has two tabs, Active and Archived (your archived projects). It also has a field to find a project (Enter opens the first match), New project and From a template….

The active projects form a table, with sub-projects indented under their parent. For each project you see: its Health (see below); its Progress: completed tasks out of all its tasks, where a repeating task counts once; how many tasks are Open; the Next due date, in red when it has passed; the People a shared project is shared with; when it was last Updated. A folded project includes its sub-projects in these figures; an unfolded one counts only its own tasks, as in the sidebar. Collapse all and Expand all are in the page's ⋯ menu. Select a row to open the project.

Health is one word, worked out on your device from rules you can check, the first that applies: Health When Late An open task's deadline has passed. The task is named, or the number of tasks past their deadline is given. Overdue An open task is due before today. The number of late tasks is given. Quiet Nothing in the project changed for a week. The number of days is given. On track Anything else, while something is open. A project with nothing open says Nothing open. Completing a task counts as a change, so it wakes a quiet project. In a shared project, health counts everyone's tasks, because it describes the project. Your statistics still count only your own. Health uses no server, no AI and nothing outside your own tasks. It works offline, and every device shows the same word.

Select a column's header to sort by it: Health starts with what needs you, and Updated starts with the newest change. Select the header again to reverse the order, and a third time to return to your own order. Projects are sorted among their siblings, so sub-projects stay under their parent. Using the keyboard: ↑ / ↓ (or k / j) move between projects. ↓ in the find field moves into the table. ← folds a project, or moves to its parent; → unfolds it. Enter opens the project. On a narrow window, the columns at the end give way. A phone shows each project's name and health. There the reason beside the health word ("1 late", the task past its deadline, "9 days") is left out, so the word tells you instead: point at it or focus it to see the reason in a tooltip, or tap it to show the reason under the word and tap again to hide it. Screen readers always read the reason.
Projects keep related tasks together, and projects can sit inside other projects.

To create a project, click + next to Projects in the sidebar, type a name and choose Create. Pick a parent project in the same form to make it a sub-project. Inside a project, quick add puts new tasks in it. See also workspaces. The Project menu at the top right of a project lets you: pick a colour, Pin to sidebar, which adds it to Favourites (see below), Move to… another project, or back to the top level; m opens the menu straight at this step. Rename it, pick an Icon…: type to search, or No icon for the dot, Archive… it, which hides it and its sub-projects from the sidebar while keeping every task, Delete project…, which moves it to the Trash. Archive and delete ask first and say what they affect. A project's open-task count shows in the sidebar on hover or focus (always on touch). A folded project counts its sub-projects. Inside a project you can also group tasks into sections and show them as a board: see Sections and boards.

All next to Projects in the sidebar (or g then Shift+P) opens the Projects page: every project in a table with its health and progress, and an Archived tab. See All projects. Pin to sidebar in the menu of a project, a label or a saved view puts it in Favourites at the top of the sidebar. Move up and Move down in its menu there, or Alt+↑ / ↓, reorder them. A pin is yours alone, even on a shared project, and syncs to your devices.
