Sub-projects work like folders: "Work" can hold "Q4 launch", which can hold more. A project's page lists its sub-projects at the bottom with their counts. Fold a project in the sidebar with its small arrow or ← / →; each device remembers its own folding and starts with the top level only. Collapse all and Expand all are in the + menu next to Projects, and the magnifier there (g then /) finds a project.

Duplicate… in a project's menu makes a copy with the same sections, sub-projects and open tasks. Choose a parent and, optionally, a Start on day to shift every due date so the earliest lands on it. Completed tasks, comments, reminders and assignees aren't copied. You can duplicate any project you can see; the copy is yours alone. To duplicate one task with its open subtasks, select it and press Shift+D, or choose Duplicate in the task panel's ⋯ menu. The copy appears right below the original and is selected. A copy works offline and reaches your other devices with the next sync. To reuse a project later, save it as a template.

When you complete the last open task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it; press Enter to accept or any other key to keep it. Projects that have had no open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice you can undo. You can turn that off in Settings → Data (each device has its own setting). To bring one back, select Restore next to it in the Archived tab of the Projects page; see Archived projects.

A completed task normally leaves the project's list and shows up under Completed in the sidebar. That suits a project you work through once. For a list you tick off and use again, such as groceries or packing, you can keep the completed tasks in the project instead.

Open the Project menu at the top right of the project and choose Show completed tasks. Choose it again to turn it off. The project's completed tasks now stay at the end of the list in a Completed group: The group starts closed and its heading shows how many tasks it holds. Click the heading to open or close it; the app remembers which on this device. The most recently completed task comes first. Complete a task and it moves into the group. Untick a task in the group and it goes back among the open tasks, in its section. A section whose tasks are all done no longer offers its own "n completed" while the Completed group is on, because the group already holds those tasks.

The setting is per project and per device, like the board layout, and it is not synced. Turn it on separately on your phone and your computer. It applies to the list layout. The board and the timeline keep showing open tasks only. Every completed task, from every project, is still in Completed in the sidebar. See Built-in views.

Every project can have a note at the top: the goal, the links you keep looking up, the rules of a shared shopping list, a packing list, who to call. It sits above the tasks in the list, the board and the timeline, so the brief is read before the work.

Select Add a note under the quick add, click the note itself, or press Shift+P anywhere in the project while no text field has focus. The note opens in place, in the same editor as task notes: start a line with - for a bullet list, [ ] for a checklist or # for a heading, press Ctrl+B for bold or Ctrl+K for a link (⌘ on a Mac). See Notes, subtasks and dependencies. To finish, press Esc or select Done. The note is saved as you type, offline too, and reaches your other devices with the next sync. A note with headings and check items is shown with those headings and boxes at rest; ticking a box happens in the editor.

In a project of your own, you. In a shared project, the owner, admins and editors can edit the note; viewers read it. When the note is empty, people who may edit see the quiet Add a note line and viewers see nothing. The roles are explained in Roles and assignments. Two people can edit the note at the same time, also offline, and both sets of changes are kept, as with task notes. Another member's change appears while you type without moving your cursor.
A note longer than about eight lines is folded with a Show more control. The choice is remembered on each device separately, so a folded note on your laptop is still open on your phone.

The project's History (in the project's ⋯ menu) lists note changes as edits of the notes, shows the text before and after, and can put back an earlier version; see Trash and history. Scripts and the API read and write the note as Markdown in the project's description; a change made there is folded into the note on the next device that opens the project. Exports and backups carry the note with the project, and importing a JSON file that lists projects with a description sets it on the projects it creates. AI assistants over MCP and the in-app assistant see the description, read-only. For an encrypted account, the note is encrypted on your devices like task notes and project names.
Views are built from the tasks on your device, so they work offline and update the moment something changes. OpenTodo comes with a handful, and you can save your own.

The built-in views are at the top of the sidebar, the less frequent ones under More. Press g, then a letter, to open one: g i for the Inbox. A project can be a list, a board or a timeline. The built-in views lists them all.
Process in the Inbox header (g p) shows one task at a time with a key for each decision, each with Undo. See Process the Inbox.
Tasks from earlier days first under Earlier, then today's by time, with This Evening and Blocked below. Anything you add here is due today. See Today and Upcoming.
Upcoming groups everything due after today by day, from Tomorrow on, and lists a task with a deadline on its deadline day. See Today and Upcoming.
Review (g r) walks a weekly review in seven steps with live data, and Statistics (g Shift+S) shows what you completed, created and let slip, computed on your device.
Anytime, for when you have time
Anytime lists the open tasks with no due date, no deadline and no start date, grouped by project. See Anytime.
Someday holds the tasks you parked with n. They stay out of Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts. See Someday.
The Filter action in a list's header shows only quick wins, tasks under 30 minutes, tasks over an hour or tasks without an estimate. See Narrow a list by duration.
Describe what you want on the New view page, press s and name it. The saved view is pinned to the sidebar with a live count and syncs to all your devices. See Saved views.
A dashboard puts up to six saved views side by side, for a morning review on one screen. See Build a dashboard.
Display mode shows a view full screen in large type with a clock, for a wall tablet or an e-ink panel. See Display mode.

Each device can open on a different view, a display included: pick it in Settings → General → Start view, or with Start view on this device in a saved view's menu. If that view is deleted, the device opens on the Inbox.

Views that sort by date (Today, Upcoming, labels, filters) can't be reordered by hand. Projects and the Inbox can. Filter queries has ten ready-made examples to copy. Track habits? Save the query habit as a view named "Habits": every habit with its streak, one click from its month history. A project with custom fields? Save cost > 1000 or no client as a view, or turn on Columns in its list.

Display mode shows one view full screen, in large type, with a clock and nothing else: no sidebar, menus, quick add or task panel. It is made for a tablet on the fridge or an e-ink panel by the door, readable from across the room.

Choose Display mode in the header of Today or Upcoming, in a project's menu, or in a saved view's menu. Each opens its own address, which you can bookmark: /display/today (or just /display): the clock and date, the tasks from earlier days and today's tasks, what was done today ticked below them, and the next three days as columns. /display/upcoming: the next seven days as columns. /display/project/<id>: the project's open tasks by section. /display/view/<id>: a saved view with its own grouping and sort. Exit, in the bottom corner, or Esc returns to the same view in the app. The menu next to it makes this display the start view on this device, so a tablet opens straight into it after a restart.

Options go in the address, so a bookmark keeps them: Option Effect size=m, size=l, size=xl text of about 20, 24 (the default) or 32 px contrast=high black on white (white on black in dark mode), no soft tints motion=none nothing animates or fades days=1 … days=7 how many day columns eink=1 high contrast, no motion and a clock without seconds, for e-ink For example, /display/today?eink=1&size=xl. The options apply only to the display; your theme and preferences stay as they are.

The display reads the copy of your tasks on the device, so a task added or completed on a phone appears within seconds, and the list stays on screen when the network drops. A line at the bottom says when the device last synced. A task can be completed or reopened with its checkbox or, on a keyboard, with Space or Enter on the focused row (arrows or j and k move). Only tasks you may edit have a checkbox: on a project you only view, nothing can be changed. The keys are in Keyboard shortcuts.

Use a viewer account. A display is signed in like any device. For a screen others walk past, create an account for it ("Fridge") and share the household project with it as a viewer: the server refuses every change from that account. A display signed in as you can tick your tasks, and the rest of the app is one address away. Lock the device. The display hides the menus but is not a lock: turn on the tablet's kiosk, screen pinning or guided-access mode, and keep the screen awake in its settings (the display also asks the browser to). Sign in again now and then. Sessions last 90 days by default; whoever runs the server can change that with OPENTODO_SESSION_DAYS. Browsers. Android tablets and e-ink tablets with Chrome or another Chromium browser work; the Kindle browser does not. To show a list with no account on the device at all, use a public link on a display.
Each view is built from your device's tasks, so it works offline. Today and Upcoming have a page of their own; for views you make yourself, see Saved views.

Quick add at the top of a list adds to it. To open a view, press g, then the letter: View Shows Shortcut Inbox Tasks that aren't in a project yet; Process walks them one at a time g i Today Tasks due today or with a deadline today, earlier ones first g t Upcoming Tasks due after today, and undated tasks with a deadline ahead, grouped by day g u Anytime Open tasks with no date and no start: things to do whenever there is time g n Someday Tasks you parked for later, by project g o Next Each project's next action, by context g Shift+N Waiting Tasks waiting on someone or something g Shift+W Assigned to me Open tasks assigned to you, across projects g a Calendar Your dated tasks by Day, Week or Month, as you last left it g d, g w, g m Completed What you finished, newest first, under a heading per day; Show more at the end reaches older days g c Filter Any search you can describe g f Trash Deleted tasks and projects g x Updates What changed in your shared projects g h Review Your weekly review g r Statistics What you completed and let slip g Shift+S The sidebar keeps Inbox, Today, Upcoming and Calendar at the top; the rest wait in More, a menu on a computer. Inbox and Today show open-task counts; a project shows its count on hover or focus. Deferred and parked tasks (When a task starts) are not counted. Each project can also be shown three ways: as a List, as a Board with a column per section, or as a Timeline of its dates with arrows between tasks that wait for each other. Press v
Anytime, for when you have time

Anytime lists every open task that has no due date, no deadline and no start date, grouped by project: the things you could do whenever there is a moment; quick add here adds an undated one. A task leaves it as soon as it gets a date, from any device.

Someday holds the tasks you parked: ideas and maybes you don't want to see every day; quick add here parks what you add. They stay out of Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts, and are listed here by project and in their project's Later group. Press n on a task to park it or bring it back.

The Filter action in the header of the Inbox, Today, Upcoming and project lists offers Quick wins (15 minutes or less), Under 30 min, Over 1 h and Unestimated. Turn one on to see only matching tasks; its chip in the header has a × to clear it. Your choice stays on that device. Set estimates with e.
Focus shows one task and a large timer, and nothing else to pick from. Open it with g Shift+F, from Focus on this task in the menu of the task panel, or by typing focus in Search and commands.

Without a task of your own choosing, Focus takes the first open task of today's focus, the up to three tasks you pick in the Daily check. When you complete it, or press n for the next task, the next one of today's focus follows. When none is left, Focus says so and offers Choose a task, which finds any open task by name. Change task in the screen's menu does the same at any time. The task's notes and subtasks are shown below the timer. Tick subtasks there; Edit the notes opens the task panel.

Choose the timer in the screen's menu or in Settings. It can't change while a session runs. Pomodoro: 25 minutes of work, then a 5 minute break, and a 15 minute break after every fourth session. All four numbers are yours to change. Flowtime: counts up from 0:00 until you select Done, then offers a break. Countdown: asks for a length first, from 5 to 180 minutes, and remembers the last one on this device. When a session or a break ends, Focus says what ended and how long you worked, and offers the next step: start the break, complete the task, or the next task.

Key What it does Space Start, pause or resume Enter Complete the task and end the session b Take a break now, or end the break n Next task of today's focus Esc Back to where you were; the session keeps running The keys don't fire while you type, for example in a new subtask. Press g Shift+F to come back to a running session.

Each stretch of work is a time entry on the task: starting starts an entry, pausing ends it, resuming starts a new one, and completing the task or starting a break ends it. Breaks are never logged. The entries sync like any other change, so your phone shows the time after the laptop syncs. When the app can't log time, the timer works the same and nothing is written. The timer itself stays on the device: it is not synced or exported, and it is cleared when you sign out. The timer counts from the clock, so a reload, a laptop that slept or a tab in the background still shows the right time.

Break reminder (off until you turn it on) shows a notice on any screen after 90 minutes of work without a break: Take a break starts a short break, Not now asks again after another 90 minutes. Pauses don't count as work. Sound plays a short tone when a session or a break ends while the app is on screen. If the tab is in the background and you allowed notifications on this device, a system notification says the session is done; select it to come back to Focus.

All of this is in Settings → General → Focus: the timer, the lengths, the long break, starting breaks and the next session automatically, the break reminder and its length, and the sound. These settings follow your account to every device.

Capture first, decide later. When the Inbox has piled up, select Process in its header (or press P there, g p anywhere) and decide each task in turn, keyboard only if you like. One task is shown at a time with its notes, date and labels, and "4 of 17" tells you how far you are.

On a screen at least 1024 px wide the Inbox keeps the selected task beside the list: move with j and k or click a row and its details follow, ready to edit. Enter opens the task as its page; Esc clears the selection. Each row says where its task came from and when, such as "From email · 3 d ago" or "From a calendar app · 2 h ago". Process is the header's main button, also P, and the header says how many tasks are left to sort.

Key Decision t Due today s Schedule: pick a day (see below), or type a date (fri, 3/11) and press Enter m Move to a project a Delegate: move it into a shared project and assign it to someone there, in one step l Labels. This one doesn't move on, so you can add a label and then decide y Park it in Someday c Complete Delete Move to the Trash j or Space Skip it for now k Back to the previous task Enter Open the task's panel to edit anything else; Esc comes back Every decision moves on to the next task and shows Undo for a few seconds. The buttons under the card do the same by mouse or touch. Delegating needs a project you share with someone; until you have one, the button says so. A task you date, move or park has a place, so it leaves the Inbox (where planned tasks go).

s opens a sheet with the same choices as the panel's Do on: Today, Tomorrow, This weekend and Next week, each with its date, a field that shows what it understood before you press Enter, and a calendar. When the task has a deadline, choices counted back from it come first, on number keys: 1 On the deadline, 2 1 day before, 3 3 days before, 4 1 week before, 5 2 weeks before, 6 1 month before. A choice that would fall before today isn't offered, and the deadline is marked in the calendar. Esc closes the sheet without a change.

The queue is the Inbox in its order when you start. Tasks you decide stay counted, so "4 of 17" doesn't jump; tasks captured meanwhile, on any device, join the end; a task someone moves out of the Inbox elsewhere drops out, and the mode tells you. When nothing is left you see Inbox zero and the way back. Esc returns to the Inbox with the task you were on selected. It all works offline, like any edit, and with Vim keybindings on, x, dd, :triage and :q work too.

Under the title, Today says in a sentence or two what stands out: "Three things matter today. Renew the passport is 2 days late, Monday is already full, and Mia answered about Boiler." It names at most three things, in this order: What is late, in red: the task and how many days late it is when there is one, otherwise how many. Tasks waiting for another task are left out. A full day, in amber: today when its estimates go past your day length, otherwise the first day of the coming week that is already full. Replies waiting for you: who answered about which task, or how many. Opening the task clears it. When nothing stands out it says so, with how many tasks are planned and the time they add up to.

Each part of the sentence leads to what it talks about. Click or tap it, or reach it with Tab; a part is underlined when you point at it. A task's name ("Renew the passport", the task a reply is about, tomorrow's first task) opens the task. Esc brings you back. A count of late tasks ("2 tasks are late") selects exactly those tasks in Today's list and scrolls to them, so the selection bar can reschedule them in one go. From the Daily check it opens Today first. A full day ("Monday is already full") opens Upcoming at that day. Replies ("3 replies are waiting") open your notifications. Following a part changes nothing.

Choose Hide briefing in the menu (…) of Today or Upcoming. The title and the date stay. The choice belongs to your account, so your other devices hide it too once they sync; Show briefing in the same menu brings it back. The Daily check always opens with the sentence.

Once you have completed the last task, or closed the day, it reads All done for today. and tells you how tomorrow starts: "Tomorrow starts with 4 tasks; the first is Standup at 9:30 AM." On a day with nothing planned and nothing done it reads Nothing is planned for today. instead.

Upcoming's briefing counts the tasks of the next seven days, names the days that are already full (or says every day still has room), and says how tomorrow starts. The Daily check opens with the same sentence as Today.

Your device works the briefing out from your own tasks, so it works offline, needs no connection and is never written by an AI. It changes as you work and as your other devices sync. The day length is the one in Settings → General → Calendar grid, set per device. The sentence follows your interface language; task titles and names stay as you wrote them.
Today (g t) and Upcoming (g u) are the two views most people live in: one for the day, one for the days ahead. The other built-in views are listed in The built-in views.

Today, under its briefing, is where most people start. A task you add here with quick add is due today. Tasks planned for an earlier day sit in Earlier at the top, each date in red. Move all to today and Reschedule… in its header move the whole group at once, with Undo. Above five tasks the group starts folded; this device remembers once you open or close it. Below are today's tasks, sorted by time; a timed task shows its time alone, since the heading already says Today. A deadline brings a task into Today too: a task whose deadline is today shows up even if it has no due date or is planned for later. If the deadline has already passed and the task isn't planned for today, it sits under Earlier. Each task is listed once, and the Today count in the sidebar counts the same tasks. A task whose start date has come shows up in Today too, with a Started chip, and stays until you complete it, give it a date or defer it again. Deferred and parked tasks stay out of Today, unless their due date or deadline has come: a hard date always wins. Tasks you marked for This Evening are listed in their own group below the day's tasks. Tasks waiting for another task gather in a Blocked group at the end, folded so they don't crowd the day; select the heading to open it (your choice is kept on this device). When the task they wait for is completed, they move up among today's tasks by themselves. In Upcoming and other lists, blocked tasks stay in place, dimmed, with a lock. To push a task to later,

A task you add here with quick add is due tomorrow unless you type a date. Upcoming lists everything that has a date after today, under headings like Tomorrow and the weekday names. Scan the next few days, move what won't fit, and spot empty days. A task with a deadline but no due date is listed under its deadline day, after the tasks due that day, so you see it while there is still time to plan it. A task with both dates is listed under its due date only; its row shows the deadline countdown. Deferred and parked tasks are left out until they start, except one without a project or due date, listed under its start day.

The Inbox holds tasks with no project and no plan. A due date, a start date or Someday takes a task out; clear it and the task comes back. Subtasks leave with their parent. A deadline alone doesn't. Planned tasks without a project wait, folded, at the end of the Inbox under Planned, no project, and don't count toward Inbox zero. To see the hours, switch to Week: timed tasks as blocks on a grid (Time blocking). Subtasks show up on their own in both views, with their parent's name.
When the built-in views aren't enough, describe the tasks you want with a filter query and save the result as a view of your own. A view's menu can make an automation rule from it.

Describe what you want on the New view page (g f), then save it. For example, blocked lists every task waiting for another one, and due <= 7 days & p1 shows urgent tasks for the coming week. Build the query from conditions or type it: see Labels and filters, and Filter queries for ten examples. To save it, press s in the results or choose Save as view, type a name in the card that replaces the header and press Enter. The view keeps its display options, is listed in the Views group of the sidebar (folded on a new device), pinned to Favourites, and synced to all your devices. Its live count is on the views list (g v) and in its header, not in the sidebar.

Under a view's header (Views › name), the toolbar shows its conditions in words, such as Label is waiting. The funnel opens the filter panel to change them (/ jumps to the query). Display options sets List or Board, the grouping and order, whether completed tasks are listed, and which properties rows show; each choice is saved to the view and syncs. Filter queries has every option. The All link next to Views (or g v) opens the list of all your saved views and boards to rename, reorder, pin or delete them. Every saved view has the same menu, wherever you open it: the ⋯ button on its row in the sidebar or the views list, its header, or a dashboard. With a row focused, . (or Shift+F10) opens it too. Rename. Pin to sidebar and Start view on this device: a check mark shows which apply. Pin to sidebar (called Pinned to sidebar before) adds the view to Favourites or takes it out; it stays in the Views group either way. Move up and Move down: unavailable at the top or bottom of the list, with the reason shown. Opened from Favourites, they move the view among your favourites. Delete view… asks for confirmation first. Deleting a view never touches your tasks.

A dashboard (a board) puts up to six saved views side by side, each with its count and first ten tasks: "Due this week" and "Waiting on others" for a morning review. Open the views list (g v), choose New board, then Empty board, name it, then add saved views as panels from the dashboard's header. Panels stack on a phone. Move between panels with Tab, and through a panel's tasks with j / k.

In Arrange, choose Rule next to a panel to set what a dropped card gets: labels added or removed, a priority, a date (today, tomorrow, next week or none), Someday, a section, completed or reopened. A bolt marks a column with a rule; others take no drops. Drag a card onto a column, or press Shift+→ / Shift+← to move the selected card to the next column with a rule. A message names the changes, with Undo. A card that still doesn't match the column's filter stays there, marked Not matching, until you leave the board. New board also offers the Eisenhower matrix: four filters by priority and date, Urgent and important to Neither, each with a rule. Each device can open on a saved view or a dashboard: see Choose where the app opens.

Once a week, look back at what happened and set up the week ahead. Open Review in the sidebar (under More) or press g r. It is the weekly rhythm of Open Loops; the Daily check and the Monthly look are in the page's menu.

The review walks you through one step at a time, starting with the first that is not done. The stepper at the top shows every step: a check when it is done, a small number for what is left. Select a step to jump to it, or use Back and Next below the step ([ and ]). On the last step, Next becomes Finish review. The steps come in three phases: Get clear Inbox: done when the Inbox is empty. Process the Inbox walks it one task at a time (Process the Inbox). Mind sweep: a few prompts ("Calls to return", "Promises to someone") and a quick add that catches into the Inbox. Get current 3. Look back: what you completed this week, and what is still open from earlier ("2 from earlier"). Done when nothing is. 4. Waiting: what you assigned to someone else or what waits for another task. 5. Projects: one card per project, least recently reviewed first, with its outcome (the first lines of its note), its next action and whether it has stalled. r marks it reviewed, q adds a next action, Enter opens it, a archives it, j skips and k goes back. Done when every project was reviewed in the last seven days and has a next action. Your mark is yours: in a shared project, the others keep their own. 6. Look ahead: what is due in the next seven days. Get creative 7. Someday: what you parked. n brings a task back. Lists use the usual keys, offline too.

Finish review records the time. It syncs to all your devices, so your phone knows when you last reviewed on your laptop. In the sidebar, Review gets a small dot once the last review is more than seven days ago, or if you never finished one; point at it to read why ("Review due · last weekly review 9 days ago"). With nothing due there is no dot, and the tooltip says when you last reviewed. With Open Loops on, the dot also covers the Monthly look, and in Open Loops first the Daily check. When Review is inside More, its dot and these words are on the Review item in the More menu; More itself carries no dot. What you completed and let slip is in Statistics and the weekly digest.
Press Ctrl+K (⌘+K on a Mac) anywhere in the app to find anything or do anything by name. It also works while you are typing in a field, except in a task's notes, where the same keys insert a link.

Use the shortcut, or the magnifying glass at the top of the screen. On a phone the box opens as a sheet from the bottom. Type, move with ↑ and ↓, and press Enter; Esc closes it and returns you where you were. With nothing typed, the box lists what you can do right now (for the selected task, the project or view you are in) and what you picked most recently on this device.

Search, Add, Commands and Ask (when the assistant is on) switch what the box does: the strip at the bottom names their first characters, and a phone shows buttons. + adds a task with quick add, > lists commands and ? asks the assistant; typing it again returns to Search. Esc returns to Search first. The last search result is always Add "…" as a task; Ctrl+Enter picks it. On screens without a quick add, q opens the box in Add mode.

Tasks, by title and by the text of their notes. Open tasks come first; completed ones are marked. Deleted tasks never show up. Picking a task opens its project with the task's panel open. Projects (archived ones are marked), labels, saved views and dashboards, and the Settings sections you can see. Matching ignores case and accents and finds words by their start or by letters in order: cafe finds Café, rp finds Renew passport. Exact matches come first; among equal matches, what you picked often on this device comes first. At most 50 results are listed; keep typing to narrow them down.

If what you type is a filter query, such as @errand & p1, due <= friday or #Work & overdue, the box lists the matching tasks and offers Open as a new view. Plain words are always a text search, so a half-typed query never shows an error.

Every action has a name in the box: go to any view, calendar or Settings section; act on the selected task (complete, priority, labels, assign, estimate, deadline, defer, park, This Evening, schedule, skip an occurrence, move to the Trash); act on the project, saved view, label or section you are in (everything in their menus, such as Pin to sidebar or Archive); save the current filter as a view; create a task, project, label or dashboard; sync now; show the keyboard shortcuts; turn Vim keybindings on or off; search Help for what you typed. Each command shows its keys (G then U), so the box also teaches them. Commands are listed only when they apply: with no task selected there are no task commands, and a viewer of a shared project doesn't see the ones that would change it.

The search runs on your device, over the data already stored there. Nothing you type is sent to the server, and nothing is indexed on it. This works offline and for end-to-end encrypted accounts too: your device holds the decrypted text and searches that.

Open Statistics under More, or press g Shift+S. Choose this week, this month, this quarter, this year or last week with the arrow keys. Weeks start on your first day of the week, and days begin at your day start: with 04:00, a task completed at 01:30 counts for the day before. A period to date is compared with the same days of the previous one: on 10 October, this month is 1–10 October against 1–10 September. The four tiles: Done: tasks and subtasks completed. Each day of a recurring task counts once; a skipped habit day never counts. On time: of the completions whose task had a due date, the share done on or before that day. Streak: days in a row with a completion, up to today (or yesterday while today has none yet), and your best run in the last 53 weeks. Tracked: your own time entries that started in the period, against the estimates of the tasks they were tracked on, and how many of those tasks have no estimate. Each panel answers one question: Am I keeping up? Completed and created as two lines: per day up to a month, per week for a quarter, per month for a year. Where does my time go? Tracked time per project (the top five, then "other"; Inbox for tasks without a project), or completions per project when nothing was tracked. A year of done tasks: every day of the last 53 weeks, shaded by how much you completed, whatever the period. When do I get things done? Completions by weekday and hour, the hours starting at your day start. How good are my estimates? For tasks with

In Settings → Notifications → Weekly digest, turn on an email for your review day: last week's numbers, what is still open, what is due in the next seven days, projects without a next action, when you last reviewed, and a link to the review. What counts as without a next action is in Places. Pick the day and hour; your time zone and language come from the browser and are shown on the card. The digest uses the same definitions as Statistics, your day start included. It needs outgoing email set up by the server owner, contains task names, and is not available with end-to-end encryption: turning encryption on switches it off. A failed send is retried for six hours.
Sections divide a project into parts, like "Planning" and "Waiting". A project can be a list with headings, a board with a column per section, or a timeline of its dates.

Open a project and select + Add section at the bottom of the list or after the last column of a board. Type a name and press Enter. Each heading shows how many open tasks it holds. Tasks without a section are listed first under No section.
Select the + on a section heading and type: the task goes straight into that section. You can also open any task and choose a Section in its panel.
Rename, reorder or delete a section

Use the ⋯ menu on a section heading (or press . with the heading focused): Rename (F2) Colour… and Icon… mark the section before its name. Move it up or down (left or right on the board). Delete section… asks first and says how many open tasks move to No section. The tasks aren't deleted. Fold a section with the small arrow next to its name. Folding is remembered on that device only.

At the top of the project, choose Board (or press v). Each section becomes a column, with No section first. v cycles through List, Board and Timeline; you can also choose one directly. The choice is remembered per project on each device. On a phone the board shows one column at a time: swipe sideways or tap a dot above the columns; "No section" is a column only while it has open tasks.

Drag a card to another column, or to a place within a column. On a touch screen, press and hold the card first. Keyboard: select a card and press Shift+→ or Shift+←. Panel: open the task and pick another Section. Moving with the keyboard or the panel puts the card at the bottom of the new column. Cards show up to three custom field values as badges, such as Cost 1,200, and +2 for the rest.
See a project on a timeline
Choose Timeline at the top of the project (or press v until it shows): tasks become bars from start to deadline that you drag to reschedule. See A project on a timeline.
Get around the board with the keyboard

Key Does h / l or ← / → Jump to the previous or next column j / k Move up and down within a column Shift+← / Shift+→ Move the selected card to the previous or next column a Add a task to the selected card's column Enter Open the card

Moving a task to another project removes it from its section, because sections belong to one project. If a section is deleted while another device moves a task into it, the task ends up under No section. Nothing is lost. Sections are exported and come back on import.
A simple flow: To do, Doing, Done. By place: Kitchen, Bathroom, Garden for a renovation. By week: This week, Next week, Later for a launch plan.

Choose Timeline at the top of the project (or press v until it shows). Each open task is a row, in list order under its sections and with subtasks indented. Its bar, in the project's colour, runs from its start to its due date or deadline, whichever is later; a task with a single date gets a one-day bar, and the part before today is dimmed. A long bar carries the task's name; a short one is followed by its length, such as 1 day. A thin mark shows the due day inside a longer bar and a diamond shows the deadline. A task whose deadline or due day has passed is late: its bar turns red and says how late it is, such as 2 days late. A note that would cross the today line is moved just past it, and one at the end of the timeline sits before its bar. A green line marks today, with Today above it. Tasks with no dates, or parked in Someday, wait under Unscheduled at the end. Drag a bar to move all its dates by the same number of days. The due time stays the same. Drag the left or right end to set the start or the deadline. If the task has none yet, one is created. Drag an unscheduled task from its name onto a day to give it that due date. Keyboard: select a task with j and k, then ← and → move its dates a day. Shift+← and Shift+→ move its deadline, starting from the due date when it has none. Enter opens it. Days and Weeks change the scale. [ and ] move the visible range, and t comes back to today. When one task waits for another in the same project, an arrow joins them and the waiting

A task, or a comment on it, can carry files and links: a receipt, a photo of a whiteboard, a PDF, the link to a design. Open a task and use Attachments below its subtasks, or the paperclip in the comment box.
Add a file or a link

Pick, paste or drop. Choose Attach › Choose files… to pick files, paste an image or a file into the task panel, or drop files onto it (a drop zone appears while you drag). In the text. An image pasted into the notes or a comment is attached and shown in place (details). Links. Choose Attach › Add a link… and paste an http or https address. A link is stored as a link: the server never downloads it. Offline. Adding a file without a connection works: the attachment appears at once, marked "waiting to upload", and uploads after the next sync. Other devices show it as "uploading" until the file has arrived on the server. Images show a thumbnail; other files show their name, type and size. Open shows the file in a new tab when the browser can display it safely (images, PDF, plain text, audio and video); everything else, and every file of an encrypted account, is downloaded instead. You can rename your own attachments and remove them; a removal can be undone from the notice that follows.

Attachments belong to their task: everyone who can see the task can see its attachments, viewers of a shared project included, and anyone who can comment can attach files. Only the person who added an attachment can rename it. The author, a project admin and the owner can remove it.

The server owner sets a size limit per file (25 MB unless changed) and a total per account (1 GB unless changed) in Settings → Server → Attachments, and can turn attachments off. Settings → Data shows how much of your total you use. Removing an attachment frees your total at once; the file itself stays on the server for the Trash retention period (30 days unless changed), so a removal can be undone from any device, and is then deleted for good. Purging a task from the Trash deletes its files immediately.

On an account with end-to-end encryption, the file name, its type, a link's address and the file's bytes are encrypted on your device before they leave it. The server stores and serves only the encrypted bytes and never holds a key. Turning encryption on or off re-uploads existing files in the new form as part of the switch, and replaces each of your links with a copy in the new form.

Files are only ever served to signed-in people who can see the task. A file is never shown as a web page: documents that could run code (HTML, SVG and the like) are always downloaded, and every file is served with headers that stop the browser from running anything in it.

Files live under <data>/attachments/, one file per attachment, written once and never changed. Backups include them after the database, the ZIP export (GET /api/v1/export?format=zip) adds them to a user's export, and opentodo restore puts them back. The optional OPENTODO_ATTACHMENTS_MAX_FILE_MB and OPENTODO_ATTACHMENTS_QUOTA_MB preset the two limits on the first start; after that the owner's settings decide. The public demo has attachments turned off. The routes are described in the API reference.

A project can give its tasks a few typed fields of its own: a cost, a client, a stage, a link. Every task of the project can then hold a value for each, and you can see and filter them like any other property.
Define the fields of a project

Open the project, open the ⋯ menu and choose Fields… (or press Shift+F). Type a name, pick a type and select Add field: Type Holds Text up to 2,000 characters Number any number, shown with your language's digit grouping Date a calendar day Choice one of the options you list, one per line Link an http or https address Checkbox on or off A project has at most 30 fields, and two fields of one project cannot share a name. The type of a field is fixed once it exists. In the same dialog you can rename a field, edit the options of a choice, move a field up or down (drag it, or press Alt+↑ / ↓ on its handle) and delete it. Whoever may edit the project's tasks may manage its fields. Viewers of a shared project see the values but not the Fields… item. The Inbox has no fields.

Open a task: the Fields group of the panel lists the project's fields in order, each with an editor that fits its type. A number or text is saved when you press Enter or leave the field, a choice opens with Enter or Alt+↓, and a link has a button that opens it in a new tab. Clear a value to leave it empty. Values work offline and sync like every edit; two people editing different fields of one task both keep their change.
See values on rows, cards and columns

Rows and board cards show up to three values as small badges, such as Cost 1,200 or Paid, and +2 for the rest. On a wide screen a project's list offers a Columns button above its tasks: one column per field, read-only, with the task panel for editing. The choice is remembered per project on that device.
Move a task or delete a field

A task moved to another project keeps its values, but shows only the fields of its new project; move it back and they reappear. Deleting a field asks first and says how many tasks hold a value: the values stay in the data and in the export, hidden. Renaming an option of a choice field in place (same line) updates the tasks that held the old text.
Use a field's name in a filter query: cost > 100, client = "Acme", "Order date" <= friday, paid = true, or no client for tasks without a value.

Projects say where a task belongs. Labels say what kind of task it is, across all projects: @call, @errand, @waiting, @deep-work. Filters then let you ask questions like "every call I need to make this week".
Add a label to a task

Pick whichever is quickest: Type it in quick add: Phone the bank @call. Select a task and press L, start typing, and press Enter. The picker stays open so you can add more. Open the task and use Labels in the panel. If the label doesn't exist yet, typing its name and pressing Enter creates it. On a task row, labels show as small chips with the label's colour and name, two at most, then "+2" for the others (hover or focus them to read every name). To remove one, open the task and select the × on the chip. Labels are personal. In a shared project, other members don't see the labels you add.

Once you have a label, the Labels group in the sidebar lists your labels; it starts folded on a new device. The number of open tasks for each is on the labels page (g l) and in the label's header, not in the sidebar. Select one to see all its tasks, grouped by project; a task you add there with quick add gets the label. Pin to sidebar in a label's menu (in the sidebar, on the labels page or in the label's header) adds it to Favourites at the top of the sidebar. All next to Labels (or g l) opens the labels page, where you rename, recolour, reorder, merge and delete labels: see Manage labels.

Open Filter in the sidebar (or press g f) and type a query. Results appear as you type, grouped by project. Rather not type? + Condition above the input builds the query for you (the builder). A query combines small pieces: Piece Means Example @name has this label @call #name in this project #Work ##name in this project or its sub-projects ##Work p1 … p4 priority p1 today, tomorrow, overdue, no date due then, or not at all overdue due <= 7 days due within the next week due before friday search: text words in the title or notes search: invoice blocked, unblocked waiting for an open task, or not unblocked & today completed include completed tasks #Home & completed Join them with & (and), | (or) and ! (not), and use brackets to group: (@call | @errand) & due <= 7 days That reads: tasks labeled call or errand, due within the next seven days. A few more: #Work & p1 & due <= tomorrow: the most important work for today and tomorrow. overdue & no project: overdue tasks still sitting in the Inbox. @waiting & !#Work: everything you're waiting on, outside work. Names with spaces go in quotes: #"Client A". Upper and lower case don't matter. If you mistype, a message under the box says where, and the previous results stay visible. Press Enter to jump from the box to the first result, and Esc to go back. ↑ and ↓ in the box bring back your recent queries. The full language, with ten worked examples, is in Filter queries.
Save a filter as a view

When a query is useful, keep it: press s in the results, give it a name, and it appears under Views in the sidebar, and in Favourites until you unpin it. Its live count is in the Filters overview (g v) and its page header. Saved views sync to your other devices. See Views for grouping, sorting and dashboards.

Labels for context work well: @call, @computer, @errand, @home. Then a view like @errand & due <= 2 days is your shopping list. A @waiting label plus a pinned "Waiting on others" view makes follow-ups hard to forget. Filters run on your device. They're instant, and they work offline. Labels and saved views belong to one workspace, so the same name can exist in two of them.

All next to Labels in the sidebar (or g l) opens the labels page: every label with its colour, its number of open tasks, a drag handle and a ⋯ menu. The sidebar rows and the label's own page have the same menu, with Pin to sidebar to add the label to Favourites.

Rename: double-click a label, or focus it and press F2. A name another label already has is refused, and the old name stays. Edit… in the menu opens a panel with the name, the colour swatches (arrow keys move between them), and buttons to move the label. Reorder: drag a label by its handle (on a phone, press and hold the handle so scrolling the list still works), or focus it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. Alt+Shift+↑ / ↓ moves it to the top or bottom. The new position is announced to screen readers. . or Shift+F10 opens the menu of the focused label.

Merge into…: type to find the label to keep. A confirmation names both labels and how many tasks change. Tasks with the first label get the second one instead, and the first is deleted. Handy when you end up with both "Errand" and "errand". Delete label…: the confirmation says how many tasks carry it. It's removed from them; the tasks stay. If two of your devices created the same label while offline, both copies get a duplicate badge, and the labels page offers to merge them. Swap chooses which one is kept. Every change is saved on this device first and syncs to your other devices, also when you make it offline. Labels are personal: in a shared project, other members don't see yours (see Labels and filters).
A task can say where it happens: the post office, a client's address, the parcel locker. The location shows on the task panel's Where line, with a small map and Open in maps.

Open a task and choose its location on the Where line, or Add → Location. In the field you can: type an address and pick a result (when maps are on); type coordinates such as 45.4642, 9.19 and choose Use 45.4642, 9.19; pick one of your saved locations. Use my location asks the browser for your position. Pick on the map lets you click a point. With maps on, both fill in the nearest address. Clear removes the location. Every change is one edit that Undo takes back, and it works offline except the address search. Open in maps opens your phone's maps app, or the position on openstreetmap.org on a computer.

Save for reuse keeps a task's location under a name such as Office. A task linked to a saved location follows it: rename the location or move its pin, and every linked task shows the change. Delete it, and the tasks keep the address they had. Locations, in the sidebar's More group, lists your saved locations with their open tasks and a map of all of them. Open one to see its tasks as a list; a task you add there gets that location. Rename, reorder or delete a location from its menu. Saved locations are yours alone; they are never shared.

Maps use OpenStreetMap data. Tiles and address searches come from the provider your server uses (OpenFreeMap and Photon by default) through your server, so the provider sees your server, the area shown and what you type into the search, never your account, your tasks or your own address. To turn maps off on all your devices, switch off Settings → General → Maps. Locations keep working with coordinates and Open in maps. The server owner can turn maps off for everyone; see Maps. With end-to-end encryption, locations and saved locations are encrypted like task titles. A device that is locked shows Encrypted and no map.

A rule says when something happens, which tasks it is for, and what to change. When the label waiting is added, move the task to the Waiting section of Work. Rules run on your server, so they work while every device is closed. Open More → Rules.

Choose New rule, name it, then: When: a task is created, completed or reopened; a label is added or removed; a task is assigned to you or moved to a project or section; a task is due (at its time, 09:00 for a date without a time); a task's date passes (at the start of the next day); or on a schedule, at a time on chosen weekdays. Only for tasks that: optional conditions, all of which must hold: project (with its sub-projects), labels, priority, date, deadline, assignee, blocked. The editor shows how many open tasks match now. Then: priority, date, start, deadline, assignee, labels to add or remove, project and section, complete or reopen, a comment, an in-app notification, or a delivery to one of your webhooks. A rule saved offline is listed at once and runs after the next sync. Times use the time zone your devices report and your day start.

A rule writes the same changes you would: completing a repeating task moves it to its next date, and a moved date carries its reminders along. A change the task already has is not written. Each change appears in the task's history as Rule (name), and Restore this value undoes it like any edit. Rules fire only for your own edits, never for a teammate's change in a shared project or for an import. A rule never moves tasks into or out of a shared project.

An account runs at most 60 rule runs a minute and 2,000 a day, a run changes at most 500 tasks, and you can have 50 rules. A rule that keeps hitting the per-minute limit is paused with Paused: it ran too often and you get one notification; turn it back on when it is fixed. Rules that trigger each other stop after three in a row. Pause all rules at the bottom of the page pauses every rule of yours until you resume.
History in a rule's menu lists its recent runs (the last 100, for 30 days) with the tasks each one changed. The history is kept on the server, so it needs a connection.
Turn a filter into a rule

A saved view's menu and a board column's Rule dialog offer Make an automation rule. The editor opens with the column's changes as actions and the filter's project, label, priority, date and similar terms as conditions; terms a rule cannot use, such as a text search, are named.
Conditions and actions use ids and dates, which the server reads for every account, so rules work with end-to-end encryption. The comment action is not available: the server cannot encrypt a comment.

Settings → Server → Automations turns rules off for every account. The optional variable OPENTODO_AUTOMATIONS=off (or on) sets it and makes the switch read-only; another value stops the server at startup. A demo instance never runs rules.

Some tasks come back: pay the rent, water the plants, the weekly one-to-one. Make them repeat once and OpenTodo moves them forward each time you complete them. Add a reminder and you'll get a nudge when it matters.

Open the task, click its date and choose Repeat: pick Every day, Every weekday, Every week on Thursday, Every month on day 22 or Every year, named from the task's date. Custom… takes any rule, such as every 3 months, and shows the next three dates so you can check it does what you meant. Set a rule in the task panel under Repeat, or type it straight into quick add: Water plants every Monday creates the task with the rule and its first date. See Repeat and remind for the phrases in each language. Repeating tasks show a ↻ symbol on the row. To stop repeating, select the × next to the rule.

every day, every weekday, every 2 weeks, every 3 months, every mon, wed, fri, every 15th, every last friday, every 2nd tuesday and every year all work. Add after completion to count from the day you finish, and until 2026-12-31 or for 10 times to end the series. Rules are in English. See Repeat rules for the full list and the recurring task rules reference for every detail.
Complete, skip or split off one occurrence

Completing a repeating task records that occurrence and moves the task to its next date. Skip (Shift+S) moves on without recording a completion; This occurrence only (Shift+O) splits the current occurrence off as a normal task while the series moves on. See Repeat rules.

Turn on Track as a habit under Repeat (for rules like every day, not after completion). The row shows a flame chip with your streak; the task panel shows your best streak and a month grid of done, skipped and missed days, counted on your device. Skip keeps the chain without adding to it; a scheduled day that passes undone breaks it. A daily habit due Monday and completed Wednesday misses Tuesday and Wednesday. Save the query habit as a view to list your habits. See Habits.

Open a task and select + Add reminder under Reminders: at the due time, a set time before or after it, relative to the deadline, or at a fixed date and time. A task can have several reminders, and relative ones move with the due date. See Task reminders.

While OpenTodo is open, a reminder pops up in the corner of the screen with snooze and dismiss buttons, without a connection and without any permission. To get reminders when the app is closed, turn on notifications for each device in Settings → Notifications. See Task reminders.
Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project, your reminders are yours alone: other members don't see them and don't get them. You can add reminders even if you can only view the project.

For bills, use a day-of-month rule (every 1st) plus a 1 day before reminder. A reminder on a task without a time fires at 09:00 for "at due time". Give the task a time if you need it earlier. Deleted tasks don't remind you. If you restore one, its reminders come back.
A repeat rule is typed into the Repeat field of a task, as described in Recurring tasks and reminders. This page lists the rules and explains what happens to each occurrence.

Rule Repeats every day, every 3 days daily, or every few days every weekday Monday to Friday every week, every 2 weeks weekly or fortnightly every monday, every mon, wed, fri on those weekdays every month, every 15th monthly, on the same day or a fixed day every last day, every last friday at the end of the month every 2nd tuesday the second Tuesday of each month every year once a year on the same date Two extras work with any of these: After completion: every 2 weeks after completion counts from the day you actually finish, not from the due date. Good for things like "change the water filter". An end: add until 2026-12-31 or for 10 times to stop the series. Rules are stored in English, whichever language you typed them in. Every detail is in the recurring task rules reference.
Complete, skip or split off one occurrence

When you complete a repeating task, that occurrence is recorded in Completed, and the task moves to its next date. If it was overdue, it jumps to the next date from today, so missed occurrences don't pile up. The buttons under the rule handle the exceptions: Skip (Shift+S) moves to the next date without recording a completion. Use it when this week's run is cancelled. This occurrence only (Shift+O) splits the current occurrence off as a normal task you can change freely, while the series moves on. Use it when this week's meeting is on Thursday instead. Changing the title, notes, project, priority, labels or time of a repeating task changes the whole series. Reminders on a repeating task carry over to each occurrence; see Task reminders.

A reminder gives you a nudge at a moment you choose. Reminders are personal, even in shared projects (see Recurring tasks and reminders), and the reminders reference has the details on snooze, web push and privacy.

Open a task and select + Add reminder under Reminders. Choose one of: At due time, 10 minutes before, 30 minutes before, 1 hour before or 1 day before, Custom offset…, for any number of minutes, hours or days before or after, once the task has a deadline: On the deadline, 1 day before the deadline or Custom before the deadline…. These count from 09:00 on the deadline day and follow the deadline, not the due date, At a specific date and time…, for a fixed moment that doesn't depend on the due date. Its date and time fields work like the ones under Due: type the date and time in your format or pick them from the calendar and the list of times (see Dates and times). Reminders are listed with their day, date and time in your format, for example Tue 3 Nov, 09:00. A task can have several reminders. Reminders relative to the due time move with it: change the due date and they follow, and on a repeating task they carry over to the next occurrence. If the task has a date but no time, "before" and "after" count from 09:00 that day.

While OpenTodo is open, a reminder pops up in the corner of the screen with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss. This works without a connection and without any permission. To get reminders when the app is closed, turn on notifications for each device in Settings → Notifications. On an iPhone this needs the installed app. See Notifications. Snoozing or dismissing on one device applies to all of them.

For bills, use a day-of-month rule (every 1st) plus a 1 day before reminder. A reminder on a task without a time fires at 09:00 for "at due time". Give the task a time if you need it earlier. Deleted tasks don't remind you. If you restore one, its reminders come back. Alarms you add in a calendar app connected over CalDAV become reminders here, and your reminders appear there as alarms.

A to-do list tells you what to do. A calendar tells you when. Time blocking puts the two together: give tasks an estimate, drop them on the Day or Week calendar, and you can see at a glance whether your day is realistic.
Estimate how long a task takes

Select a task and press e, then type 20, 45m, 1h or 1h30 and press Enter. In the task panel, Estimate also has buttons for 15 minutes up to 2 hours. In quick add, write +30m or +1h30. The estimate shows on the task row, like 45m or 1h 30m.

Choose Calendar in the sidebar, then Day, Week, Month or Plan in its header, or press g d, g w, g m or g Shift+C. Timed tasks are blocks as tall as their estimate; dated tasks without a time wait in the Unscheduled lane. The sidebar opens the calendar the way you last left it on this device. See Day, Week and Month.
Month shows six weeks at a glance, each day with its open tasks and planned total. Drag a task onto another day to move it. See See the month.
Plan a project on a timeline
For work that spans weeks, switch the project to Timeline. Each task is a bar from its start to its deadline, so overlaps and gaps show; drag bars to reschedule. See Sections and boards.
Plan counts meetings and repeating tasks too. See Plan the next two weeks.
Place a task on the calendar

Drag a task from the Unscheduled lane onto a time slot, or select it in any list and press s to place it with the keyboard. Drag the bottom edge of a block to change how long it takes. See Place tasks on the calendar.
Each day's header adds up the estimates of its open tasks against your day length, for example 4h 15m / 8h, and is marked when you've planned more than the day holds. See See whether the day fits.

When the server owner has turned on calendar feeds, events from your Google, Outlook or Apple calendars appear in Day and Week beside your tasks: read-only, marked when they overlap a task, and never counted in the day's total. See Other calendars in Day and Week.

On a phone the Week is a list: each day with its unscheduled tasks and its timed tasks in order, so nothing is squeezed into seven columns. Tap a task to select it, tap again (or press Enter) to open it. In Settings → General → Calendar you can set when the grid starts and ends (6:00 to 22:00 by default; you can still scroll beyond) and how long your working day is (8 hours by default). These settings belong to each device, so your phone and laptop can differ.

Estimate generously at first. After a week you'll know how long "quick" things really take. Leave gaps. A day planned to the minute falls apart at the first phone call. Quick wins, under the Filter action in a list's header, shows tasks of 15 minutes or less, good for filling a short gap. Dates and times you set on the calendar are ordinary due dates, so they show up in Today and Upcoming as well, and in calendar apps connected over CalDAV, estimate included.
The calendar shows your dated tasks by day, week, month or as a two-week plan. Dragging and keyboard moves are in Place tasks on the calendar; estimates and the grid settings are in Time blocking.

Choose Calendar in the sidebar, then Day, Week, Month or Plan in its header, or press g d, g w, g m or g Shift+C. The sidebar opens the calendar the way you last left it on this device. Tasks with a date and a time appear as blocks at that time, filled in their project's colour. The block is as tall as the estimate. A timed task without an estimate gets a 30-minute block with a dashed edge. Tasks with a date but no time wait in the Unscheduled lane at the top of their day. Past days are dimmed. A red line marks the current time, in today's column. +N shows a day's other all-day events. Use ‹ and › (or [ and ]) to go back and forward, and Today (or t) to come back. Week starts on your first day of the week; the hours and block times follow your time format (9 AM or 09:00). Both are set in Settings → General → Date and time and follow you to all your devices.

Month shows six weeks at a glance, starting on your first day of the week, with today marked and the days of other months dimmed. Each day lists its open tasks: the timed ones first by time, then the rest by priority. A crowded day shows the first few and +N more, which expands the day in place. When a day's tasks have estimates, the day shows the planned total against your day length, in red when it is over. Drag a task onto another day to move it. It keeps its time. Select a task with j and k, or by clicking it. The arrows then move it a day (← →) or a week (↑ ↓), into the next month if needed. Enter opens it, and Esc clears the selection. With no task selected, the arrows move between days. q adds a task due on the day you're on. [ and ] go to the previous and next month, and t comes back to today. Switching between Day, Week, Month and Plan keeps the date you're looking at. On a phone, each day shows how many tasks it has, and the tasks of the day you tap are listed under the month. Tasks in a project where you're a viewer are shown but can't be moved.

Plan shows the next 14 days as columns, seven to a row. Each day lists its tasks with their time, estimate and priority, under a bar of planned time against your day length. The bar counts task estimates, busy meetings from other calendars, and the coming occurrences of repeating tasks, which are dimmed and move with the task itself. Drag a task onto another day, or select it and press the arrows: a day (← →) or a week (↑ ↓). q adds a task on the focused day, c completes the selected one. Choose 7, 14 or 21 days in the page's menu; this device remembers it. On a phone the days are listed vertically.
Once tasks have estimates, the Day and Week calendar is where you decide when to do them. Opening the calendar and the Month view are covered in Day, Week and Month.
Place a task on the calendar

Drag a task from the Unscheduled lane onto a time slot. Its due date and time become that slot. The grid works in 15-minute steps. To plan from your lists, open the side list with Plan from a list and drag tasks from there onto the calendar. To change how long something takes, drag the bottom edge of its block. Dropping a block back on the Unscheduled lane keeps the date and removes the time.

Every move works without a mouse. In Today, a project or any list, select a task and press s. The Day view opens with the task ready to place. Move it with the arrow keys: ↑ / ↓ by 15 minutes, ← / → by a day. Press Enter to place it, or Esc to cancel. On the calendar itself, j / k select tasks, the arrows move the selected one, Shift+↑ / Shift+↓ shorten or lengthen it, and u takes it off the grid while keeping its date.

Each day's header adds up the estimates of its open tasks and compares them with your day length, for example 4h 15m / 8h. When you've planned more than the day holds, the header is marked as over capacity. That's your cue to move something. Tasks that overlap in time are shown side by side, with a marker, so nothing hides behind something else. Completing a task removes its block and lowers the day's total. Your day length and the hours the grid shows are set per device in Settings → General → Calendar; see Adjust the grid.

Calendar feeds work in both directions: Other calendars in OpenTodo. Subscribe to the iCal address of a Google, Outlook, Apple, Fastmail or Nextcloud calendar, and its events appear next to your tasks in Day and Week. You see your real free time while you plan. Your tasks in your calendar app. Create a private feed address, then subscribe to it from Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar. Your dated tasks show up there as events. Both directions are read-only. Events from other calendars can't be moved or edited in OpenTodo, and calendar apps can't change your tasks. For two-way sync with apps that support it, use CalDAV. Calendar feeds are off until the server owner turns them on under Settings → Integrations → Calendar feeds. The server fetches the calendar addresses itself; private network addresses follow the owner's webhooks setting.

Copy the calendar's iCal or webcal:// address from its app, then open Settings → Integrations → Calendar feeds, choose Add calendar and paste it, with a name and a colour if you like. The server fetches the calendar straight away and then on its own schedule, and its events appear in Day and Week beside your tasks. Other calendars in Day and Week has the steps for each calendar app, what the events look like, how refreshing works, and the limits.

In Settings → Integrations → Calendar feeds, under Your tasks as a calendar, choose Create feed URL. The address is shown only once, so copy it right away. Then subscribe to it: Google Calendar: Other calendars → + → From URL. Outlook: Add calendar → Subscribe from web. Apple Calendar: File → New Calendar Subscription. The feed holds your open tasks due from 30 days ago to a year ahead, including tasks in projects shared with you. Tasks in archived projects are left out. Repeating tasks repeat in the calendar app too. A task with a time and an estimate becomes an event of that length. A task with a time but no estimate becomes a 30-minute event, and a date-only task becomes an all-day event. Completed tasks drop out. Calendar apps refresh subscriptions on their own schedule, which can be every few minutes or once a day.

Anyone who has the address can read the tasks in it, so treat it like a password. Rotate creates a new address. The old one stops working at once, so calendar apps need the new address. Revoke turns the feed off. The panel shows when the address was created and when a calendar app last fetched it.

With end-to-end encryption on, the server can't read your task titles. In the task feed they appear as "Encrypted item". Dates and times are still correct. Events from your other calendars are stored unencrypted on the server, like any other data the server fetches for you.
The public demo refuses calendar feeds, both subscriptions and the task feed, because they make the server fetch arbitrary addresses. See Demo instance.

With calendar feeds turned on by the server owner, you can subscribe to up to ten of your other calendars. Their events are read-only in OpenTodo and count toward a day's planned total only in the Plan; they're there so you can see your real free time while you plan.

Copy the calendar's iCal address from its app: Google Calendar: Settings → the calendar → Integrate calendar → Secret address in iCal format. Outlook: Settings → Calendar → Shared calendars → Publish a calendar → the ICS link. Apple iCloud: Calendar → the calendar's share button → Public Calendar, then copy the webcal:// link. Fastmail and Nextcloud: the calendar's Share or Export menu offers an iCal or .ics address. In OpenTodo open Settings → Integrations → Calendar feeds and choose Add calendar. Paste the address, and optionally give the calendar a name and a colour. webcal:// addresses work too. The server fetches the calendar straight away and then on its own schedule: as often as the calendar asks (between every 30 minutes and once a day), and every hour by default. Refresh now in a calendar's menu fetches it at once. Each calendar's row shows when it was last refreshed. When fetches fail, the row shows the error and the time of the last successful refresh. A calendar that keeps failing is retried less and less often, up to every six hours. Disable stops fetching it and hides its events. Delete removes it and its events from every device.
What you see in Day and Week

Timed events are drawn as blocks in the calendar's colour, next to your task blocks. When a task and an event overlap, both get the overlap marker. All-day and multi-day events appear as chips above each day's unscheduled lane. Events marked as free in their calendar are drawn as an outline only, so the slot still reads as free. Events never count toward the day's planned total here; only the Plan counts busy ones, overlaps once. Events can't be dragged, resized or completed. Tab onto an event and press Enter, or click it, to see its time, location and calendar. The Calendars button in the calendar's toolbar hides or shows events on this device only. Your choice is kept when you reload. Events are cached on each device, so Day and Week still show them offline, as of the last refresh. The toolbar then says Calendars as of and the time. Weeks your device has not loaded yet show no events while you're offline.

Up to 10 calendars per person. A calendar may be up to 2 MB. Events from 30 days ago to a year ahead are kept, up to 5,000 per calendar. Repeating events are expanded on the server. A repeat rule OpenTodo doesn't understand shows its first occurrence only, and the calendar's row gets a warning. A calendar whose events repeat so much that expanding them would take more than a few seconds keeps the occurrences found so far, with a warning that some events are left out. Refresh now, adding a calendar and changing its address count toward 12 fetches per person per hour. Calendars on a private network (your NAS, a home server) are refused unless the server owner allows private network targets for webhooks. The same switch applies to both.

Share a project with people who have an account on the same OpenTodo server: your partner for the house move, a workspace team. Everyone sees the same tasks, edits sync within seconds, and each task has a comment thread.

Open the project and select Share at the top (or press Shift+S). Type the person's email address. Pick a role and select Share. The project appears on their devices the next time they sync, with all its tasks. Shared projects show a people icon in the sidebar. Email works only for people with an account on your server; anyone else gets an invite link (next section).

An invite link adds one person to the project, with or without an account. In Share, select Create a link…, pick a role, optionally an email and an expiry, then copy it and send it yourself. It is shown once and works once; the dialog lists and revokes waiting links. See Invite people.

A link creates a new account only when its creator is the owner or an admin of the server, open sign-up is on, or the server owner switched on Invite new people (Settings → People → Project invite links). See Who can bring new people.

A public link shows a project's open tasks to anyone with it, no account needed, view-only or with ticking, also full screen on a display; a Public badge marks the project. See Public links, or task pages for one task.

Viewers see the project and comment, editors also change tasks and the project's note, admins also manage the project and its members, and the one owner can also delete or hand it over. Change roles next to a name in Share; Remove takes someone out. See Roles and assignments.
Sign-up is closed by default. An invite link is the quickest way in; the owner or an admin of the server can also create a server invitation under Settings → People → Members. See Invite people.
Leave or hand over a project
Leave next to your name in Share takes the project off your devices; everyone else keeps it. The owner hands it over with Make owner first. See Roles and assignments.
In a shared project, a task is assigned to one member under Assignee or with Shift+A; Assigned to me (g a) lists everything assigned to you. See Roles and assignments.
Every task has a comment thread under Comments, with @mentions, replies and simple formatting; everyone who can see the task can comment, offline too. See Comments and activity.
Updates (g h) lists the latest changes in all your shared projects; Activity inside a project shows its changes only. See Comments and activity.

Labels and reminders stay personal. Only you see the labels and reminders you add to a shared task. Moving a task out of a shared project to your own project or Inbox makes a copy there and removes the original for everyone. Only the owner deletes a shared project. It disappears for every member; its open tasks go to the owner's Inbox. End-to-end encryption and sharing don't mix. Shared projects are never encrypted, and an account with encryption on can't share new projects.

Sharing by email reaches only people with an account on your server. Everyone else gets an invite link from the Share dialog or a server invitation from Settings; Sharing and comments has the overview.

An invite link adds one person to the project, whether or not they have an account yet. Open Share and select Create a link… under Invite with a link. Pick the role they get. Owners can also invite admins; admins can invite viewers and editors. Optionally enter their email: then only an account with that address can use the link. Choose how long it stays valid (1 hour to 30 days, 7 days by default) and select Create link. Select Copy link and send it yourself. If your server sends email and you entered an address, Send by email (on by default) mails it for you; the dialog says where it went and still shows the link once. The link is shown only once and works once. The dialog lists the links still waiting, with their role, email, expiry and creator; Revoke stops one from working. Creating and revoking links need a connection. When the person opens the link they see who invited them, the project and the role: Already have an account? They select Sign in to join, sign in (with single sign-on too), and select Join project. Someone already signed in just selects Join project. New to the server? They select Create an account, choose a name and password, and land in the project. This option appears only when the link is allowed to create accounts (see below). Otherwise the page tells them to get an account on the server first, then come back and sign in. A link stops working when it expires, is revoked or has been used, when the project is deleted, or when the person who created it

New accounts are created through a project link only when one of these is true: the link was created by the owner or an admin of the server; open sign-up is on for the server; the server owner switched on Invite new people in Settings → People → Project invite links. It is off by default. When none applies, the Share dialog says so under the new link, which then works only for people who already have an account. The switch is checked when a link is used, so changing it also affects links already sent.

Sign-up on an OpenTodo server is closed by default. The quickest way to bring someone into one project is an invite link. To invite someone to the server without a project, as its owner or an admin, go to Settings → People → Members, optionally enter their email, choose how long the link stays valid, and select Create invitation. Copy the link and send it yourself, or, if the server sends email and you entered their address, leave Send by email on. The link works once. If you're not an admin of the server and your invite link can't create accounts, ask whoever runs it to invite the person, or to switch on Invite new people. Once they've joined, you can share projects with them yourself.

Every member of a shared project has a role that says what they can do, and every task in it can be assigned to one of them. Both are set in the Share dialog and the task panel; Sharing and comments has the overview.

Role Can viewer see the project and its tasks, and comment editor also add, edit, complete and delete tasks, assign them, and edit the project's note admin also rename, recolor and archive the project, and manage members owner everything, including deleting the project and handing it over Every project has exactly one owner. To change someone's role, open Share and pick a new one next to their name. Remove takes them out of the project.
