If you're used to Vim, turn on Settings → General → Keyboard → Vim keybindings. It's off by default and applies to that device only. With it on, a small indicator shows the mode (Normal, Insert or Command), and you get: counts like 3j, gg and G for the first and last task, dd to delete, x to complete, o to add a task below and i to edit, J / K to move the selected task, a command line on : with :today, :project <name>, :new <title>, :sync and :help. All the usual shortcuts keep working. With Vim keybindings on, the ? list includes a Vim section.

A passkey makes signing in quicker and safer, and two-factor authentication adds a second lock to your password. All of it lives in Settings and involves nobody outside your server. These settings need a connection to your server; offline they're read-only.

A passkey lets you sign in with your fingerprint, face or device PIN instead of typing a password. It can't be phished or reused on another site, and your password keeps working as a fallback. Open Settings → Account and find the Passkeys card. Select Add passkey and give it a name you'll recognise, like "Work laptop". Confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN when your device asks. Next time, choose Sign in with a passkey on the sign-in screen, or pick it from the suggestions in the email field. Add a passkey on a second device too, so losing one isn't a problem. You can rename or delete passkeys in the same list. One marked as suspicious looks like a copied passkey; delete it if you don't recognise the device. No Passkeys card? Passkeys need a secure https:// address on your server; ask whoever runs it.

With two-factor authentication, signing in takes your password plus a six-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone. Set it up under Settings → Account → Two-factor authentication and save the recovery codes it shows once. Signing in with a passkey skips the code. The steps are in Two-factor authentication.
When you enter a code, tick Remember this device for 30 days and that browser won't ask again for a month. See Remember this browser.
Each recovery code works once, in place of a code from the app, if you lose your phone. See Recovery codes.

Open Settings → Account, select Change password in the Password card, enter your current password and a new one of at least 10 characters. Changing it signs you out everywhere else; the device you're on stays signed in and API tokens keep working. Forgot it? If your server sends email, choose Forgot password? on the sign-in screen and enter your address: a reset link valid for 24 hours arrives by email, and the screen answers the same whether or not the address has an account. Otherwise ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link; an owner who can't receive mail: see recovering owner access.

Settings → Account → Recent activity lists sign-ins and token changes on your account from the last 90 days. If you see one you don't recognise, change your password, choose Sign out everywhere and tell your server's owner.

Some changes, like creating an API token or turning off two-factor authentication, ask for your password or a code again unless you entered one in the last ten minutes, so someone who finds your unlocked laptop can't change them.
Settings → Account → Session → Sign out ends your session on that device and removes your tasks from it. Changes that haven't been sent yet are uploaded first when you're online.

End-to-end encryption encrypts your task titles, notes and comments on your devices, so even your server only stores scrambled text. If your server uses a company or family login (single sign-on), you can link it under Settings → Account → Linked accounts and sign in with it.
Two-factor authentication is the second lock on your account, next to passkeys and your password. It needs a connection to your server; offline it's shown read-only.

With two-factor authentication, signing in takes your password plus a six-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone. Any app that supports time-based codes works; your server makes and checks the codes itself, without contacting anyone. Open Settings → Account → Two-factor authentication and select Set up two-factor authentication. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or type in the key shown under it. Enter the six-digit code the app shows. Save the recovery codes that appear. They're shown only once: download them as a text file or write them down and keep them somewhere safe. From then on, sign-in asks for a code after your password. Signing in with a passkey skips the code, because the passkey already checks it's you.

When you enter a code, you can tick Remember this device for 30 days so that browser doesn't ask again for a month. The list of remembered browsers is under Two-factor authentication, where you can forget them.

Each recovery code works once, in place of a code from the app. Use one if you lose your phone. Settings shows how many you have left and lets you generate a new set, which replaces the old one. If you lose both your phone and your recovery codes, the owner of your server can reset your two-factor authentication. Your server's owner can also make two-factor authentication required. If so, you'll be asked to set it up when you sign in, and you can't turn it off. Turning two-factor authentication off asks for your password or a code again, unless you entered one in the last ten minutes (Confirm it's you).

Your tasks are yours. You can download all of them at any time, and bring tasks in from other places. Nothing is locked in. The export includes your automation rules (rules), and importing your own export restores them with their ids.

Open Settings → Data and select Download export (JSON) in the Export row. You get one file with all your projects, sections, tasks and subtasks, labels, reminders, saved views, saved locations, time entries and which workspace each belongs to, including completed tasks and items in the Trash. Shared projects you're a member of are included too. The file is plain JSON, so you can open it in any text editor, keep it as a backup, or load it into another OpenTodo server. The JSON file lists your attachments but doesn't contain the files. To take the files with you, select Download export with files (ZIP) instead: you get the same JSON file plus every attached file, in one ZIP. Importing the JSON file alone brings back links and the names of files, but not the files themselves. The person who runs your server can also set up automatic backups of the whole server. A Markdown vault is not an export: it keeps your projects as files in two-way sync, but leaves out comments, attachments and time entries. Use the JSON file to keep everything.

Open Settings → Data, select Import data (or press g then Shift+I) and choose a file: an OpenTodo export, a CSV file with a title column, or a JSON export from another task app. Nothing is written straight away. You check the format OpenTodo detected, choose the options, read a preview that says what will happen to each row, and then import. The tasks reach all your devices on their next sync. Import step by step walks through the preview and the options; the import formats reference has each format and how fields are mapped.

A template is a project you want to start again and again, saved as a small file in the export format. Save as template… in a project's menu writes one. + next to Projects in the sidebar, then From a template…, starts a fresh project from it, with the dates counted from a start day you choose. The downloads on open-todo.app/templates are template files too. Project templates has the details and the difference from Import.
Importing the same file twice won't double your tasks: rows OpenTodo imported before, and tasks that look like ones you already have, are skipped unless you choose Import them anyway. See Duplicates.
Every import appears under Past imports. Undo removes everything that import created and leaves the rest alone. See Undo an import.

Import needs a connection to your server. Files can be up to 20 MB and 50,000 rows, unless your server allows more. Comments aren't imported (the export lists each comment's reactions); the members a task's notes mention come back with the task. Time entries come back from your own export; entries another member tracked on a shared task are left out, with a note in the preview. Workspaces come back by name, and one you don't have is created for you; their members and groups aren't imported. The full list covers attachments, CSV dates and JSON files that aren't recognised.
An import never writes anything until you've seen what it will do, and it can be undone afterwards. The overview is in Import and export.

Open Settings → Data, select Import data (or press g then Shift+I) and choose a file. OpenTodo accepts: an OpenTodo export, for moving to another server or restoring (the ZIP export brings its attached files too), a CSV file, from a spreadsheet or a script, with a title column and optional columns for project, due date, priority, labels and more, JSON exports from other task apps, in the common shapes those apps use. Nothing is written straight away. OpenTodo first shows a preview: Check the format it detected. You can change it if it guessed wrong. Choose the options: which project gets tasks that have none, the time zone for dates, whether sections stay sections or become labels, and what to do with possible duplicates and with rows that have errors. Read the preview table. Each row says what will happen: created, updated, skipped (with the reason) or an error (with the reason). Problems are listed first. Import. The import runs on the server, and the tasks reach all your devices on their next sync. Recurring rules, reminders, subtasks, sections and completed tasks come across where the file has them. Anything OpenTodo can't store is listed as a warning on its row, never dropped silently.

Importing the same file twice won't double your tasks. OpenTodo recognises rows it imported before, and flags tasks that look like ones you already have (same title, project and due date). Those are skipped unless you choose Import them anyway. For an OpenTodo export, items that already exist on the server are kept as they are, unless you choose to overwrite changed fields.

Every import appears under Past imports, with a summary. Undo removes everything that import created and leaves the rest alone. Tasks you added later to an imported project move to your Inbox rather than disappearing. You can then import the same file again, for example with different options.

Import needs a connection to your server. Files can be up to 20 MB and 50,000 rows, unless your server allows more. Comments aren't imported. The preview tells you how many there were. Attachments in a file from another app come across as links when they're web addresses. Anything else, like a file on someone's computer, is listed as a warning. Attached files count towards your attachments total, like files you add yourself. A file over the limit is skipped and listed under the import's errors. In a CSV file, write dates as 2026-10-15 and put a time like 09:30 in a due_time column. The import reference lists every column, with an example file. If a JSON export from another app isn't recognised, convert it to CSV. Every field OpenTodo stores can be written as a CSV column. A template file is better started with From a template… than imported; see Project templates. The import formats reference has the details: each format, how fields are mapped, recurring rules and reminders.
A template is a project you want to start again and again: a trip checklist, a client onboarding, a weekly review. It's a small file in the same format as an export.

Open a project's menu and choose Save as template…. You get a file with the project, its sub-projects, sections, open tasks and the labels they use, with the dates as they are. Completed tasks, assignees, comments and reminders are left out. On an encrypted account the dialog warns you that the file isn't encrypted.
Start a project from the library

Select + next to Projects in the sidebar, then From a template… (or New project from a template in the command palette). The dialog opens on the template library that comes with OpenTodo: trip planning, moving house, a weekly review and more, grouped by category, in your language where a translation exists. It works offline. Type to search titles, summaries, labels and tasks; ↓ moves to the templates and Enter opens one. You see its description, how to use it, how to make it yours, and a preview of every section and task with when it falls ("day 3", "week 2"). Nothing is created yet. Choose a Start on day (today unless you change it) and an optional parent project, and select Create. Esc goes back to the library, and again closes the dialog.
Start a project from a file

In the same dialog, Upload a file… takes a template file you saved or downloaded. You see what it holds and choose the start day and parent the same way. Dates move together so the template's first day lands on your start day; times stay the same. You can start the same template as often as you like: each time is a new project.
The downloads on open-todo.app/templates are template files. Open them with Upload a file… to get fresh copies counted from your start day.

The library lives in the templates/ folder of the OpenTodo repository: one folder per template, written by hand in a short YAML format, with optional translations. Propose a new one with a pull request; the format and the bar for the library are on GitHub. Templates are shared under CC BY 4.0.

From a template and Import do different things with the same file: Import creates it once, with the ids and dates in the file (importing it again skips everything as existing), while From a template makes a fresh copy on your device, also offline. When you import a template file, the preview points you to From a template. The import itself is described in Import step by step.
Deleting something in OpenTodo doesn't make it vanish. It goes to the Trash first, and every change to a task is kept in its history, so a slip of the finger is easy to undo.

Open Trash in the sidebar (or press g x). It lists deleted tasks and projects, newest first, with when they were deleted and how many days they have left. Select Restore next to an item. It comes back exactly where it was: A restored project returns to its place in the sidebar, with all its tasks. A restored task returns to its project. If that project is still in the Trash, the task goes to your Inbox instead. With the keyboard: j / k to select, r to restore.

Delete permanently removes one item for good, and Empty Trash removes everything in it. Both ask you to confirm, and both need a connection. Once something is permanently deleted, it's gone from every device and from the server, and it can't come back. Items are also deleted for good automatically after 30 days in the Trash. Your server's owner can change that period or turn it off.

Deleting a task also deletes its subtasks. Deleting a project hides it and its tasks everywhere. Its sub-projects move up a level, so they aren't lost. Reminders on deleted tasks stay quiet. Restore the task and they work again. Deleted items are still in your export until they are deleted for good.
See what changed on a task

Open a task and select the History tab below its details: every change, grouped into versions, newest first, with who made it, from where and when. Projects have a History too, in the ⋯ menu of the project's header. See Task history.
Next to each change in the history is Restore this value, and Restore this version puts back everything a version changed. See Task history.

After you change several tasks at once, a notice with Undo stays for ten seconds; Ctrl/⌘+Z undoes too. Tasks moved to the Trash in bulk come back with it, and so do the originals of a move into a shared project (the copies go to the Trash). Undo works offline. See Change several tasks at once.
The Activity tab of a task shows who created it, completed it, moved it or changed the date, newest first, also offline. See Task history.

Archiving is different from deleting: an archived project disappears from the sidebar, but it isn't in the Trash and isn't deleted after 30 days. OpenTodo offers to archive a project when you complete its last task, and archives projects without open tasks for 30 days. See Archived projects.

Open the Projects page (All next to Projects in the sidebar, or Show archived projects in Settings → Data) and select Restore next to the project under Archived projects. See Bring back an archived project.
Every change to a task is kept, so you can see what happened and put any value back.
See what changed on a task

Open a task and select the History tab below its details. Changes are grouped into versions, newest first: everything one person changed from one device within a few minutes is one version, with a one-line summary such as "Renamed and rescheduled", who made it, where (this device, another device, the API, a calendar app, a public link, or an AI assistant) and when. Select a version to see each change: the old value struck through and the new one next to it, shown the way the task shows them (dates in your date format, priorities, labels, project and section names). A change marked not applied arrived after a newer one and never took effect; you can still restore it. Changes made by an AI assistant read "AI assistant (token name)" for your own assistants and "AI assistant" for someone else's in a shared project, and can be restored like any other change. Ticks made through a public link read "Public link (link name)" for the project's owner and admins and "Public link" for everyone else; they are written as the link's creator, but the version names the link, not them. Projects have a History too: open it from the ⋯ menu in the project's header; it opens beside the list. History is loaded from your server, so it needs a connection. Offline, the tab says so instead of showing anything out of date.

Next to each change in a version is Restore this value. Select it to set the field back to that value. To put back everything a version changed at once, select Restore this version; a confirmation lists the fields first. Restoring is a change like any other: it syncs to all devices and shows up in the history itself as a new version, so you can always undo the undo. Each field is restored as its own change, so if someone edits the same field on another device at the same time, the later edit wins for that field.

The Activity tab of a task shows who created it, completed it, moved it or changed the date, newest first. Quick changes by one person within ten minutes are grouped into one line, such as "You changed the due date and priority"; select it to see each change. Comments appear as one short line that opens the comment. Activity works offline; your changes that are not synced yet are marked pending. In shared projects this includes everyone's changes. See Sharing and comments.

Archiving is different from deleting. An archived project disappears from the sidebar, but it isn't in the Trash and isn't deleted after 30 days: it and its tasks are kept as they are. Archive a project from its Project menu. When you complete the last task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it. The weekly review walks every project, with an Archive key. Projects without open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice that has an undo button. To switch automatic archiving off on a device, untick the option under Settings → Data. A pinned project leaves Favourites while it is archived and comes back with it.

Open the Projects page (All next to Projects in the sidebar, or g then Shift+P) and select the Archived tab; it shows how many there are. Show archived projects in Settings → Data opens it straight there. You see every archived project, sorted by name, with its parent project and how many open tasks it has. Select Restore next to one, and it's back in the sidebar with all its tasks. With the keyboard, Tab to the button and press Enter. Restoring works offline, like any change, and the project comes back on your other devices after they sync. Restoring brings back that one project. If you archived a project with sub-projects, they stay in the list until you restore each of them. A project you restore by hand isn't archived automatically again on that device. In a shared project, only the owner or an admin can restore it, the same people who can archive it. Deleted projects are a different matter: they go to the Trash.

Open Settings from the menu of your name at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then s. On a wide screen the sections are listed in the left column with the first, Account, open beside it; on a phone the list comes first and each section is its own page with a ← Settings link back. The list starts with your profile card (initials, name, email, role) and Search settings, then the sections, each with an icon and a line saying what's inside, grouped under You, App, Data and, for the people who run the server, Server. Search settings finds a setting by name or by what it does; matches are listed under their section and Enter opens the first with that row focused. The command palette (Ctrl/⌘+K) searches the same index: "passkey" lists Account › Passkeys. Every section has its own address, such as /settings/integrations, to bookmark or share. Older links still work. In a section, the main setting is a card; thin lines divide the rest. Each leads with a heading and one sentence saying what it is for, then its settings as rows: label and description on the left, the control on the right (below the label on a narrow screen), and a badge with the current state. Forms with several fields open from a button; actions that remove something ask you to confirm first and say what will be lost. Some settings follow your account to every device; others belong to the device you're on, marked "this device", so your phone and laptop can differ. Each section page has a Help button in its header t
Your account and how the app looks for you: Settings: You.
Account: your profile, Sign out here, password, two-factor authentication, passkeys, linked accounts, end-to-end encryption and recent activity.
Appearance: Mode (System, Light or Dark), one of eight colour themes, Density and which More destinations the sidebar shows, all following your account.
How the app behaves: Settings: App.
General: the language, start view, date and time, calendar grid and keyboard. Date and time Date and time: the date format, time format and first day of the week, on all your devices.
Notifications: push notifications for reminders on this device, and a test that shows whether they arrive. The weekly digest emails last week's numbers on your review day.
Capture: quick add parsing and its languages, voice capture, the bookmarklet and extension, and email to task.
About: version, docs, feedback and support.
Connections to other tools, and your data: Settings: Data.
Integrations: calendar apps (CalDAV), calendar feeds, webhooks, API tokens, the in-app assistant and AI assistants over MCP.
Data: export and import, attachments, the sync status of this device, and archiving and restoring projects.
Owner and admins only; Server and the access policies inside People are for the owner alone. Every row: Settings: Server.
People: users and their roles, invitations, the two-factor policy, single sign-on and project invite links.
Server: backups and restore, attachment limits and the audit log. Running the server: Running with Docker.
The You group of Settings holds your account and how the app looks for you.

Profile: your initials, name, email and role. Session: Sign out here removes your tasks from this device; changes not yet sent are uploaded first, and the app asks you to confirm. Sign out everywhere signs out every device and revokes your API tokens and app passwords. Password: Change password opens the form. See Account security. Two-factor authentication: a code from your phone on top of your password. The badge shows whether it's on, and the card warns when only a few recovery codes remain. See Two-factor authentication. Passkeys: sign in with your fingerprint, face or device PIN. See Account security. Linked accounts: connect a single sign-on login, if your server offers one. Linking also lets you confirm sensitive changes with that login; while single sign-on is off, the links are kept. If the owner turned it on, your picture at the provider becomes your profile picture when you sign in or link; a picture you upload yourself is never replaced, and one you remove is not fetched again. See Single sign-on. End-to-end encryption: encrypt your task text on your devices, and keep its recovery key. See End-to-end encryption. Recent activity: sign-ins and token changes from the last 90 days.

How you work chooses how much the app shows Open Loops, its method for everything on your mind: Lists only, Companion (screens name the move they serve) or Open Loops first (the Loop home and a sidebar by the Places). It syncs to your devices and never changes a task; see Set up in ten minutes.

These choices follow your account to every device, also when you change them offline: Mode: System follows your device's light or dark setting (the default), Light and Dark keep the app that way whatever the device says. Theme: the colour of buttons, links, the focus ring and selected items: Emerald (the default), Blue, Indigo, Violet, Rose, Orange, Teal or Graphite. Each tile previews its theme; with the keyboard, the arrow keys move between them. On a phone the tiles are one row of swatches you can scroll sideways. Density: Comfortable (the default) or Compact, which makes task rows, group headers and the sidebar tighter. On a touch screen every target stays full size in both. Haptic feedback: on a phone or tablet that can vibrate, a short tick when you complete a task or pick one up with a long press. On by default; turning it off on one device turns it off on all of them. Computers without vibration do not show the switch. Sidebar: one switch per destination of the sidebar's More group (Anytime, Someday, Assigned to me, Completed, Updates, Trash, Filter). A destination you switch on moves up next to Inbox, Today, Upcoming and Calendar. Under Open Loops first the sidebar follows the Places, so these switches wait, kept, until you choose Lists only or Companion. Mode and theme apply at once, without a reload. They never change other people's app. Priority colours (P1 to P4), warnings and errors, and the colours of your projects, labels and views keep their meaning in every
The App group of Settings is about how the app behaves. Settings marked "this device" belong to the device you're on; the others follow your account.

Language: the language of the app on all your devices. See The app in your language. Start view: the view this device opens on, including Display: Today and Display: Upcoming for a tablet or a wall panel; a project or saved view display is pinned from the display's own menu. See Views and Display mode. Date and time: how dates and times look and where weeks start, on all your devices (see below). Calendar: when the Day and Week grid starts and ends, and how long your working day is. See Time blocking. Keyboard: Show shortcut hints prints the keys in the app itself (next to quick add, beside the sidebar's destinations, in prompts) as well as in tooltips and menus, and Vim keybindings turns the Vim layer on; both for this device. See Keyboard shortcuts. Focus: the timer of the Focus screen, its lengths and breaks, the break reminder and the sound, on all your devices.

Four choices that follow your account to every device, also when you change them offline: Date format: System (the way this browser writes dates), Day-month (14 Oct, 14/10/2026), Month-day (Oct 14, 10/14/2026) or ISO (2026-10-14). Each option shows today's date in that format. Month and weekday names are written in the interface language. Time format: System, 12-hour (3:00 PM) or 24-hour (15:00). Week starts on: System, Monday, Sunday or Saturday. It decides where the Week view and the calendar of a date field start, and which days this week and last week cover in filters. My day starts at: Midnight (the default) or a time up to 06:00. If you work past midnight, set it to when your day really ends: until then the app still treats it as the previous day. See When a day ends. The Preview shows which day is today, a due date, a date, a due time, a comment time and this week as they will appear. A change applies at once everywhere in the app, without a reload. With a numeric date order on Automatic, quick add reads dates like 3/11 in your date format too.

Push notifications for reminders on this device, and a test that shows whether they arrive. See Notifications and Push notifications. Weekly digest: an email on the day you choose with last week's numbers; it needs outgoing email from the server owner. See the weekly digest.

Quick add: turn natural-language parsing on or off, and pick the languages it understands. Dates like 12/11 follow your date format. See Quick add syntax. Voice capture: dictate tasks into quick add. Off until you turn it on, and the app explains first what your browser does with the audio. See Quick add syntax. Bookmarklet and extension: the Add to OpenTodo bookmarklet, to save the page you're reading as a task. See Capturing pages. Email to task: your own secret address; an email sent there becomes an Inbox task, with the subject as its title, the text as its description and the attachment names listed, up to an hourly limit. Anyone who knows the address can add tasks, so keep it private: New address replaces it, and the old one stops working at once. See Email to task.
The Data group of Settings connects OpenTodo to other tools and manages your data.

These cards connect OpenTodo to other tools. Some appear only when the person running your server has switched the feature on. Calendar apps (CalDAV): see your tasks in calendar and reminder apps such as Apple Reminders, Thunderbird or Nextcloud Tasks, with an app password. Each project is a list, and the Inbox is its own list. On a plain http:// address app passwords would travel unencrypted, so use HTTPS outside your home network. See Calendar apps. Calendar feeds: show your Google, Outlook or Apple calendars in Day and Week, and get a private address that lets calendar apps show your tasks. The server owner turns it on here. See Calendar feeds. Issues: open GitHub or GitLab issues assigned to you become tasks that complete when the issue closes. The server owner turns it on here. See Issue import. Webhooks: send a message to another service, such as Home Assistant or n8n, when tasks and projects change; each request is signed with the webhook's secret. The owner's Allow private network targets lets receivers on your LAN or the server itself be reached, for everyone; leave it off on a public server. See Webhooks. API tokens: keys for scripts and the ot command-line client. A token is shown once, when you create it. Read-only tokens can't change anything; tokens for an AI assistant that can make changes work only through the assistant tools and never on the rest of the API. See HTTP API and Command-line client. Assistant: the in-app assistant, when the server owner has turne

Download export (JSON) saves everything you can see in one file, the Trash included, as a personal copy or to move to another server; and Download export with files (ZIP) adds your attached files. Import data brings in tasks from a file. See Import and export. Attachments shows how much of your total your files use and how large one file may be (see Attachments). The sync status of this device is shown too. Projects: archive projects automatically after 30 days without open tasks. Show archived projects opens the Projects page at its archived projects, where Restore brings one back. See Archived projects.

OpenTodo speaks English, Deutsch, Français, Español, Italiano and Português. Pick one in Settings → General → Language; each is listed in its own language, so you can find yours whatever the app shows now. System uses the first language of your browser that the app has, and English otherwise. The option names the language it picked, for example System (Deutsch). Your choice belongs to your account: every device you sign in on switches to it after the next sync, also when you changed it offline. The app switches at once, without a reload.

Every menu, button, message and notice of the app. Dates and times: month and weekday names, and on System the order of day and month and the clock, follow the language. Your browser's region is kept when it is the same language, so Swiss German stays Swiss German. Your own date and time formats still win. Quick add and voice try the language you picked first, then your browser's languages, unless you chose their languages yourself in Capture. See Quick add syntax. Reminder notifications on your phone or computer, including Snooze 10 min and Dismiss. See Notifications. Messages from the server, such as a wrong password, are shown in your language.

Your tasks, projects, labels and comments are never translated. Filter queries and repeat rules keep their English keywords (due <= tomorrow, every weekday), so a saved view works in every language. The guide in Help and this documentation are in English; Help says so in your language. The browser extension follows your browser's language. See Capturing pages.

A language is loaded the first time you pick it and then kept on the device, so switching later works offline. If it cannot be loaded (for example on a new device without a connection), the app stays in its current language, the setting says so, and your choice applies as soon as it can.
The Server group of Settings is for the people who run the server. Only the owner and admins see it; Server and the access policies inside People are for the owner only.

Users: everyone with an account, their role and last sign-in. Make someone an admin (owner only; admins manage members), deactivate or reactivate an account, reset a password, or delete an account. When the server sends email, a reset offers Send reset email (the link goes straight to the person; you never see it) beside Create reset link (you deliver the link yourself). Members: invite people with a single-use link. With outgoing email, Send by email mails it to the address you enter. See Invite people. Two-factor policy (owner only): optional, required for the owner, or required for everyone. An account that must use it and has not set it up can still sign in, but can only set it up until it does; API tokens are never affected. See Two-factor authentication. Single sign-on (owner only): sign-in through an OpenID Connect provider you already run, such as Authentik, Keycloak or Authelia; the server contacts only the issuer you enter. See Single sign-on. Project invite links (owner only): Invite new people (off by default) lets links that members create in a project's Share dialog also create accounts; links from you or an admin always can. It applies to links already handed out too, since links are checked when used. See Who can bring new people.

Backups: scheduled backups of the whole server (every account, task and the sync log) to a folder, S3 or WebDAV, the last run and its result, and the next one. Restore from a backup puts the whole server back to an archive from the destination or one you upload: you see a verified preview first, type RESTORE to confirm, and the server restarts into the restored data. Undo last restore puts the previous database back, and old safety copies can be deleted to free space. See Backups. Attachments: turn attachments on or off, and set the size per file (25 MB unless changed, up to 2048 MB) and the total per account (1 GB unless changed; 0 means no total). See Attachments. Outgoing email: the SMTP server this server sends mail through, for password resets, sign-up confirmations and invitations; nothing is sent until it is configured. The card shows whether it's configured, the server and From address, and the last test. Configure opens the form, where fields set by OPENTODO_SMTP_* variables are read-only. Send test email sends a message to you and shows the mail server's answer when it fails. See Outgoing email. Speech to text: the speech service for dictation, see Speech to text. Branding: name and logo, see Branding. Audit log: sign-ins, tokens, invitations, exports and setting changes, and who made them; task content is never recorded. Recording client addresses is off by default, turning it off erases every stored address, and behind a reverse proxy the address comes from X-Forw

Most problems have a quick fix. Start with the section that matches what you see; each links to the full steps. If nothing helps, whoever runs your server can look at its logs, or you can open an issue on GitHub.
A task seems to be missing
Look for a duration filter chip in the list's header, then in Completed, the Trash, archived projects and folded parents. Where to look, in order.
Changes don't show up on my other device
Offline · 3 pending at the top right means the changes are still waiting on that device; click the status to sync right away. What Sync error, Signed out and Locked mean.
Check the email address and that Caps Lock is off. OpenTodo doesn't send reset emails: ask the owner or an admin of your server. Forgotten passwords, two-factor phones and the owner account.
The demo says my sandbox expired
Sandboxes are deleted after two hours without activity. Select Start a new sandbox. How long a sandbox lasts.
Push notifications must be on for each device in Settings → Notifications. What to check, and iPhones.
I can't install the app or add a passkey
Both need your server to be on a secure https:// address. What to ask whoever runs your server.
Select the × on the wrong chip, or put the words in double quotes: Read "Next Friday". More ways to stop it.
I can't edit a shared project
Your role in that project is viewer, which is read-only. Who can change it.
I can't share a project with someone
You can only add people who have an account on your server. Invitations and encrypted accounts.
The app looks out of date
The app updates itself when your server is updated. What to do if something still looks old.
If a part of the app fails to display, you see a message with a Reload button. Why reloading is safe.
Yes. Each device keeps a full copy of your tasks, and changes are sent when you're back online. See Offline and sync.
On your devices and on the OpenTodo server you use. Nothing goes to anyone else: the app has no tracking and no analytics, and it only talks to your own server.
Is there an app in the app stores?
No. OpenTodo is a web app that you install from your server's address, and it then behaves like any other app. See Installing the app.
Can I use OpenTodo on my own, without a server?
OpenTodo needs a server to sign in and sync, but it can be small: a single container on a Raspberry Pi or a cheap virtual server is enough. To try it first, use the demo. See Running with Docker.
Can I move my tasks from another task app?
Usually, yes. OpenTodo imports CSV files and the JSON exports of other task apps. See Import and export.
Can several people use one server?
Yes. The owner invites people, each person has their own account and private tasks, and projects can be shared between them. See Sharing and comments.
Nothing. OpenTodo is free software under the AGPL-3.0 licence. There's no subscription and no paid tier.

These are the problems that involve your server: a task that isn't where you expect it, changes that stay on one device, an account you can't get into, and shared projects. The shorter list is in Troubleshooting and FAQ.
A task seems to be missing

Check these places, in this order: A duration filter. If Quick wins, Under 30 min, Over 1 h or Unestimated is on, a chip with that name sits in the list's header and the list shows only matching tasks. Clear it with the chip's × or from the Filter action. Completed. It may have been ticked off by accident. Open Completed and reopen it. Trash. It may have been deleted, or its project was. See Trash and history. An archived project. Tasks of archived projects don't appear in Today or Upcoming. A folded parent or section. Select the small arrow to unfold it. A shared project you left or were removed from. Ask its owner. The New view page with search: word (add & completed to include finished tasks) searches titles and notes.
Changes don't show up on my other device

Look at the status at the top right of both devices. Offline · 3 pending means the changes are still waiting on that device; they're sent as soon as it's online. Click the status to sync right away. Sync error: hover over it to see the reason. If the server is down or being updated, it clears up once the server is back. Signed out: your session ended. Sign in again; waiting changes are sent afterwards. Locked: your account uses encryption. Enter your passphrase on that device. See Offline and sync for what each status means.

Check the email address and that Caps Lock is off. Passwords are at least 10 characters. After several failed attempts, the server makes you wait a little before trying again. Forgot your password? OpenTodo doesn't send reset emails. Ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link. If you are the owner, see recovering owner access. Lost your two-factor phone? Use one of your recovery codes instead of the code. Without them, the server owner can reset your two-factor authentication.
The demo says my sandbox expired
Demo sandboxes are deleted after two hours without activity, after 24 hours at most, and every night. Select Start a new sandbox to get a fresh one. Nothing from the old sandbox is kept.
I can't edit a shared project
Your role in that project is viewer, which is read-only. Ask the owner or an admin to make you an editor. See Sharing and comments.
I can't share a project with someone
You can only add people who have an account on your server. Ask an admin of the server to invite them first. Accounts with end-to-end encryption turned on can't share new projects.
These are the problems that live on one device: notifications, installing, passkeys, quick add and the app itself. The shorter list is in Troubleshooting and FAQ.

Inside the app, reminders pop up while it's open. To get them when the app is closed, push notifications must be turned on for each device in Settings → Notifications, and on an iPhone only the installed app can receive them. Notifications lists the messages you might see and what to do.
I can't install the app or add a passkey

Both need your server to be on a secure https:// address. If the browser offers no install option, or Settings has no Security section for passkeys, ask whoever runs your server. Instructions per device are in Installing the app.

If a word was read as a date, project or priority by mistake, select the × on its chip before you press Enter, or press Backspace twice at the end of the line. Text in double quotes is never interpreted: Read "Next Friday". You can also switch parsing off in Settings → Capture → Quick add. See Quick add syntax.
The app looks out of date

The app updates itself when your server is updated. An open tab shows A new version of OpenTodo is ready with a Reload to update button; a screen whose code changed in the update reloads on its own. If something still looks old, close it completely (all tabs or the installed window) and open it again. If a tab says A newer version of OpenTodo is open in another tab, reload it: the other tab updated the data stored on this device, and the older tab can no longer save changes.

If a part of the app fails to display, you see a message with a Reload button in its place; the sidebar and other screens keep working. Your tasks are stored on the device and aren't lost by reloading. If a change can't be made (for example moving a task under one of its own subtasks), a message at the bottom of the screen says why.

Type one line in the quick-add box (press q in any task view) and OpenTodo picks out the due date and time, project, labels, priority and estimate: Meeting with Sarah next Wed at 3pm #work @call p1 +30m creates Meeting with Sarah, due next Wednesday at 15:00, in project Work, with the label call, priority 1, estimated at 30 minutes. Everything runs in your browser. The parser needs no network, sends nothing anywhere, and gives the same result on every device for the same line, date, languages and projects. The created task stores the resolved date, so other devices never parse the line again.

As you type, each thing OpenTodo recognises shows up as a chip under the input and is tinted in the line itself (underlined in high contrast), and the title preview (→ Meeting with Sarah) shows what will be saved. Nothing is hidden: if there is no chip, the text stays in the title. The same line works in the list, the phone's add sheet and the command bar's Add mode, and gives the same task everywhere. The command bar lists what it understood as one row per field, with the token that sets each one; the phone's sheet shows plain chips, and buttons under them (date, priority, label, estimate, project) start a token for you. To… Do this Keep a word literally ("may" is not May 1st) Click the × on its chip, or press Backspace at the end of the line: the first press highlights the last chip, the second dismisses it. The text itself is not changed. Never parse some text Put it in double quotes: Watch "Next Friday" tomorrow → title Watch Next Friday, due tomorrow. The quotes are removed from the title. Turn parsing off on this device Settings → Capture → Quick add → Parse natural language in quick add. Quick add then saves the line exactly as typed. A dismissed chip stays dismissed while you keep typing; it comes back only if you edit that word. Backspace only highlights a chip when that chip's text ends the line; otherwise Backspace deletes text as usual.

In the command bar's Add mode (q on screens without a quick add, or + in the box), what quick add understood is a row per field: When, Project, Label, Priority and Estimate, plus Deadline, Repeats, Reminder and Time spent when you type them. Each row shows its value, or how to set it (#, @, p1, +30m). Click a row, or move to it with ↓ and press Tab: a set field's words are selected so you can type over them, and an empty field gets its token at the end of the line. The × on a row keeps its words as text. Enter adds the task and keeps the box open for the next one; Shift+Enter adds it and opens it. On a phone, the add sheet shows plain chips for what it understood, and buttons under them (date, priority, label, estimate, project) that start a token for you.

Token Meaning Examples #name Project, including sub-projects. Case-insensitive; spaces, - and _ are ignored. An exact name wins, otherwise a unique prefix; #Home/Docs picks Docs under Home. If nothing matches, or a prefix fits several projects, the token stays in the title and a grey chip says so. #work, #trav (Travel), #sideproject (Side Project), #Home/Docs @name Label, matched ignoring case. A name with no label yet creates one when you press Enter; its chip says New label until then. Use as many as you like. @call, @waiting-for p1–p4 Priority, 1 highest, 4 default. p1, P3 +duration Estimate in minutes, from 1 minute to 7 days (10080 minutes). Shown on the task row. +30, +30m, +45min, +2h, +1h30, +1.5h spent/estimate Time already spent and an estimate (see Time spent). 30m/2h, 1h/1h30, 45min/2h The same works when you edit a title in the task panel: type tomorrow p1 after the title and press Enter, and the date and priority are set with the title left as it was; only what you typed in this edit is read, and Undo takes it back. Type # or @ and a list of your projects or labels opens under the field, narrowed as you type; arrows move, Enter or Tab picks, Esc closes it. When nothing has that name, the last entry creates it. Without the +, 45min and 2h also work, except that 2h is left alone when French, Spanish or Portuguese is active, because those languages write times as 15h.

Draft the offer 30m/2h creates the task with a two-hour estimate and one closed time entry of 30 minutes ending now, in the same step; the preview shows a Spent 30 min chip beside the estimate, and the row reads 30m / 2h. Both parts need a unit (h, m, min), so Pay rent 30/12 stays a date, and Réunion 15h with French active is still a meeting at 15:00. +30m remains an estimate only. Units are not translated: the token works the same in all six languages. Backspace on the chip keeps the text in the title, like every token.

Vocabulary is bundled for English, German, French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese. The active languages are the interface language when you picked one, then your browser's preferred languages that are bundled, plus English, which is always on; all of them are matched at the same time. With the interface language on System the order is your browser's, as before. Settings → Capture → Quick add can override the list on this device. Quick add still takes the view's context for anything the line does not set: today in Today, tomorrow in Upcoming, the current project in a project view, the current label in a label view. Anything the line does set wins, so Plan trip next Monday #travel typed in Today goes to Travel on Monday. Labels add up instead: @call typed in the errand label view gives the task both labels, so it stays in the view you added it from. A task added in Someday is parked, unless the line sets a date (Read Proust tomorrow is due tomorrow instead).

Quick add can also be dictated. Voice capture is off by default and is switched on per device in Settings → Capture → Voice capture; it is not synced, so turning it on for your phone leaves your laptop as it is. Browsers without speech recognition (Firefox, for example) show the switch disabled with an explanation, and quick add has no microphone button there. Who recognises speech. By default your browser does, and some browsers send the audio to their vendor. If the server owner connected a speech service, Recognition offers This server's speech service too. Each phrase is then recorded in the browser and sent once through your server to that service, which returns the text. Neither keeps the audio or the text. The statement you confirm names the service's host. With voice capture on, press the microphone button in quick add or Shift+V anywhere outside a text field (plain v already toggles list and board in a project). Words appear in the box as they are recognised; when you stop talking, press the button again or press Esc, the final transcript is inserted at the caret and parsed exactly like typed text, chips included. Nothing is saved until you press Enter, so you can correct the line by hand first. Spoken forms of the tokens are turned into their typed forms first, in the active quick-add languages (English is always on): Said Becomes "renew insurance hashtag home priority two" renew insurance #home p2 "standup at nine thirty am" standup at 9:30am "call the dentist tomo

Before voice capture can be switched on, Settings shows this statement and waits for you to confirm: Speech is recognised by your browser, not by OpenTodo. Depending on the browser, your audio may be sent to the browser vendor's speech service (for example Google for Chrome, Apple for Safari) and handled under their privacy policy. OpenTodo asks the browser to recognise speech on this device when it offers that choice. Your OpenTodo server never receives audio or transcripts. Only the task you save with Enter is stored and synced, like a typed one. The microphone is used only while you dictate; the browser asks for permission the first time. OpenTodo's code never records, stores or sends audio: the Web Speech API hands it text. On-device recognition is requested whenever the browser reports it available for the language (Chromium's processLocally); OpenTodo never asks the browser to download a speech model. The browser asks for microphone permission on your first dictation, not when you switch the setting on.

A rule and reminders can be typed in the same line. Each gets its own chip and is removed from the title. An unknown #name stays in the title unless you pick Create project from the list. The server and the REST API do not parse lines; the ot CLI does with ot add --natural. Some ideas are listed under future ideas.

Estimates are stored in the additive task field estimate_minutes (integer 1–10080 or null; see api.md and sync.md). @name tokens are stored as label ids in the task's labels list, never as names; a new label is written as its own operation before the task, so both sync together and work offline.

The New view page (g then f, New view in the views list or the sidebar's More) lists the tasks that match a one-line query such as: @work & due <= tomorrow & p1 Queries run entirely on your device, over the data the app already holds: they work offline, make no network request, and the results update live as you edit tasks or as changes from your other devices arrive.

query := or or := and ( "|" and )* and := not ( "&" not )* not := "!" not | "(" or ")" | term term := "@" name label | "##" name | "#" name project with / without sub-projects | "p1" | "p2" | "p3" | "p4" priority | ("due" | "created" | "deadline" | "start" | "completed") cmp date | keyword | "search:" text | "origin:" text where the task came from | "workspace:" name the task's workspace | "tracked" ("<" | "<=" | "=" | ">=" | ">") duration tracked time | field ("<" | "<=" | "=" | ">=" | ">") value custom field | "no" field custom field without a value field := a word that is not a reserved word | '"' chars '"' value := number | "true" | "false" | date | word | '"' chars '"' cmp := "<" | "<=" | "=" | ">=" | ">" | "before" | "after" date := "today" | "tomorrow" | "yesterday" | weekday | YYYY-MM-DD | INT "days" | INT "days ago" | period period := ("this" | "last" | "next") ("week" | "month") | INT ("week" | "weeks" | "month" | "months") "ago" weekday := "monday" | "tuesday" | "wednesday" | "thursday" | "friday" | "saturday" | "sunday" keyword := "overdue" | "today" | "tomorrow" | "no date" | "no project" | "no labels" | "no time" | "no deadline" | "no start" | "completed" | "open" | "subtask" | "someday" | "deferred" | "evening" | "blocked" | "unblocked" | "habit" | "origin" | "no origin" | "tracked" duration := INT ("m" | "min" | "mins" | "minutes")? | NUM "h" (INT ("m" | "min")?)? name := word | '"' chars '"' text := word | '"' chars '"'

! (not) binds tightest, then & (and), then | (or). @errand | @call & p1 means @errand | (@call & p1). Use parentheses to group: (@errand | @call) & p1. & and | are the only connectives. There is no implicit "and": @work p1 is an error, write @work & p1. Whitespace between tokens is ignored, so due<=tomorrow and due <= tomorrow are the same.

A bare name (@errand, #Work) runs until whitespace, a double quote, or one of the operator characters & | ! ( ) < > =. Any other character, including #, -, /, . and non-Latin letters, is part of the name. Put names with spaces or operator characters in double quotes: #"Client A", @"follow up". Inside quotes, \" is a literal quote and \\ a literal backslash. Keywords, comparison words, weekday names, label names and project names all ignore case: #work, #Work and #WORK are the same.

Term Matches @name tasks carrying the label with that name #name tasks in the project with that name ##name tasks in that project or in any of its sub-projects, at any depth p1 … p4 tasks with that priority (p1 is the highest, p4 the default) due <cmp> <date> tasks whose due date compares as asked; a task without a due date never matches created <cmp> <date> tasks whose creation day, in your time zone, compares as asked deadline <cmp> <date> tasks whose deadline compares as asked; a task without a deadline never matches. deadline <= 3 days includes deadlines that have passed start <cmp> <date> tasks whose start date compares as asked; parked tasks and tasks without a start never match completed <cmp> <date> completed tasks whose completion day, in your time zone, compares as asked; open tasks never match. completed = last week is what you finished last week overdue due before today: the tasks of Today's Earlier group today due today tomorrow due tomorrow no date no due date no time a due date without a time of day no deadline tasks without a deadline no start tasks with no start date and not parked someday parked tasks deferred tasks whose start date is after today evening tasks marked for This Evening blocked tasks waiting for another task that is still open (Blocked by) unblocked tasks not waiting for any open task habit recurring tasks tracked as a habit; save habit as a view to list every habit with its streak no project Inbox tasks (no project) no labels tasks with no la

A custom field is named like a project or label, ignoring case, in every project you see that defines a field of that name; quote names with spaces: "Order date" <= friday. The words the grammar already uses (due, created, deadline, start, completed, no, origin, tracked, the keywords and p1 to p4) keep their meaning, so a field named "due" is reached only through its quoted name, "due" <= tomorrow. How a field compares depends on its type: Type Terms Number cost > 100, cost <= 99.5, cost = 0 Date "Order date" <= friday, "Order date" = this week: the date grammar above Text, link, choice client = "Acme" only, ignoring case; client > "A" is an error Checkbox paid = true, paid = false (an unset box is unchecked) no client lists the tasks of projects that define Client and have no value for it. A value is only compared while its task is in a project that defines the field. A name that no project defines is not an error: the view warns No field named "budget" and the term matches nothing.

A query matches open tasks only, unless completed or open appears somewhere in it, or it compares the completion date (completed >= this week). completed on its own lists only completed tasks, p1 & completed the completed priority-1 tasks, and completed | open both. Deleted tasks never match, and neither does the record a skipped day of a habit leaves (it is neither completed nor open). Parked and deferred tasks match like any other unless you exclude them: !someday, !deferred. Like the other cross-project views, the New view page leaves out tasks of archived projects.

Dates compare calendar days in your local time zone, the same way Today and Upcoming do; the time of day is ignored. Expression Meaning (when today is Saturday 2026-10-10) today, tomorrow, yesterday 2026-10-10, 2026-10-11, 2026-10-09 monday … sunday the next such day, today included: friday is 2026-10-16, saturday is 2026-10-10 2026-12-01 that date 3 days three days from today: 2026-10-13 7 days ago seven days before today: 2026-10-03

A period stands for several days. Weeks start on the first day of the week you chose in Settings → General → Date and time (the browser's choice until you pick one), the same on all your devices; months are calendar months. Expression Days (when today is Friday 2026-10-16 and weeks start on Monday) this week, last week, next week 2026-10-12 to 10-18, 2026-10-05 to 10-11, 2026-10-19 to 10-25 2 weeks ago 2026-09-28 to 10-04 (1 week ago is last week) this month, last month, next month October, September, November 2026 3 months ago July 2026 Against a period, = means within it, < (before) before its first day, <= up to its last day, > (after) after its last day and >= from its first day. A single day works the same way, so due = this week lists everything due this week, completed >= last month everything completed since the first of last month, and due < this month everything due before the first of this month. Every date term takes periods: due, created, deadline, start and completed. A saved view keeps the period itself, so a view of completed = last week always shows the previous week. People sharing a project may start their weeks on different days; each sees their own week. before is the same as < and after the same as >. today on its own is the keyword (due today); due = today is the same comparison written out, and due <= today also includes overdue tasks. Only English weekday names are accepted.

A filter shows the workspace you are in, like every list. A query with a workspace: term anywhere looks at the tasks of every workspace instead, and the term picks the ones you want: (workspace: Home | workspace: Work) & due = this week lists both, whichever workspace you are in, and !workspace: Work & today lists today's tasks everywhere but Work. Labels and projects in such a query are matched by name in every workspace. A task belongs to its project's workspace; a task without a project belongs to the workspace it was added in. A name that matches no workspace warns No workspace named "…", like a label. A saved view that names a workspace counts every workspace's tasks in the sidebar too.

Names are looked up every time the query runs, so renaming a label or project is picked up immediately. When several labels or projects share a name (two devices can create the same name while offline), the term matches any of them. A name that matches nothing is not an error: the view shows a warning such as No label named "errands", that term matches no task, and the rest of the query still works. A saved or remembered query therefore survives a rename or deletion.

A query that does not follow the grammar shows a message under the input, and the previous results stay on screen until the query is valid again. Positions count characters from 1: Query Message @errand & Expected a term after "&" at position 9 (p1 | p2 Missing ")" at end of query @work p1 Expected "&" or "|" before "p1" at position 7 p1 & urgent Unknown term "urgent" at position 6 p5 Priority must be p1, p2, p3 or p4 at position 1 due today Expected a comparison (<, <=, =, >=, >, before or after) after "due" at position 1 due > 7 Expected "days", "weeks" or "months" after "7" at position 7 due = last year Expected "week" or "month" after "last" at position 7 completed > 2 weeks Expected "ago" after "weeks" at position 15 no & Expected "date", "project", "labels", "time", "deadline", "start", "origin" or a field name after "no" at position 1 cost > Expected a value after ">" at position 6 tracked > soon Expected a duration such as 30m or 1h30 after ">" at position 11 workspace: & p1 Expected a workspace name after "workspace:" at position 1 An empty query shows a short usage hint and no results.

You can also type a query straight into the search box (Ctrl+K): it lists the matching tasks and offers to open them as a new view. g then f opens the page with the cursor in the query input, at the bottom of the filter panel. Results update about 150 ms after you stop typing. Under the header, the toolbar repeats the query's conditions in words, with the filter and display buttons on the right. Results are grouped and ordered as a saved view would show them: by project (Inbox first, then projects in sidebar order, each heading showing the project's path, Work › Client A), then by due date and priority. Display options changes the grouping, the order, the layout, completed tasks and what rows show before you save. Enter in the input runs the query at once and moves to the first result; Esc returns to the input. In the list, the usual keys work: j / k, Enter to open, c to complete, 1–4 for priority, L for labels, Delete. ↑ / ↓ in the input step through the last 20 distinct queries you ran on this device. The history lives in the browser's local storage for the app, is never synced, and is cleared when you sign out.

In the filter panel, above the query input, the builder shows the same query as conditions you can read: Label is errand, Due on or before tomorrow, Priority is P1, No project. Conditions. + Condition opens a small dialog: choose what to filter on (label, project, priority, one of the five dates, a state such as Due earlier or Waiting on another task, text in the title or notes, origin, workspace (with more than one), tracked time or a custom field), then its value. Labels and projects are picked from a searchable list. Click a condition to change it. Groups. A group is a block headed All of these (every condition must match, &) or Any of these (one is enough, |). + Group adds one inside, up to three levels deep. Change the heading to switch between the two. Not. The Not switch in a condition's dialog, or the Not button on a group, matches the tasks it would otherwise leave out (!). Keyboard. Tab reaches every control. Inside a group, the arrow keys move between conditions, and Delete or Backspace removes the focused one. Both ways. The query input stays under the builder (Edit as text jumps to it). Every change in the builder rewrites it, with only the parentheses the grammar needs, and anything you type that parses updates the builder. What is saved is always the query text, so saved filters, ot and the API see exactly what they saw before. What it cannot show. A double !!, or groups nested deeper than three levels, stays editable as text; the builder shows a short notice i

A query you come back to can be saved as a view: it keeps the query and its display options, and syncs to all your devices like your tasks do. Save. On the New view page, press s while the results have focus (or choose Save as view). The header becomes a card: type a name and press Enter, or Esc to cancel. The view is created with the current query, grouping, order and display options, listed under Views in the sidebar and pinned to Favourites, and opened at /views/<id>. Saving works offline; other devices show the view after they sync. Edit. A view shows its conditions in the toolbar. The filter button, a condition chip or / opens the same filter panel as the New view page, with a count for the changed query before you save. Enter or Save saves a changed query for every device, Esc discards the change. A query that does not parse shows the error and is not saved. Display options. The sliders button at the right of the toolbar opens them, reachable with Tab: List or Board (one column of cards per group), Group by (project, due date, priority, label, none), Order by (due date, priority, manual order, created, title), Completed tasks (hide or show) and Show on rows (date, project, labels, estimate, assignee, deadline, start, origin); the direction is under More options. Defaults are list, group by project, order by due date ascending with undated tasks last, completed hidden, everything shown. Grouping by due date shows Earlier, Today, Tomorrow, then each later date and finally
