The OpenTodo app for Android opens your own OpenTodo server, like the installed web app, and adds what only a phone app can do: reminders on time without a push service, sharing files from other apps, home-screen widgets and fingerprint unlock. It needs Android 8.0 or later and an OpenTodo server; it talks to nothing else.

On first start the app asks for your server's address, the one you open in the browser (for example todo.example.com). It checks the address and says what is wrong when it can't connect: No connection: the first start needs the network; the screen tries again when it's back. Not an OpenTodo server: the address answers, but not like OpenTodo. Check for typos. Certificate not trusted: the phone doesn't trust the server's certificate. If your server uses its own certificate authority, install it in Android's security settings; the app trusts certificates you installed there. Address refused: the app needs https://. Plain http:// works only for addresses on your own network (such as 192.168.1.4:8080 or nas.local), after a warning. Then sign in as usual. After the first start the app also opens offline, with your local copy. To use another server, long-press the app icon and choose Change server. This removes the current server's data from the phone (the offline copy, scheduled reminders, widget data and fingerprint unlock); changes not yet synced are lost.

In Settings → Notifications, turn on Notifications through the app. The app schedules the next seven days of reminders on the phone itself and refreshes them about once an hour, so a reminder you add on your computer reaches the phone too. Details in Notifications.
The app appears in Android's share menu for links, text, photos and files, also on phones without Google Play services. See Capturing pages.

Two home-screen widgets: Today shows your tasks for today with the time of the last update, and Quick add opens the app's quick add. The widgets show what the app last saw; open the app to refresh them. While an encrypted account is locked, the Today widget shows only counts.
With end-to-end encryption, the unlock screen offers Unlock with fingerprint or face next time.

No trackers, no analytics, no advertising. The app stores the server address, the scheduled reminders, the widget data and, if you turned on fingerprint unlock, the encrypted account key, only in its private storage, excluded from Android backup.

A task can carry an estimate; time tracking records what it actually took. Each stretch of work is one time entry: when it started, when it ended (nothing while it runs) and an optional note. Entries are stored on your device first, work offline and sync like your tasks.

In any task list, select a task and press y to start tracking it; press y again to stop. With the task panel open, y acts on the open task. The row's actions menu (.) and the panel's ⋯ menu offer Start tracking or Stop tracking. Only one entry runs at a time: starting another task ends the running entry at that moment. Completing the task you are tracking stops the entry in the same step. Completed and deleted tasks offer no start, and viewers of a shared project cannot track.

While an entry runs, a pill in the sidebar's bottom row takes the place of your name: the elapsed time and the task's name, 1:05 · Write the report, with a Stop button inside it; activate the pill to open the task. With the sidebar collapsed to icons it shows the time alone and opens a menu with Open the tracked task and Stop. On a phone the bar shows the time as a pill that opens a sheet with Open and Stop. The time counts in minutes, then as hours and minutes from one hour, and turns to a caution colour after 12 hours in case you forgot to stop. Screen readers hear it once when tracking starts and once when it stops. If you stop the entry on another device, the indicator disappears here after that device syncs.

The task panel's Time tab lists the task's entries, newest first, with their day, times, duration and note, and in a shared project who tracked each one. It shows the total, Start tracking or Stop tracking, and Add time: Type a duration, 45m, 1h30 or 90 (minutes). On today it ends now; on another day it ends at 17:00. Or choose Enter a start and an end and type both times. Add a note if you like. An end before the start is refused. The ⋯ menu of each of your own entries edits its start, end and note, or deletes it. Other members' entries can be read, not changed. The start, the end and the note are separate fields, so edits made on two devices at once are both kept.

Once a task has entries, its row shows the tracked time with the estimate, 35m / 1h, or 35m tracked without one. It takes the estimate's place in the line under the title, as one item. A running entry counts up to the current minute. Rows and the Time tab show the task's total, everyone's entries included. Today's header adds 3h planned · 1h 20m tracked: the estimates of the open tasks listed, and your own entries that started today, each counted whole on the day it started even across midnight, with your day start applied.

Statistics shows the time you tracked in the period, per day and per project. The filter terms tracked and tracked > 1h list tasks by their tracked time; see Filter queries. In quick add, 30m/2h means 30 minutes already spent and a two-hour estimate.

Export time entries in Statistics downloads a CSV of the chosen period, made on your device. Its columns are date, start, end, minutes, task, project, labels (joined by ;) and note, then one column per custom field of the projects present. Times are in your time zone, a running entry has no end and counts up to the export, and the file starts with a byte-order mark so spreadsheets read it as UTF-8. The server writes the same file for ot time export and the API; see Command-line client and the HTTP API.

In a shared project every member reads every entry, and each entry names its author. Only the author edits an entry; the author, project admins and the owner can delete it. Statistics and Today count only your own entries. With end-to-end encryption the note is encrypted on your device; the times stay readable so the server can total and export them. The server's CSV and AI assistants then show [encrypted] for the note.

A task can repeat. The rule is a short English phrase stored in the task's recurrence field, for example every weekday or every 3 days after completion. The same grammar is implemented by the server (internal/recurrence) and the web app (web/src/lib/recurrence.ts), and both are tested against one shared file of test vectors (web/src/lib/recurrence.vectors.json), so every device and the REST API compute the same dates. Every example on this page is one of those vectors.

every <pattern> [after completion] [until YYYY-MM-DD | for N times] Rules are case-insensitive and extra whitespace is ignored. A rule is at most 200 characters. What gets stored is the canonical form: lowercase, single spaces, weekday names spelled out, ordinals with the correct suffix. Every 2nd Tuesday is stored as every 2nd tuesday. Pattern Examples Meaning day, N days every day, every 3 days Daily, or every N days (1–999). week, N weeks every week, every 2 weeks Every 7 × N days. weekday every weekday Monday to Friday. month, N months every month, every 6 months Same day of month; a day the month does not have becomes its last day. year, N years every year, every 2 years Same date; 29 February becomes 28 February in common years. weekday names every monday, every mon, wed, fri, every tuesday and thursday Any set of weekdays, full names or three-letter abbreviations, separated by commas or "and". day of month every 1st, every 15th, every 31st That day of each month; in shorter months the last day. last day every last day The last day of each month. last weekday every last weekday The last Monday–Friday of each month. ordinal weekday every 2nd tuesday, every first monday, every last friday 1st/first to 4th/fourth or last of that weekday in each month. every 2nd is the 2nd day of each month; every 2nd tuesday is the second Tuesday.

Add after completion to a day, week, month or year interval to count from the day the task is actually completed instead of from its due date: every 3 days after completion, every week after completion. Calendar patterns (weekdays, days of month, ordinals) cannot be completion-relative.

until YYYY-MM-DD: no occurrence after that date, e.g. every day until 2026-12-31. for N times: the series has N occurrences in total, e.g. every weekday for 10 times. Skipped occurrences do not count. Only one end condition per rule.
How the next occurrence is computed

All dates are floating calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD), like due itself; the computation never converts through a time zone, so daylight saving changes have no effect. The due time, if any, is kept. A deadline on the series moves by the same number of days as the due date: every monday due 12 October with the deadline 14 October is next due 19 October with the deadline 21 October, also when an overdue series catches up. Skipping and "this occurrence only" move it the same way. The completed occurrence and a detached copy keep the deadline they had. A start date moves the same way, so a task deferred until two days before it is due is deferred again before the next occurrence. This Evening stays on the series. Parking a repeating task in Someday clears its due date and so ends the repetition. Calendar rules: the next occurrence is the first matching date strictly after the current due date. If that date is already in the past (the task was overdue), it is instead the first matching date after today: overdue tasks catch up rather than piling up, and no missed occurrences are generated. Interval rules keep their rhythm while catching up (every 3 days due on the 1st, completed on the 10th, moves to the 13th). Completion-relative rules: the next occurrence is counted from the local date of completion. every 3 days after completion due Monday and completed on Wednesday is next due Saturday; completed on the Sunday before, it is next due Wednesday. Month ends: every month due 31 January

Complete: a completed copy of the current occurrence (the occurrence record) goes to Completed, and the task moves to its next occurrence. When the end condition is reached the task completes like any other task. Skip (Shift+K, or Skip in the detail panel): moves the task to the next occurrence without recording a completion. Completion-relative rules skip as if completed today. Skipping the last occurrence is not possible; complete or delete it. For a habit, a skip also writes that day's occurrence record marked skipped, in the same batch as the move, so the history can tell a skipped day from a missed one. A skipped record is not a completion: it is not listed in Completed, does not match completed filters and does not count towards for N times. A task that is not a habit skips exactly as before, with no record. This occurrence only (Shift+O, or the button in the detail panel): makes a standalone copy of the current occurrence, without a rule, and moves the series to its next occurrence. Edit or move the copy freely. Every other edit (title, notes, project, priority, labels, due time, rule) applies to the series, because the series is the task. Reopen an occurrence record and it becomes a standalone open task; the series is not moved back. Reopening a series that ended keeps its rule, so its next completion continues the schedule.

The calendar's Plan draws the occurrences that would follow the current one inside the days it shows, dimmed, and counts their estimates in each day's total. They are computed on each device from the rule, the due date and the completed count with the same calculation as the preview, so every device draws the same ones. They are never written: no operation, no row, nothing to sync. They can't be moved, selected or completed; move the task itself and they follow. An end condition stops them. Every other view shows the current occurrence only.

The rule is stored in task.recurrence and occurrence records point back with task.series_id (see sync.md). An occurrence record's id is derived from the series id and the occurrence date (SHA-256, formatted as a UUID), and the next due date is a pure function of the rule and dates every device shares. Two devices that complete the same occurrence offline therefore write the same record and the same next due date, and end with one Completed entry once they sync. A for N times count is the number of occurrence records, so it converges without a counter; skipped records of a habit are left out of the count on every device and on the server. A habit's skip writes the same record id a completion writes, with every field of the record in one batch under one timestamp. Two devices that skip the same day therefore end with one skipped record, and when one device completes a day while another skips it, per-field last-writer-wins keeps the later batch whole: the day reads as done or as skipped, never as a mix, and the streak is unbroken either way. A completion through the REST API, CalDAV or an assistant writes no skipped field; if it lands after a device's skip of the same day, the record keeps skipped: true with the server's completion time, and the day still reads as skipped. Skipped a day by mistake? Set the task's date back to that day and complete it: the completion writes the same record with skipped: false, so the day reads as done. The history grid itself is read-only. The RE

A recurring task with a calendar rule (any rule except after completion) can be tracked as a habit: turn on Track as a habit under the repeat rule in the detail panel. The task stays an ordinary recurring task; the flag is the boolean habit field, synced like any other. Its streaks and month history are computed on each device from the series and its occurrence records (web/src/lib/habits.ts, pinned by web/src/lib/habits.vectors.json); nothing about them is stored and the server computes nothing, so two devices with the same rows show the same numbers, offline too. A task whose rule is removed or made completion-relative keeps the flag but shows no habit statistics until it has a calendar rule again. The rules: Scheduled days are the dates the rule matches plus every date that has an occurrence record: a record proves the day was scheduled even if the rule changed since. Weekday and month rules match the date itself; interval rules (every day, every 2 weeks, every month) step back from the current due date by the interval, months clamped to the month's length (every month due on the 31st was due on 28 February). Days before the habit's first record are not part of its history. Done and skipped days have a record. A missed day is a scheduled day before the current occurrence without one. The current occurrence (the task's due date) is pending: it never breaks the streak, whatever today is. Once the day has passed the streak chip says it is at risk. The streak counts done days

A task can carry any number of reminders (OpenSpec change reminders). Open a task, then use the Reminders section of the detail panel. You can also type reminders in quick add: Dentist tomorrow at 15:00 remind me 30 min before (see Repeat and remind). Relative reminders fire a number of minutes before or after the task's due time ("30 minutes before"). A task with a date but no time counts as due at 09:00. A task whose time is fixed to a time zone fires relative to that exact instant, wherever your devices are. When the due date or time changes, on any device or through the API, the reminder moves with it; recurring tasks carry their relative reminders to the next occurrence. Without a due date a relative reminder is kept but does not fire. Deadline reminders fire a number of minutes before or after 09:00 on the task's deadline ("1 day before the deadline"), in your device's time zone. They follow the deadline when it changes, on any device or through the API, and never move with the due date. Without a deadline the reminder is kept but does not fire. A device on an older version leaves them untouched. Absolute reminders fire at a moment you pick and never move with the due date. They work on undated tasks and are shown in each device's local time.

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project your reminders are yours alone: other members never see or receive them, and you can add them with any role, viewer included. When someone else moves the task, your relative reminders follow as soon as one of your devices syncs.

In the app. While the app is open, a reminder whose time has come appears as a notification in the corner with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss (focus moves to it; Esc dismisses). This needs no network and no permission, and is skipped for completed or deleted tasks. When the tab is in the background and the browser allows notifications, a system notification is shown instead. Web push. In Settings → Notifications each device can enable push so reminders arrive while the app is closed. Enabling asks for the browser permission and registers the device with the server; disabling or signing out removes it. The server checks for due reminders every 30 seconds and sends each one once per firing time to every enabled device of the reminder's owner (reminders are personal), then records the delivery on the reminder (an op by device server) so all devices know it fired. A reminder that falls due on a completed task is not sent; the server records it as dismissed instead (also an op by device server), so it is not checked again. Reopening the task does not bring that firing back; set a new time or snooze it to be reminded again. System notifications offer Snooze 10 min and Dismiss; these work offline and are uploaded on the next sync. Their text and the due date are written in the account's interface language, which the service worker reads from the synced preferences row on the device (English when there is none). If the app is focused when a push arrives, the remind

A reminder does not fire, in the app or by push, while its task is deleted or while the task's project, or any project above it, is in the Trash. It is not marked as delivered either, so restoring the task or the project brings it back: a reminder whose time is still ahead fires on time, and one whose time passed while it was in the Trash is delivered once, late, on the next check (the same rule as for reminders that fell due while the server was down). Dismiss or snooze it if you no longer need it. Purging the task from the Trash removes its reminders.

Snoozing sets a new firing time (in 10 minutes, in an hour, or tomorrow at 09:00) and the reminder fires again, also by push. Dismissing silences the current firing. Both are ordinary synced edits: when one device dismisses and another later snoozes the same reminder, the later edit wins on every device.

For an account with end-to-end encryption the server never puts a title in a push, even for devices that opted in to titles: it cannot read it, and ciphertext would be useless. The notification uses the content-free text; in-app reminder toasts still show the decrypted title from the device.

Nothing to configure. The VAPID key pair is generated on first use at <data>/push_vapid.pem and travels with backup archives. OPENTODO_PUSH=off turns push off entirely (routes answer 404, no outbound requests); in-app reminders keep working. Push requires the app to be served over https (OPENTODO_BASE_URL), as browsers only allow push subscriptions on secure origins. See self-hosting and API.

Many tasks start as "deal with this page later". OpenTodo can receive a page from three places, and all of them open the same capture screen at /share on your own server: From How Works offline Phone or desktop share sheet Install the app, then choose OpenTodo in the share menu Yes, once the app has been opened online Any desktop browser The bookmarklet from Settings → Capture The popup opens from the app's offline cache once the app has been loaded in that browser Chromium and Firefox The browser extension in extension/ Same as the bookmarklet in Capture screen mode The capture screen proposes: Title: the page title, or the link's host name when there is no title. The title field is a regular quick-add line, so typing tomorrow #work p1 into it sets the date, project and priority. Description: the selected or shared text, followed by the link. The link is also kept as the task's origin. Project: the Inbox by default; pick any project. Files: anything shared along with the page (photos, PDFs, documents) or a screenshot from the extension, each with its name, type and size and a thumbnail for images. Remove any you don't want; they're saved as attachments of the new task. A share that carries only a file proposes the file's name as the title. Press Enter to save or Esc to cancel. Nothing is saved until you confirm. Saving creates an ordinary task on the device first and syncs it like any other quick-add task, so it works with no network and reaches your other devices when the n

A task saved from a shared link also remembers that link as its origin. The task's row shows a small chip with the link's host (example.org), and the task panel an Origin chip; both open the page in a new tab, and the page title you shared is their tooltip. On a row the chip is quiet, like the counts at the end of the row; on a board card it ends the line under the title. A link to an issue on GitHub, GitLab, Jira (*.atlassian.net) or Linear is recognised on your device, without opening it: the chip reads the issue (owner/repo#7, ENG-123) and the task is listed by origin: github, origin: gitlab, origin: jira or origin: linear in a filter. Self-hosted trackers are kept as ordinary links. The link still ends the description, so your notes read as before. To forget the origin, remove the Origin chip in the task panel; the description keeps the link. The command palette also finds a task by its issue id (eng-123) or the shared page title. Tasks from email carry an Email origin without a link, and imported tasks carry their source (origin: todoist). A message saved from Gmail or Outlook on the web with the extension's Quick save reads Gmail or Outlook, opens the message, has the subject as its tooltip, and is listed by origin: gmail or origin: outlook.

The web app manifest declares a Web Share Target (POST /share with title, text, url and files), so the app is offered for links, text, images and documents. The browser adds OpenTodo to the share menu once the app is installed: Platform Install Share Android, Chrome / Edge / Samsung Internet Menu → Install app (or Add to Home screen) Share from any app → OpenTodo Android, other browsers (Vivaldi, Brave …) or a device without Google Play services (GrapheneOS, /e/OS, LineageOS) Usually only a home-screen shortcut, which Android cannot list in the share menu See below Windows, ChromeOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Share from apps that use the system share dialog macOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Support for receiving shares varies by version; use the bookmarklet or extension iOS and iPadOS, any browser Share → Add to Home Screen Safari does not support share targets for web apps; use the bookmarklet in Safari instead Firefox (all platforms) Firefox does not install web apps as share targets Use the extension or bookmarklet

The Android app is in the share menu as soon as it is installed, also on phones without Google Play services. Links and text open the capture screen as above; photos and files (up to ten, 20 MB each, 25 MB together) are handed to it the way the browser extension hands over a screenshot, and stay on the phone until you save. A share that arrives before you have entered a server waits until you have.
OpenTodo is missing from the share menu on Android

Android lists a web app in the share menu only when it was installed as a real app (a WebAPK), not as a home-screen shortcut. Chrome creates that app through Google Play services, Samsung Internet through its own service. Other browsers such as Vivaldi or Brave, and any browser on a device without Google Play services (GrapheneOS without sandboxed Google Play, /e/OS, LineageOS), add a shortcut instead. OpenTodo then opens normally from the home screen but cannot receive shares. Nothing on your server can change this. To check: open Android Settings → Apps. If OpenTodo is listed there, it is installed as an app; if not, it is a shortcut. What works instead: Install from Chrome: remove the shortcut, open your server in Chrome and choose Install app. On GrapheneOS this needs sandboxed Google Play installed in the same profile. Email to task: share the page to your email app and send it to your secret inbox address, if the owner turned email capture on. Copy and paste: share → Copy, then paste the link into quick add. Some apps put the link inside the shared text instead of the link field. The capture screen then takes the last http(s) link from the text and moves it to the end of the description. After an update that adds or changes the share target, the browser may need the app to be opened once (or reinstalled) before the share menu entry appears. If a share reaches the server before the app has been opened since the update, the title, text and link still arrive, and the captu

Settings → Capture shows an Add to OpenTodo button generated for your server's address. Drag it to the bookmarks bar (or use Copy bookmarklet and paste the code as the address of a new bookmark). Clicking it on any page opens a small popup with the capture screen, prefilled with the page's address, title and the text you selected. The bookmarklet contains no password or token. It only opens your server's /share page in a popup, where your normal sign-in applies. Its source, with your server's address in place of https://todo.example.com: javascript:(function () { var e = encodeURIComponent var s = String(window.getSelection ? getSelection() : '').slice(0, 16384) var u = "https://todo.example.com/share" + '?url=' + e(location.href) + '&title=' + e(document.title) + (s ? '&text=' + e(s) : '') if (!window.open(u, 'opentodo-capture', 'popup,width=480,height=640')) alert('Allow pop-ups for this site to capture it to OpenTodo.') })() If nothing happens, the browser blocked the popup: allow pop-ups for the site you are on. Some sites block bookmarklets with their own security policy; the extension works there.

extension/ holds a small Manifest V3 extension for Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi) and Firefox 128 or later. The toolbar button and Alt+Shift+O (change it at chrome://extensions/shortcuts or in Firefox's Manage Extension Shortcuts) open a popup: one line with the page's title, the text you selected, a project and a label picker, the page as the task's origin (remove it with its cross), and Save. Enter saves, Esc closes without keeping anything. Right-click to start from something else with Add to OpenTodo: on a link, the link's text is the line and its address the origin; on an image, the file name is the line and the image's address starts the description (the extension never downloads the image). On a message open in Gmail or Outlook on the web, the subject is the line and From: with the sender starts the description; the message body is never read. Two modes, chosen in the extension's options: Capture screen (the default): Save opens your server's capture screen in a popup window with the line, the text and the address, where you check and save as above. The extension holds no token and sends nothing itself. Quick save: paste a full-access API token (create one per browser, so you can revoke it alone). Save then creates the task at once and shows Saved with a link to it. While you type, the line is previewed as chips (date, project, labels, priority, reminders) in your account's language; a #name that is no project shows a grey chip and stays in the

If the device is not signed in, the capture screen first shows the sign-in form with a note, then continues to the capture screen with the shared page intact. Until you save, the shared title, text and link stay in the page's memory only: they are removed from the address bar and are not written to storage or sent to the server (the server's request log records paths, never query strings). Reloading the sign-in page therefore loses the shared content; share it again.

The title is cut to 500 characters, the text to 16 KB with a [truncated] note. A link is kept only if it starts with http:// or https://; anything else (javascript:, data:, file: …) is dropped and the rest of the share is shown normally. Shared content is shown as plain text, never as HTML, and the capture screen never opens the shared link. There is no auto-save: a link to /share cannot create a task without you pressing Save. At most 10 files per share, none larger than the server's limit per file (25 MB unless the owner changed it); a larger file is listed as refused and the task is saved without it. On the public demo, files are not attached. Shared files are listed by name, type and size and never shown as web pages; an HTML file is attached as a file that downloads.

OpenTodo imports tasks, projects, sections, recurrence rules and reminders from files: its own JSON export (for moving between instances or recovering), CSV from a spreadsheet or a script, and the JSON exports of other task managers. Open Settings → Data → Import data in the web app (or press g then Shift+I), or drive the same endpoints from a script; see API below. Every import works in two steps: Preview. The server reads the file and reports, row by row, what would happen: create, update, skip (with a reason) or error (with the row number and the reason), with totals that also count new sections, recurring tasks and reminders, and file-level notes (for example comments that are not imported). Nothing is written. Import. The server runs the import as a background job. Every created or changed field becomes an ordinary operation in the op log, stamped with server time and the device id import, so every device receives the imported data on its next sync under the usual last-writer-wins rules. A whole import can be undone later. Import runs on the server, so it needs a connection: the Import screen disables the file picker while offline and keeps showing the last loaded job list.

The format is detected from the content, in this order; the preview shows what was detected and the format option overrides it. Format id Recognised by Notes opentodo a top-level "format": "opentodo-export" Exact round trip, see below things-db a SQLite database with Things 3's tables a copy of Things' main.sqlite, see Things google-tasks-json "kind": "tasks#taskLists", or items of kind tasks#taskList Google Takeout's Tasks.json, see Google Tasks trello-json top-level id, name and lists, cards, checklists arrays one Trello board, see Trello microsoft-todo-json lists with wellknownListName, or with tasks that have importance and dueDateTime or isReminderOn written by a PowerShell script, see Microsoft To Do apple-reminders-json an array whose every element has identifier and isCompleted written by a Shortcut, see Apple Reminders anydo-json categories and tasks arrays, tasks with categoryId and status Any.do's data request, see Any.do json-items top-level items and projects arrays "projects / sections / items" backups json-lists a top-level lists array lists of tasks; each list becomes a project json-generic a top-level array of objects, or a tasks array a generic task list todoist-csv a header starting with TYPE and containing CONTENT, PRIORITY, INDENT one project exported from Todoist, see Todoist todoist-backup a ZIP of todoist-csv files Todoist's backup of every project ticktick-csv a preamble starting with Date:, then a Folder Name, List Name, Title, Kind header TickTick's

The file from Settings → Data → Download export or GET /api/v1/export. Labels, projects (with their sub-project tree), sections, custom field definitions (fields, deleted ones included), tasks (with subtasks, completion, tombstones and their fields values), reminders and saved views are recreated with their original ids and field values, so importing an export into an empty account and exporting again gives an equivalent file (comments aside, see below). Because ids are kept, nothing needs remapping: a task's section_id, a recurring series and its occurrence records (series_id, whose ids are derived from the series id), a reminder's task_id, a task's blocked_by and a dashboard's panels all point at the same entities as before. Every task field is carried: recurrence (stored in canonical form, for example Every Monday becomes every monday), series_id, section_id, notes_doc (rich-text notes), due including a zoned tz, estimate_minutes, ical_extra, origin (where the task came from, unchanged) and every custom field value in fields, including values of definitions that were deleted or belong to another project. The preview counts the definitions it creates as fields. What is handled differently, and why: Comments are not imported. A comment keeps its author, and the sync engine only accepts comments whose author_id is the account writing them; the authors in an export are accounts of the exporting instance (and other members of shared projects). Comment creation is also rate-limi

A single CSV does not name its project, so its tasks go to the target project. Things 3 has no export, but its database can be copied, as Cultured Code's support article "Accessing the Things database" explains. Quit Things first. On a Mac, open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/, then the ThingsData-… folder, and copy Things Database.thingsdatabase. Upload its main.sqlite (right-click the folder and choose Show Package Contents), or a ZIP of the whole folder. On iPhone or iPad the article describes a diagnostics code that sends Things Database.aar; tap it to unpack it into the same folder. The file is read from a private copy on the server, read-only, using only Things' own tables, and deleted after the preview or import. A SQLite file that is not a Things database is refused with 400 invalid_file. UTF-8, with a header row. Comma, semicolon and tab separators are detected from the header; quote fields that contain the separator. Header names are case-insensitive and spaces or dashes count as underscores (Due Date is due_date). Only title is required. An object with projects, sections, items and optionally labels, notes and reminders arrays joined by ids. Source Becomes projects[].name, parent_id project and sub-project; the source inbox (inbox_project: true) maps to the target project projects[].description (or notes, note) the project's note, for created projects only items[].content, description title, description items[].project_id, section_id project, section sections[] sections of their project, created even when empty, in file order (with sections: section; deleted ones are skipped) items[].parent_id subtask items[].priority counted upwards in the source: 4 → 1, 3 → 2, 2 → 3, 1 → 4 items[].due.date due date (date-times with a zone are converted) items[].due.is_recurring, due.string recurrence rule from the due string (every tue 4pm → every tuesday, every! 2 weeks → every 2 weeks after completion); a string that cannot be expressed is a warning reminders[] (item_id) type: "relative" with minute_offset → reminder that many minutes before the due time; type: "absolute" with due.date → reminder at that time; location reminders and is_deleted ones are dropped (location with a warning) items[].labels label names items[].checked, completed_at, added_at completion, completion time, creation time deadline ({date}) the task's deadline notes[], duration dropped with a warning on the item Items and projects marked is_deleted are skipped.

{"lists": [{"id", "title", "tasks": [...]}]}; each list becomes a project with its title. Tasks read title, notes (description), due (RFC 3339; converted to the chosen time zone), status: "completed" and completed (completion time), parent (a task id) or nested subtasks, and starred / important (priority 1). recurrence (string, RRULE array or {pattern: {type, interval, daysOfWeek}}) becomes a rule and reminderDateTime (or the other reminder keys of json-generic) a reminder. links are dropped with a warning; tasks marked deleted are skipped.

Projects are matched by name, ignoring case, against existing non-deleted projects; otherwise created. Tasks without a project go to the target project (option) or the Inbox. Sections: see Sections. Recurrence and reminders: see Recurrence and Reminders. Subtasks are resolved after the whole file is read, so row order does not matter. A subtask joins its parent's project. A parent that is missing, invalid or would form a cycle leaves the task at the top level with a warning. Labels are matched by name, ignoring case; missing ones are created. Dates: plain dates stay dates; date-times without a zone keep their wall clock; date-times with a zone become the wall clock of that instant in the chosen time zone (default: the browser's zone in the web app, UTC through the API). Due dates are always stored floating. A deadline is a date only: a time on it is dropped with a warning, keeping the day as written. The preview counts the tasks that get a deadline. Completion: a completed row keeps its source completion time, or the import time when the source has none. Unsupported attributes (attachments that are not web addresses, comments, assignees, links, location reminders, recurrence rules the grammar cannot express) never block a row: the task is imported and the row carries a warning naming what was dropped. Custom fields: see Custom fields.

Trello custom fields, Asana's extra columns and Linear estimates become custom fields of the task's project. A field of the same name (ignoring case) and type in that project is reused; otherwise one is created, and the preview counts it under new fields. A choice field gets the values in the order they first appear. A value is dropped with a warning when the project already has a field of that name with another type, when the project already holds 30 fields, or when the task goes to the Inbox (fields belong to a project). Undo removes the fields the import created and leaves fields that were there before.

With sections: section (the default) a row's section becomes a real section of the task's project: an existing live section with the same name (ignoring case) is reused, otherwise one is created once per project, after the existing ones. A subtask's section is looked up in the project it ends up in. Tasks without a project (the Inbox, when no target project is chosen) cannot hold sections, so their section becomes a label, with a warning. sections: label turns every section into a label named like it (the behaviour before sections existed), sections: ignore drops them. Re-importing a file finds the sections it created by name (and, for json-items, by source id), so nothing is duplicated.

A recurrence becomes a rule of the recurrence grammar, stored in canonical form, when the grammar can express it. Accepted, in this order: The grammar itself: every day, every 2 weeks, every monday, friday, every 15th, every last friday, every 3 days after completion, … until 2027-01-01, … for 10 times. An iCalendar RRULE, with or without the RRULE: prefix (FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2, FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR), when it maps exactly onto a rule (as for CalDAV). Common spellings: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, annually, biweekly, fortnightly, every other day|week|month|year, weekdays, every workday, every weekend, each … and ev … for every …, and every! … for "after completion" (every! 3 days → every 3 days after completion). A trailing time of day (every tue 4pm, every day at 09:00) is removed: the due time carries it. A structured object {frequency|freq|type|unit, interval, days|daysOfWeek|byday} (also under pattern), e.g. {"frequency": "weekly", "days": ["MO", "TH"]} → every monday, thursday, and an array of RRULE strings. Anything else (hourly rules, starting …, every other monday, an interval combined with weekdays, free text) is shown in the preview as a warning on the row, recurrence "every 3 hours" not supported; imported without a rule, and the task is imported without a rule. A recurring task without a due date gets the rule's first date from today in the chosen time zone, as in the app. Imported recurring tasks are series of their own (no series_id).

Reminders are created together with their task (a task that is skipped, for example as already imported, brings none) and belong to you, like every reminder. Value Becomes a number, or a string of digits relative reminder that many minutes before the due time 30m, 1h, 2 days, 15 min before relative reminder before the due time an ISO 8601 duration (-PT15M, -P1D) relative reminder; a negative duration is before the due time a date-time (2026-10-20T08:00, with or without zone) or a date absolute reminder at that time (floating values in the chosen time zone, a date at 09:00) an object with offset_minutes (negative = before), minute_offset / minutes_before (minutes before) or offset / trigger (a duration) relative reminder an object with datetime, at, remind_at, fire_at, time, date or due.date absolute reminder type: "location" dropped with a warning A relative reminder fires at the due time plus its offset, with a date-only due counting as 09:00, in the chosen time zone. On a task without a due date it is kept but does not fire (the row says so). A reminder whose time has already passed at import time is imported dismissed, with a warning, so no stale notification is sent. Offsets beyond one year are dropped with a warning.

Tasks from Todoist, TickTick, Things, Linear, Google Tasks, Trello, Asana, Microsoft To Do, Apple Reminders and Any.do keep where they came from as their origin, written in the import's operations like every other field and shown as a chip on the row. Tasks from a generic CSV or JSON file get none, and the preview has no origin column. Duplicate detection still uses the importer's own memory (below), not the origin.

Checked in this order: Own export: an id that already exists is skip (exists) or, with existing: overwrite, update. A source row recorded by an earlier, not undone import of the same format for this account is skip (already_imported). Importing the same file twice therefore creates nothing the second time. CSV rows without an id column are recognised by their content. A row whose title (trimmed, ignoring case), project and due date match an existing open task is skip (possible_duplicate), unless the duplicates option is import, in which case it is created with a warning.

Option Values Default format a format id from the table above detected targetProject id of one of your projects Inbox timeZone IANA zone, e.g. Europe/Rome UTC (the web app sends the browser zone) sections section, label, ignore section duplicates skip, import skip errors skip_rows, abort skip_rows existing skip, overwrite (own export only) skip With skip_rows, bad rows are reported and everything else is imported; a bad row never leaves a partial task. With abort, any row in error fails the job before anything is written and names the first bad row.

One import job per account runs at a time; starting a second one answers 409 conflict naming the running job. Files may be at most OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB megabytes (default 20, allowed 1–200) and 50,000 rows; larger files answer 413 too_large. Ops are written in batches of at most 1,000 and progress is saved after each batch. If the server restarts mid-import, the job shows failed with the counts of what was written, and undo removes it. Undo tombstones every project, task, label, section, reminder and saved view the job created, through the op log: they disappear from every view and from other devices after their next sync, and stay in the export with deleted_at. Entities the job only updated are left alone. As when deleting in the app, open tasks you later added to an undone project move to the Inbox, open tasks you later put into an undone section move to "No section", and undone labels are removed from your other tasks. Undo is idempotent. After an undo the same file can be imported again. Webhooks see an import as one import.completed delivery per finished job and one import.undone per undo, not one event per task. See Webhooks → Imports. Job records (status, options, counts, row errors) are operational metadata kept in the server database; they are not part of the export.

The preview reads the whole file once. CSV is streamed record by record; a JSON file is decoded in one piece and takes roughly five times its size in memory, so the largest default file (20 MB of JSON) peaks around 100–120 MB during the preview and the start of the job, released afterwards. Typical imports of a few thousand rows stay under 10 MB. On a 1 GB Raspberry Pi keep the default or lower OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB.

All routes require a session or a bearer token, like the rest of the API. Uploads are multipart/form-data with a file part and the options either as one JSON options part or as individual fields named like the options. # Preview (nothing is written) curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/preview" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -F file=@tasks.csv -F timeZone=Europe/Rome # Start the job → 202 {"job": {"id": "…", "status": "running", …}} curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -F file=@opentodo-export.json -F 'options={"existing":"overwrite"}' # Follow it, list jobs, undo curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" curl -sS -X POST "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>/undo" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" See docs/api.md for the response shapes and error codes.

Optional, per account, off by default (OpenSpec change e2ee). When it is on, your devices encrypt the content of your tasks before it is synced, so the server, its backups and every server-side integration hold only ciphertext for it. Sync, offline use and conflict-free merging keep working because ciphertext travels through the unchanged operation log as an ordinary string value. Turn it on in Settings → Account → Encryption. Automation rules work with encryption: their conditions and actions use ids and dates. Only the comment action is unavailable.
What is encrypted, what is not

Encrypted, in your personal data (Inbox, your own projects, labels, saved views): Entity Encrypted fields task title, description, ical_extra, notes_doc (the rich-text note document, encrypted as one opaque string; its ciphertext must fit the 256 KB document limit, so an encrypted note document is capped at about 196 KB), origin (where the task came from: the whole object, serialised as JSON and encrypted into one ciphertext string, because its title, link and id name the page, mail or issue; the server accepts that string wherever it accepts the object) project name, description and notes_doc (the project's note) label name section name saved view name, query comment body (your comments on your own tasks) attachment name, mime (the file type), url (a link's address), and the file itself, as an encrypted file (see below) custom field the field's name and options, and every text, link, date and choice value on a task (fields.<id> with a string value) time entry note (the time entry's note) review tomorrow_note (the line for tomorrow you leave when you close the day) Everything else stays plaintext, because views sort and group by it, reminders and calendars schedule with it, and the server needs it to merge and authorize: due (date, time, zone), priority, completed_at, deleted_at, created_at, position, project_id, parent_id, section_id, labels (the list of label ids on a task), recurrence, estimate_minutes, assignee_id, number and checkbox values of custom fields, a custom fie

Protected against: Someone who reads the server's disk, database file, backups (local, S3, WebDAV) or database dumps: they see ciphertext for the fields above. The server operator browsing the data, and server-side integrations (CalDAV, the MCP endpoint, webhooks, the REST API with an API token): they see ciphertext or a placeholder. A server or a bug moving a ciphertext to another field or task: the value is bound to entity, entityId and field and fails authentication; the app shows "[Cannot decrypt]" and keeps the operation. Not protected against (honest limits): Metadata. Everything in the plaintext list above, plus how many tasks, projects and labels you have, when you edit what, from how many devices, and the approximate length of each text. A malicious or compromised server serving tampered JavaScript. The web app is delivered by the same server it protects you from. A server that changes the code can capture the passphrase or the key on the next load. This is inherent to web-delivered end-to-end encryption; a future change may verify release signatures in the service worker. Your devices. The device is the trust boundary: local storage (IndexedDB) holds plaintext and the account key (as a non-extractable CryptoKey). Malware, a browser extension with access to the page, or someone with your unlocked device can read everything. "Lock this device" forgets the key and pauses sync but leaves already synced data in local storage; Sign out clears local data. Weak passphrases.

Key hierarchy, all generated and used in the browser with the built-in Web Crypto API (no dependency): Account key: 256 random bits, AES-256-GCM. Kept on each unlocked device as a non-extractable key in IndexedDB. Passphrase key: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 over your passphrase (NFC-normalised) with a 16-byte random salt and 600,000 iterations, producing an AES-KW key. Recovery key: 256 random bits, shown once as 56 base32 characters in 14 groups of four (52 for the key, 4 for a checksum). HKDF-SHA-256 (fixed salt, info opentodo/e2ee/recovery-kek/v1) turns it into an AES-KW key. The account key is wrapped (AES-KW, RFC 3394) under both. The key record — {version, kdf, salt, iterations, wrappedByPassphrase, wrappedByRecovery} — is the only key material the server stores (encryption_keys table). It never receives the passphrase, the recovery key or the account key. Value format (a string in the existing op value): "enc:v1:" + base64url( nonce(12 bytes) || AES-256-GCM(utf8(plaintext)) || tag(16 bytes) ) additional authenticated data = utf8(entity + "\0" + entityId + "\0" + field) Nonces are 96 random bits per encryption. Known-answer vectors shared by the Go and browser test suites are in web/src/lib/e2ee.vectors.json. Attached files are encrypted on the device in 1 MiB chunks, so a large file is never held in memory twice: header = "OTAT1" || chunk size (4 bytes, big-endian) || file prefix (8 random bytes) chunk i = AES-256-GCM(chunk i of the file) || tag(16 bytes) nonce i = file prefix

New device: sign in, then enter the passphrase (or the recovery key) on the unlock screen. Nothing is pulled or pushed before that; the sync status reads Locked. Afterwards the device works offline and does not ask again. Wrong passphrase: an error, and after 5 failures within a minute further attempts are delayed for the rest of that minute (on this device). Lock this device (Settings): forgets the key and pauses sync until unlocked. The command-line client: ot encryption unlock unwraps the key with the passphrase (or --recovery) on your computer and keeps it in an owner-only file next to the CLI's configuration, so ot mcp --decrypt can let a local AI assistant read and write your text. The passphrase and the key never reach the server; the assistant's AI provider does receive the plaintext it reads. ot encryption lock deletes the key file, and a passphrase change elsewhere makes it stale until you unlock again. Offline unlock works once the device has seen the key record. Unlock with a fingerprint (Android app): see below. A device that did not know encryption had been enabled notices the first ciphertext it receives, checks the key record and locks itself without applying the batch. Key record missing: only you can turn encryption off on a device, never an answer from the server. When the server says it has no key record while the device encrypts (the server was restored from an older backup, another device turned encryption off, or the server misbehaves), the device stops

In the Android app, on a phone with a fingerprint or face unlock, the unlock screen offers Unlock with fingerprint or face next time. After you unlock with the passphrase, the app keeps a copy of the account key encrypted by Android's keystore under a key that opens only with your fingerprint or face; from then on the unlock screen shows Unlock with fingerprint or face, and the passphrase still works. The copy never leaves the phone. It is deleted when you sign out, change or reset the passphrase on this phone, turn encryption off, or when the account key changes; Android makes it unusable when fingerprints or faces are added or removed. Lock this device keeps it, so the next unlock can use the fingerprint.

Change passphrase (needs the current one and a fresh sign-in confirmation): re-wraps the account key; content is not re-encrypted; other devices keep working; new devices use the new passphrase. Reset with the recovery key (forgotten passphrase): sets a new passphrase and issues a new recovery key; the old one stops working. Lost both: the content cannot be recovered by anyone, including the server owner — there is no server-side reset. Settings and the unlock screen offer only to turn encryption off and delete the encrypted content: the key record is removed and every item whose content cannot be decrypted is moved to the Trash as it syncs. Plaintext fields (dates, structure) are kept.
Enabling, plaintext that appears later, purging, disabling

Enabling re-writes every content field of your personal data as ciphertext through ordinary operations, with progress in Settings; the job is resumable after a reload. 500 tasks produce roughly 1,500 operations. A link attachment cannot change its address on the server, so each personal link is replaced by a copy with the address and name encrypted, and the plaintext link moves to the Trash. Then each attached file is downloaded, encrypted and uploaded again as a new attachment that replaces the plaintext one ("Encrypting your files: 3 of 40 files"). This part needs a connection: it stops when the network goes and continues after the next sync, and files not done yet keep their old form meanwhile. Plaintext written later — through the REST API, the CLI, email-to-task or an import — is accepted by the server and shown with a small "not yet encrypted" marker; the next unlocked device that syncs it re-writes it as ciphertext ("encrypt-on-sight"). Two devices doing that at once produce two ciphertexts of the same text; one wins and nothing is re-written again. Purge plaintext history (POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history) deletes the superseded operations of the content fields in your personal data, including the plaintext from before encryption. Winners stay, so every device still converges. The deletion runs with SQLite secure_delete, then the database is vacuumed and the write-ahead log truncated. Revision history for those fields is gone afterwards. Backups made before the p

Workspace names, members and groups are server data in plaintext, like project members; with encryption on you can create workspaces and move things between them, but not add members, groups or invite links yet. The server cannot decrypt. Each feature that needs content degrades explicitly: Feature Behaviour for an encrypted account REST API reads Return the ciphertext string in content fields, plaintext elsewhere. Scripts need the key to decrypt (format above). REST API writes Accepted in plaintext; encrypted on sight by the next unlocked device. Export (GET /api/v1/export) Ciphertext content, plaintext scheduling fields, and the wrapped key record under encryption, enough to decrypt elsewhere with the passphrase. Importing it into another account keeps the ids (so the binding still matches), but that account needs the same key record to decrypt. Import Writes plaintext like REST; duplicate detection by name/title cannot match encrypted labels and projects, so an import may create duplicates. Backups Hold ciphertext and the wrapped key record (plus any plaintext not yet purged). CalDAV Refused: /dav/ answers 403 for the account and creating an app password answers 409 encryption_enabled. Calendar clients can neither read ciphertext nor write it back, and placeholders would overwrite real titles. Calendar feed URL Encrypted titles appear as "Encrypted item" in calendar apps; dates, times, estimates and recurrence are served as stored. Subscribed calendars Events fetched from
See api.md: GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/encryption/keys, POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history, encryption and minClientVersion in GET /api/v1/me and GET /api/v1/auth/status.
OpenTodo is free and open source, made by one person in the open. These are the ways to reach that person and to help the project.
Report a problem or suggest an idea

Open an issue on GitHub. Say what you did, what you expected and what happened instead, and which version you run (the Help page shows it at the top). Every report is read. Before reporting a problem, the troubleshooting guide may already have the fix. If you found a security problem, do not open a public issue: follow SECURITY.md in the repository instead.

Join the OpenTodo server on Discord to ask a question, show how you use the app or see what other people build. It is the place for conversation; a bug report is still best as an issue, so it is not lost in the chat. Nothing in the app talks to Discord: the link opens it in a new tab only when you choose to.
Star OpenTodo on GitHub. Stars are how many people discover open-source projects, so a star is a real help. Telling a friend who pays for a task app works too.
If OpenTodo saves you a subscription, a coffee helps keep it going. It is entirely optional: OpenTodo has no paid plan and every feature is free.
Settings → About has all of these in one place: the version your server runs, Help, the documentation and the website, the issue tracker, the Discord server, the source code and the coffee button.

The first time the owner opens a new server, a short note thanks them and shows these links. It appears once per account; closing it on one device closes it on all of them. People invited to the server do not see it, and neither does the public demo. The owner can open it again from Settings → About → Welcome note.

Connect a GitHub or GitLab account and the open issues assigned to you become tasks. They show up in Today, Next and your weekly review next to everything else, and they follow the issue: when it closes, the task is completed; when it reopens, the task reopens; when it is renamed, the task is renamed. Nothing is ever written back to GitHub or GitLab. The server owner turns issue import on under Settings → Integrations → Issues. Until then the panel says so and nothing is fetched.

Create a personal access token that can read issues: GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens, with Issues: Read-only on the repositories you want (or a classic token with repo for private repositories). GitLab: Preferences → Access tokens, with the read_api scope. On a self-hosted GitLab, use its own address. Give the token an expiry date; you can replace it at any time. Open Settings → Integrations → Issues and choose Connect issues. Pick the provider, keep https://github.com or https://gitlab.com or enter your own instance, and paste the token. The token is stored on your server, outside the database and its backups, and is never shown again. Choose which issues: all issues assigned to you, or only those in up to 20 repositories or projects. You can also require up to 10 labels. Choose the project the tasks go to (or the Inbox), whether issue labels become OpenTodo labels, and how often to check: every 15 minutes to once a day. The connection checks the token at once and shows the account it belongs to. Test token checks it again later.

A new open issue becomes a task with the issue's title, its text as notes and a link back to the issue. Issues that were already closed are not imported. Closing the issue completes the task on the day it closed; reopening it reopens the task; renaming it renames the task. Your own edits win until the issue changes the same thing again. Complete a task yourself and it stays completed; rename it and it keeps your title until the issue is renamed. The notes are written once. Later edits to the issue text are not copied. Nothing is ever deleted. A task you moved to the Trash stays there. An issue that is unassigned from you, or loses a label you filter on, leaves its task as it is. With label mapping on, each issue label becomes the label of the same name, created when missing. Labels you add yourself are kept. Tasks arrive on your devices with their next sync, like tasks from any other device, and work offline like every task. Pull requests and merge requests are never imported.

Each connection shows its state first: up to date and when, failed with the last error, or stopped with the reason. Then the host and account, the project, the filter and what the last run did. Use Sync now to check at once; checks and syncs are limited to 12 an hour. A connection stops, and waits for you, when the provider refuses the token, when the host turns out to be on a private network the owner has not allowed, or when no token is stored. A restored backup never contains tokens, so after a restore enter each token again with Edit → Replace token. When the host is down, the wait between checks doubles, up to six hours.

Up to five connections per account, at most 1,000 new tasks per check; a larger backlog arrives over the next checks. Hosts on your local network work only when the owner allows private network targets (Settings → Integrations → Webhooks). Accounts with end-to-end encryption cannot use issue import: the server would write issue text into the history unencrypted. Turning encryption on stops existing connections; their tasks stay. Deleting a connection removes its token. The tasks it created stay as ordinary tasks.
